The lab implements a two-proportion effect estimate, standard error, interval, z-test, and approximate sample-size calculation; compares with statsmodels; and verifies invariants using deterministic data. Production guidance covers assignment, sample-ratio mismatch, novelty, interference, sequential monitoring, data quality, privacy, guardrails, rollout, and rollback. The aim is a trustworthy decision process, not a ritual that converts every p-value below 0.05 into a launch.
learningObjectives: Define the estimand, eligible population, randomization unit, variants, outcomes, and decision threshold before observing results.
Compute and interpret treatment effects, uncertainty, p-values, power, and MDE for common independent-arm metrics.
Distinguish statistical significance, practical significance, equivalence, noninferiority, and inconclusive evidence.
Audit an online test for assignment, exposure, SRM, multiplicity, interference, and post-randomization bias.
lessons.labGoal: Implement a two-proportion A/B estimate, interval, null z-test, and approximate power calculation, then compare with statsmodels and verify invariants.
followUpQuestions: What is the difference between statistical and practical significance?
Why is 50/50 allocation common?
What does randomization guarantee?

lessons.title: MLE vs MAP
lessons.interviewAnswer: MLE maximizes p(data|theta), treating the observed data as fixed and theta as the optimization variable. MAP maximizes p(data|theta)p(theta), equivalently log likelihood plus log prior. A zero-mean Gaussian prior often yields an L2 penalty and a Laplace prior an L1 penalty, with scaling determined by noise and prior parameters. Both return point estimates; MAP is not full Bayesian inference and is not invariant to arbitrary reparameterization. Validate the model, identifiability, optimization, and predictive calibration separately.
keyPoints: Likelihood is a function of parameters, not a normalized parameter probability
Logs turn products into stable sums
MAP adds prior information and can regularize weak data
Point estimation discards posterior shape
A converged optimizer can fit a wrong or unidentified model
lessons.description: Maximum likelihood estimation chooses parameter values that make the observed data most likely under a specified statistical model. Maximum a posteriori estimation multiplies that likelihood by a prior density and chooses the posterior mode. This chapter carefully distinguishes probability of data given parameters from a probability distribution over parameters, derives log-likelihood objectives for Bernoulli and Gaussian models, connects Gaussian and Laplace priors to common regularizers, and explains why MAP remains a point estimate rather than full Bayesian inference. You will learn how identifiability, constraints, reparameterization, boundary solutions, weak data, and misspecified likelihoods affect both methods; why maximizing a density is coordinate-sensitive; and why optimization convergence does not prove statistical validity. The worked example derives smoothed Bernoulli estimates and contrasts MLE, MAP, and posterior mean. The lab implements them from first principles and verifies against an analytic Beta–Binomial result. Production guidance covers numerical stability, calibration, prior governance, reproducibility, monitoring, and rollback when data or likelihood assumptions shift.
learningObjectives: Write likelihood and log-likelihood objectives without reversing their conditioning.
Derive MLE and MAP estimates for simple models and connect priors to regularization penalties.
Distinguish MAP, posterior mean, posterior predictive inference, and full posterior uncertainty.
Diagnose identifiability, numerical, boundary, prior, and misspecification failures in estimation.
lessons.labGoal: Derive Bernoulli MLE, Beta-prior MAP, and posterior mean, then verify each analytic formula on sparse data.
followUpQuestions: Why maximize log likelihood?
When do MLE and MAP become similar?
Why is MAP not invariant to reparameterization?

lessons.title: Linear Regression
lessons.interviewAnswer: Linear regression models the conditional mean as E[Y|X=x] = beta_0 + x^T beta and estimates beta by minimizing squared residuals. With a full-rank design, the fitted residual is orthogonal to every design column; software normally solves the least-squares system with QR or singular-value decomposition rather than forming an inverse. A coefficient is the expected change in the modeled outcome for a one-unit predictor change while other included predictors are held fixed. That is an associational interpretation unless causal assumptions justify more. I check residual structure, influential points, conditioning, train-serving feature consistency, and extrapolation, and I report intervals or out-of-sample error rather than only R-squared.
keyPoints: A linear model is linear in coefficients; transformed predictors may still be used.
Least squares projects y onto the design-matrix column space.
Coefficients are conditional associations unless identification supports causality.
Prediction intervals are wider than mean-response confidence intervals.
Use stable solvers and validate outside the training sample.
lessons.description: Linear regression is the baseline model for estimating how a numerical outcome changes with one or more predictors. Its apparent simplicity hides several separate ideas: a linear conditional-mean specification, least-squares estimation, the geometry of projection, uncertainty statements, and prediction under a stable data-generating process. This chapter develops those ideas without treating the fitted line as automatically causal. You will derive the normal equations, understand why a numerically stable least-squares solver is preferable to explicitly inverting a matrix, interpret coefficients under transformations and interactions, and separate confidence intervals for a mean response from prediction intervals for a new observation. A worked pricing example shows how centering changes the intercept but not predictions. The lab implements ordinary least squares with a QR-style NumPy solver, compares it with scikit-learn, and verifies orthogonality and translation invariants. The production section covers feature contracts, extrapolation, drift, interval coverage, numerical conditioning, and rollback. The boundary is important: linear regression can be an excellent predictive or descriptive model, but causal language requires a separate identification argument and diagnostics cannot prove that argument.
learningObjectives: State the population model, sample objective, and interpretation of a partial regression coefficient.
Derive the normal equations and explain least squares as an orthogonal projection.
Distinguish coefficient uncertainty, mean-response uncertainty, and new-observation uncertainty.
Fit and verify a stable multivariate least-squares implementation without explicit matrix inversion.
lessons.labGoal: Fit ordinary least squares from the design matrix, compare with scikit-learn, and verify projection, translation, and rank-sensitive behavior.
followUpQuestions: Why can coefficients be unstable while predictions remain stable?
When should you use heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors?
Does adding a feature always help?

lessons.title: Logistic Regression
lessons.interviewAnswer: Logistic regression assumes logit P(Y=1|x)=beta0+x^T beta, so the sigmoid maps any linear score to a probability. Maximum likelihood is equivalent to minimizing binary cross-entropy; with L2 regularization the objective is convex and usually has a unique stable solution. Exp(beta_j) is the conditional multiplicative change in odds for a one-unit increase in x_j, holding other modeled features fixed. It is not a constant probability increase. I evaluate discrimination and calibration separately, choose a threshold from costs or constraints rather than defaulting to 0.5, and watch for separation, leakage, prior shift, subgroup errors, and train-serving mismatches.
keyPoints: The linear predictor acts on log-odds, while the sigmoid returns probability.
Cross-entropy is the negative Bernoulli log-likelihood.
Odds ratios are conditional and are not constant risk differences.
Regularization stabilizes separation and correlated predictors.
Calibration, ranking, and threshold utility answer different questions.
lessons.description: Logistic regression models a binary outcome by making the log-odds of the positive class linear in the predictors. It is simultaneously a probabilistic classifier, a generalized linear model, and a tool for estimating conditional associations. This chapter connects Bernoulli likelihood, cross-entropy, odds ratios, decision thresholds, regularization, and calibration. You will derive the score and Hessian, understand iteratively reweighted least squares, and see why perfectly separated data can send unregularized coefficients toward infinity. A worked credit example distinguishes a probability change from an odds ratio and shows that the same coefficient has different probability-scale effects at different baselines. The lab implements damped Newton updates, compares probabilities with scikit-learn, and verifies finite likelihood improvement and label-complement symmetry. Production guidance treats probability estimation and decisions as different layers: validate calibration, choose thresholds using asymmetric costs and capacity, monitor class-prior and conditional drift, and provide safe fallback behavior. Logistic regression is interpretable only with careful units, encoding, interactions, and conditioning; exponentiating a coefficient produces a conditional odds ratio, not a universal risk ratio or causal effect.
learningObjectives: Derive logistic regression from a Bernoulli likelihood and interpret coefficients on odds and probability scales.
Explain Newton or iteratively reweighted least-squares fitting and the role of regularization.
Separate probability quality, ranking quality, threshold decisions, and causal interpretation.
Detect separation, calibration failure, leakage, and distribution shift in a deployed classifier.
lessons.labGoal: Implement L2-regularized logistic regression with damped Newton updates, compare with scikit-learn, and verify likelihood, probability, and label-symmetry invariants.
followUpQuestions: Why does complete separation cause trouble?
What is the difference between discrimination and calibration?
How does L2 regularization affect interpretation?

lessons.title: Decision Trees
lessons.interviewAnswer: A decision tree is a nonparametric, piecewise-constant model that recursively partitions feature space. At each node it greedily searches a feature and threshold that maximize weighted impurity reduction: Gini or entropy for classification, and usually squared-error reduction for regression. A leaf predicts its training-label distribution or target average. Trees capture thresholds and interactions without scaling, but an unpruned tree has high variance, unstable boundaries, unreliable small-leaf probabilities, and no sensible extrapolation. I tune leaf size, depth or cost-complexity pruning inside leakage-safe validation, compare against simple baselines, and evaluate probability calibration separately from discrimination. In production I version preprocessing and category handling, guard unsupported ranges, monitor leaf occupancy and delayed error, and never interpret impurity importance as causality.
keyPoints: A split is selected by weighted reduction in a declared node impurity or loss.
Greedy recursive partitioning is locally optimal, not a search for the globally best tree.
Depth, minimum leaf mass and cost-complexity pruning control variance and rule complexity.
Leaf class fractions are estimates, not automatically calibrated probabilities.
Tree explanations and feature importances describe model behavior, not causal effects.
lessons.description: Decision trees learn if-then rules by recursively partitioning feature space and assigning a constant prediction to every terminal region. This chapter derives classification impurity and regression loss reduction, explains the weighted split calculation, and separates greedy tree construction from post-pruning. It covers Gini versus entropy, thresholds, categorical encoding, sample and class weights, stopping rules, cost-complexity pruning, leaf probabilities, instability, missing values, monotonic constraints, extrapolation and interpretation. Two worked examples calculate a split and expose a leakage-prone customer identifier. The lab implements a one-level classifier from scratch, compares its threshold and predictions with scikit-learn, and verifies partition and impurity invariants. The production discussion treats the tree as a versioned decision system: input schema, category policy, leaf occupancy, probability calibration, latency, fairness, fallbacks and rollback all need explicit contracts. A tree can be transparent about its computation while still being wrong about the population or unsafe for a decision. You will also learn why validation must preserve grouped and temporal dependence, how tiny leaves create false confidence, and when a simple rule list is preferable to a statistically unstable tree.
learningObjectives: Compute weighted Gini, entropy or regression-loss reduction for a candidate split.
Explain recursive partitioning, greedy search and the piecewise-constant prediction surface.
Control complexity with leaf constraints and cost-complexity pruning under honest validation.
Audit tree probabilities, explanations, importances and production behavior without causal overclaiming.
lessons.labGoal: Build a one-level classification tree, compare it with scikit-learn, and verify impurity and partition invariants.

visualSummaries.title: How a tree learns one branch

followUpQuestions: Why does minimum leaf size regularize a tree?
Gini or entropy?
Why can a tree not extrapolate?

lessons.title: Random Forest
lessons.interviewAnswer: A random forest averages many high-variance decision trees that are deliberately made different through bootstrap samples and random feature subsets at each split. Bagging reduces variance when individual errors are not perfectly correlated; feature subsampling lowers that correlation, sometimes at the cost of weaker trees. Classification averages class probabilities or votes, while regression averages leaf predictions. Out-of-bag observations provide a useful internal estimate and permutation-importance sample, but OOB evaluation still inherits temporal, grouped and preprocessing leakage if the sampling unit is wrong. I tune leaf size and max_features before simply adding trees, assess calibration and subgroup error, and monitor latency, model size, category behavior, drift and prediction disagreement in production.
keyPoints: Bootstrap resampling changes observations; random feature selection changes available split opportunities.
Averaging reduces variance most when base predictors are individually useful and imperfectly correlated.
Out-of-bag estimates are convenient but do not repair an invalid sampling or feature pipeline.
Impurity and permutation importance have different biases and neither establishes causality.
More trees stabilize Monte Carlo variation but do not fix biased targets, leakage or domain shift.
lessons.description: Random forests combine bootstrap aggregation with randomized feature competition to reduce the variance of decision trees. This chapter develops the variance-correlation equation, explains why deep individual trees can be useful inside an average, and distinguishes bagging observations from subsampling features. It covers bootstrap multiplicity, out-of-bag predictions, max_features, tree and leaf complexity, class weights, regression and classification aggregation, probability calibration, feature importance, missing values, quantiles, extrapolation and compute scaling. A worked example computes how correlation limits ensemble variance reduction, while a second diagnoses invalid OOB evaluation for repeated customers. The lab implements bootstrap stumps and majority voting from scratch, compares them with scikit-learn's forest, and verifies sampling diversity, deterministic seeds and accuracy. Production guidance covers artifact size, parallelism, batch versus online latency, tree disagreement, schema drift, leaf support, subgroup performance, canaries and rollback. The main lesson is precise: adding trees reduces Monte Carlo noise around the forest construction; it cannot average away a mistake shared by every tree.
learningObjectives: Explain how bootstrap sampling and random feature subsets create useful tree diversity.
Derive how base-model correlation limits the variance reduction from averaging.
Use out-of-bag predictions correctly and identify when their sampling assumptions fail.
Evaluate and operate a forest under calibration, interpretation, latency and drift constraints.
lessons.labGoal: Build a bootstrap ensemble of randomized decision stumps and verify diversity, voting and a library forest baseline.
followUpQuestions: Why are individual forest trees often deep?
What does max_features control?
Can tree disagreement be used as uncertainty?

lessons.title: Gradient Boosting / XGBoost Intuition
lessons.interviewAnswer: Gradient boosting builds an additive predictor stage by stage. Starting from a constant, each new weak learner approximates the negative gradient of the chosen loss with respect to current predictions; a learning rate shrinks its contribution. With squared error, those pseudo-residuals are ordinary residuals. Tree boosting adds shallow regression trees that specialize in remaining error. XGBoost-style systems use first and second derivatives, regularized leaf scores, row and column sampling, sparsity-aware split handling and efficient histogram or quantile approximations. The main controls—number of rounds, learning rate, tree complexity and regularization—interact, so I select them with chronological or grouped validation and early stopping on an independent set. I monitor calibration, subgroup error, latency, drift and missing-value routing, and preserve a simpler fallback.
keyPoints: Boosting performs greedy optimization in function space by adding a learner aligned with the loss gradient.
Residual fitting is exact intuition for squared loss but other losses use different pseudo-residuals.
Learning rate, boosting rounds, tree depth and leaf regularization must be tuned jointly.
XGBoost's second-order and systems machinery changes efficiency and regularization, not the need for honest evaluation.
Early stopping consumes validation information and must not be evaluated on the same data as final performance.
lessons.description: Gradient boosting constructs a prediction function as a sequence of small loss-reducing corrections. This chapter derives pseudo-residuals as negative functional gradients, shows why squared-error boosting fits ordinary residuals, and explains logistic gradients, line search, shrinkage, tree depth, subsampling and early stopping. It then connects classical gradient boosting with XGBoost's second-order objective, regularized leaf weights, sparsity-aware routing and scalable split approximations. Worked examples calculate two regression rounds and explain why a repeatedly reused early-stopping set is no longer an unbiased test. The lab implements one-dimensional squared-error boosting with decision stumps, compares it with scikit-learn and verifies monotone training-loss reduction and additive predictions. Production coverage includes objective and weight semantics, missing and categorical values, class imbalance, calibration, thresholding, determinism, artifact size, latency, drift, canaries and rollback. The chapter keeps optimization and evidence separate: stagewise training can minimize exactly the wrong loss on exactly the wrong data. It also shows how derivative conventions, sample weights and learned missing directions become part of the deployed model contract and must be tested across training and serving runtimes.
learningObjectives: Derive the stagewise additive update and pseudo-residual for a differentiable loss.
Explain how shrinkage, rounds, tree complexity, sampling and regularization interact.
Connect first-order gradient boosting with XGBoost-style second-order leaf optimization.
Design leakage-safe early stopping, evaluation and production monitoring for boosted trees.
lessons.labGoal: Implement squared-error gradient boosting with stumps, compare with scikit-learn, and verify additive updates and loss reduction.
followUpQuestions: Why can shallow trees work well in boosting?
What does the Hessian do in second-order boosting?
Random forest or gradient boosting?

lessons.title: Support Vector Machines
lessons.interviewAnswer: A support vector machine learns a maximum-margin decision boundary. For binary labels y in {-1,+1}, the soft-margin linear SVM minimizes 0.5||w||² + C Σ_i max(0,1-y_i(wᵀx_i+b)); only points on or inside the margin have nonzero hinge loss and determine the solution. Feature scaling matters because the norm and distances define the margin. In the dual, predictions depend on support-vector inner products, which kernels replace with valid similarities such as the RBF kernel. C trades margin width against violations, while RBF gamma controls locality. I tune both inside leakage-safe validation, check class weights, calibration and threshold utility separately, and avoid kernel SVC when quadratic-or-worse scaling, support-vector count or serving latency violates the budget.
keyPoints: The geometric margin is tied to feature scale, regularization and the norm of the separating vector.
Soft margin uses hinge loss and slack to trade violations against a wider boundary.
Only support vectors have nonzero dual influence, but many support vectors can make inference expensive.
A kernel must produce a valid positive-semidefinite Gram matrix for the standard convex formulation.
SVM decision scores are not probabilities; calibration and decision thresholds are separate stages.
lessons.description: Support vector machines learn regularized maximum-margin boundaries and extend linear separation through kernels. This chapter derives hard- and soft-margin objectives, hinge loss, slack variables, KKT support-vector conditions and the dual prediction rule. It explains why standardization changes the geometry, how C and RBF gamma interact, what makes a kernel valid, how multiclass one-vs-one or one-vs-rest wrappers work, and why decision_function values are not calibrated probabilities. Worked examples calculate a margin and diagnose an apparently accurate but operationally infeasible RBF model with tens of thousands of support vectors. The lab trains a linear hinge-loss model from scratch, compares its labels with LinearSVC, and verifies positive margins and scaling sensitivity. Production guidance covers sparse versus dense solvers, fit complexity, kernel-matrix memory, support-vector inference cost, calibration, thresholds, schema parity, drift, privacy and rollback. The aim is not to memorize 'maximize the margin,' but to connect the margin to units, regularization, data overlap and the actual serving budget.
learningObjectives: Derive the hard- and soft-margin primal objectives and interpret hinge loss and slack.
Explain support vectors, dual coefficients and kernelized prediction.
Tune scaling, C and kernel parameters using an honest validation design.
Choose an SVM solver and probability or threshold layer that meets production constraints.
lessons.labGoal: Train a linear soft-margin classifier with hinge-loss subgradients, compare with LinearSVC, and verify margin and scaling behavior.
followUpQuestions: What happens as C increases?
How do C and RBF gamma interact?
When would you choose LinearSVC over SVC?

lessons.title: k-Nearest Neighbors
lessons.interviewAnswer: k-nearest neighbors is an instance-based, nonparametric method. At prediction time it finds the k training observations closest under a chosen representation and metric, then votes for classification or averages targets for regression, optionally weighting nearer points more. Small k produces flexible, high-variance boundaries; large k smooths toward the global prevalence or mean. Scaling, encoding and irrelevant dimensions are central because they define distance. Exact search costs roughly O(nd) per query without an index; KD and ball trees help mainly at lower intrinsic dimension, while approximate indexes trade recall for latency at scale. I choose the metric and k inside leakage-safe validation, monitor neighbor distance and label mix as support diagnostics, and never interpret proximity as causal similarity.
keyPoints: The representation and distance metric define what the model means by similar.
k controls locality: small neighborhoods have low smoothing bias and high sampling variance.
Neighbor search and the prediction rule are separate; exact, tree-based and approximate indexes have different guarantees.
High dimension makes distances concentrate and indexing less effective unless useful structure remains.
Store-and-query models require privacy, deletion, freshness and latency controls for the reference set.
lessons.description: k-nearest neighbors predicts from labels or targets of nearby stored observations. This chapter treats representation, distance and neighborhood choice as the learned model, derives uniform and distance-weighted classification and regression, and explains the bias-variance effect of k. It covers standardization, mixed and sparse data, Mahalanobis and cosine choices, ties, radius neighborhoods, class imbalance, distance concentration, intrinsic dimension, exact brute force, KD trees, ball trees and approximate search. Worked examples show how units reverse a neighbor ranking and how a large neighbor distance signals unsupported inference. The lab implements Euclidean KNN from scratch, compares it with scikit-learn and verifies self-neighbor, voting, scaling and probability invariants. Production guidance addresses reference-set versioning, embedding parity, deletion, privacy, index recall, tail latency, freshness, drift, fallbacks and rollback. The goal is to make one principle operational: a nearby point is useful only if the metric encodes task-relevant similarity and the search system returns that neighborhood reliably.
learningObjectives: Implement kNN classification and regression from a declared metric and weighting rule.
Explain how k, scaling, irrelevant dimensions and class density affect predictions.
Choose among brute-force, tree-based and approximate search using measured recall and latency.
Operate a reference-set model with support, privacy, freshness and deletion controls.
lessons.labGoal: Implement distance-weighted KNN classification, compare it with scikit-learn, and verify voting, self-neighbor and scaling behavior.
followUpQuestions: How do you choose k?
Why does scaling matter?
What should happen when no radius neighbor exists?

lessons.title: Naive Bayes
lessons.interviewAnswer: Naive Bayes is a generative classifier that estimates a class prior P(y) and class-conditional feature likelihoods, then applies Bayes' rule. Its naive assumption is conditional independence of features given the class, so log posterior scores become log P(y)+Σ_j log P(x_j|y). Gaussian NB models continuous features with class-specific univariate Gaussians; multinomial and Bernoulli variants suit counts and binary events. Smoothing prevents unseen features from forcing zero likelihood. The independence assumption is often false, yet the argmax class can remain good because classification needs correct ordering rather than perfect joint probabilities. I match the likelihood to the representation, fit vocabulary and smoothing inside validation, evaluate calibration separately, and monitor priors, token or feature drift and underflow-safe log computations.
keyPoints: Conditional independence is P(x|y)=∏_j P(x_j|y), not marginal independence of features.
Different variants encode different data-generating assumptions; multinomial counts and Bernoulli presence are not interchangeable.
Additive smoothing handles zero counts and changes rare-feature evidence.
Log-space scoring prevents product underflow and converts evidence into additive contributions.
Good classification accuracy does not imply calibrated posterior probabilities.
lessons.description: Naive Bayes combines class priors and feature likelihoods under a conditional-independence approximation. This chapter derives posterior log scores and distinguishes Gaussian, multinomial, Bernoulli, categorical and complement variants. It explains sufficient statistics, Laplace and Lidstone smoothing, absent-feature evidence, class priors, log-sum-exp normalization, correlated-feature double counting, vocabulary leakage and probability calibration. Worked examples calculate smoothed token odds and show how duplicated correlated features make a posterior unjustifiably extreme. The lab implements multinomial Naive Bayes from token counts, compares log probabilities and predictions with scikit-learn, and verifies normalization, smoothing and permutation invariants. Production coverage includes streaming count updates, vocabulary and tokenizer versioning, prior shift, numeric precision, unknown categories, privacy-sensitive text, feature drift, canaries and rollback. The key distinction is maintained throughout: a misspecified generative model may still draw a useful classification boundary, but its posterior numbers should not be treated as trustworthy risk without independent evidence. You will learn how likelihood assumptions define legal inputs, why feature absence can itself be evidence, and how a compact count model can fail when its vocabulary or deployment prevalence changes.
learningObjectives: Derive Naive Bayes posterior scores from priors and conditionally independent likelihoods.
Select Gaussian, multinomial, Bernoulli, categorical or complement assumptions for a representation.
Apply smoothing and stable log arithmetic and explain their effect on rare evidence.
Evaluate classification, probability calibration and production drift as separate concerns.
lessons.labGoal: Implement multinomial Naive Bayes in log space, compare it with scikit-learn, and verify smoothing and normalization.
followUpQuestions: Why does Naive Bayes work despite dependence?
Why use log probabilities?
How would you handle class-prior shift?

lessons.title: K-means Clustering
lessons.interviewAnswer: K-means partitions observations into k groups by minimizing within-cluster squared Euclidean distance to cluster centroids. Lloyd's algorithm alternates assignment to the nearest centroid and recomputation of each centroid as its assigned mean; each step cannot increase inertia, but convergence is only to a local optimum. The objective favors compact, roughly spherical, similar-scale groups and is sensitive to units, outliers, initialization and the chosen k. k-means++ spreads initial centers to improve starting quality, and multiple runs reduce local-optimum risk. I fit scaling inside the analysis pipeline, inspect stability across seeds and resamples, compare inertia with silhouette and downstream usefulness, and treat cluster IDs as arbitrary labels rather than discovered truth. In production I version centroids and transforms, monitor distance and occupancy, and route unsupported points safely.
keyPoints: The objective is squared Euclidean distortion, so feature units and outliers directly shape the partition.
Assignment and centroid updates monotonically reduce or preserve inertia but need not reach the global minimum.
k-means++ and repeated initializations address optimization variability, not model misspecification.
Choosing k requires stability, geometry and use-case evidence; an elbow alone is subjective.
Cluster numbers are permutation-invariant and should not be treated as semantic classes without validation.
lessons.description: K-means clustering represents a dataset with k centroids and assigns each observation to its nearest centroid under squared Euclidean distance. This chapter derives the distortion objective and both steps of Lloyd's algorithm, proves monotone descent, and explains why the solution is local and cluster labels are arbitrary. It covers scaling, whitening, outliers, k-means++ initialization, empty clusters, repeated starts, minibatch updates, high dimension, sparse vectors, spherical assumptions, selecting k, silhouette limitations, stability and downstream validation. Worked examples calculate one assignment-update round and show how units reverse a segmentation. The lab implements Lloyd's algorithm and k-means++-style restarts, compares inertia with scikit-learn, and verifies nonincreasing objective, centroid means and label-permutation invariance. Production guidance versions transforms and centroids, aligns identities across retrains, monitors distance and occupancy, handles empty or unsupported regions, and retains a safe fallback. The method is treated as a useful compression model, not an oracle that reveals natural categories. You will also learn why multiple starts solve an optimization problem rather than a geometry problem, how minibatches alter the fitted prototypes, and how unsupported assignment should be exposed instead of silently named.
learningObjectives: Derive the k-means objective and alternating assignment and centroid updates.
Explain sensitivity to scaling, initialization, outliers, shape and high dimension.
Select and validate k using stability, geometry and intended use rather than inertia alone.
Deploy versioned centroids with identity, support, monitoring and rollback controls.
lessons.labGoal: Implement Lloyd's k-means with repeated starts, compare with scikit-learn, and verify monotone inertia and centroid invariants.
followUpQuestions: Why is the mean the centroid update?
Why does k-means++ help?
What can distance to the nearest centroid indicate?

lessons.title: PCA
lessons.interviewAnswer: PCA finds orthogonal directions that capture maximum variance in centered data. With centered matrix X, the first loading maximizes ||Xv||² subject to ||v||=1; later loadings are orthogonal. Equivalently, PCA takes eigenvectors of the covariance matrix or right singular vectors of X. Scores are X V_q, and rank-q reconstruction is scores V_qᵀ plus the mean; truncated SVD gives the minimum Frobenius-error rank-q approximation. Scaling determines whether variance in large-unit features dominates. Explained variance is not importance, causality or guaranteed predictive signal. I fit centering and scaling only on training data, choose q from reconstruction, stability and downstream validation, inspect sign and subspace ambiguity, and monitor reconstruction error and score drift in production.
keyPoints: Centering is essential for ordinary PCA; standardization is a modeling choice, not a theorem requirement.
Variance maximization, covariance eigendecomposition and truncated SVD are equivalent views under the stated setup.
Components are orthogonal directions, while scores are observation coordinates and loadings are feature weights.
Signs are arbitrary and nearly tied eigenvalues make individual component directions unstable even when their subspace is stable.
High explained variance does not establish task relevance, group fairness or causal meaning.
lessons.description: Principal component analysis rotates centered data into orthogonal directions ordered by captured variance. This chapter derives PCA from a constrained variance problem, covariance eigenvectors and singular value decomposition, then proves the rank-q reconstruction guarantee. It distinguishes loadings, scores, eigenvalues, explained-variance ratios, reconstruction residuals and whitening. Practical sections cover centering, standardization, units, missing values, outliers, sparse truncated SVD, randomized solvers, component selection, sign ambiguity, repeated eigenvalues, subspace stability, visualization leakage and downstream predictive validation. Worked examples calculate a two-feature principal direction and show how unit conversion changes the result. The lab implements PCA with NumPy SVD, compares it with scikit-learn, and verifies centering, orthogonality, reconstruction and sign-invariant subspaces. Production guidance versions transforms and loadings, monitors score and residual drift, tests parity and supports rollback. PCA is presented as optimal linear compression for one declared loss—not as automatic discovery of meaningful latent causes. You will also learn how sparse truncated SVD differs from centered PCA, why nearly tied eigenvalues destabilize component stories, and when residual monitoring reveals new variation outside the deployed subspace.
learningObjectives: Derive PCA through variance maximization, covariance eigendecomposition and SVD.
Compute scores, loadings, explained variance and rank-q reconstruction.
Handle scaling, signs, tied eigenvalues, sparse data and leakage correctly.
Select and deploy a PCA subspace using reconstruction, stability and downstream evidence.
lessons.labGoal: Implement PCA with SVD, compare with scikit-learn, and verify orthogonality, reconstruction and sign-invariant subspaces.
followUpQuestions: Why does PCA minimize reconstruction error?
PCA versus factor analysis?
What does whitening do?

lessons.title: Bias–Variance Trade-off
lessons.interviewAnswer: Bias-variance decomposition explains expected squared prediction error at a fixed input. Across repeated training sets, error equals squared bias of the average predictor, variance of fitted predictors, and irreducible conditional noise. A rigid model can have high bias; a highly adaptive model can have high variance, but model class alone does not determine either, and modern curves need not be U-shaped. The decomposition is exact for squared loss under a defined data-generating process, not a universal formula for classification or distribution shift. I diagnose the practical trade-off with learning curves, repeated grouped or temporal validation, train-versus-validation gaps and error slices, then adjust representation, regularization, data volume or model class. I do not call label error or deployment shift 'variance' simply because performance is unstable.
keyPoints: Bias and variance are expectations over repeated training samples at a fixed prediction input.
Under squared loss, expected error decomposes into squared bias, estimator variance and irreducible noise.
Training error alone cannot estimate generalization or distinguish bias from variance.
More data often reduces variance but does not repair target misspecification or missing signal.
Distribution shift, leakage and optimization failure are separate causes, not terms to hide inside the decomposition.
lessons.description: Bias-variance decomposition separates expected squared prediction error into systematic error of the average fitted predictor, instability across training samples and irreducible outcome noise. This chapter derives the identity at a fixed input, defines every expectation, then integrates it over a deployment population. It distinguishes approximation, estimation, optimization, measurement and distribution-shift errors and explains why the familiar U-shaped curve is a heuristic rather than a law. Practical sections cover train-validation gaps, repeated cross-validation, learning curves, bootstrap stability, regularization, ensembling, more data, feature improvements, label quality and double descent. Worked examples compute a numeric decomposition and diagnose a model that appears high-bias only because optimization failed. The lab repeatedly fits polynomial regressions to simulated samples and verifies that empirical test error matches bias squared plus variance plus noise. Production guidance monitors retraining dispersion, segment errors, drift and decision stability. The result is an intervention framework: do not add complexity, data or regularization until evidence identifies the mechanism those changes can actually address.
learningObjectives: Derive the fixed-input squared-loss bias-variance-noise identity.
Distinguish approximation, estimation, optimization, measurement and shift errors.
Use repeated validation and learning curves without treating them as direct decomposition estimates.
Choose data, regularization, ensembling or representation interventions from a mechanism-based diagnosis.
lessons.labGoal: Estimate bias squared, variance and noise across repeated polynomial fits and verify the squared-error decomposition empirically.
followUpQuestions: Why is bias squared in the decomposition?
Does regularization always increase bias?
How does bagging reduce variance?

lessons.title: MSE vs MAE
lessons.interviewAnswer: MSE averages squared residuals and MAE averages absolute residuals. Squaring gives large errors disproportionate influence, a differentiable objective, and the conditional mean as the population-optimal point prediction. Absolute loss grows linearly, is more robust to tails, is nondifferentiable at zero, and targets a conditional median. RMSE restores target units but retains squared-loss ranking. The right metric follows operational cost and the estimand, not a universal robustness preference. I report distributional and slice errors, uncertainty over independent units, and a baseline; keep training loss distinct from selection and business utility; and verify sample weights, missing targets, inverse transforms and aggregation. A model with lower MSE can have worse typical error or worse high-stakes tail decisions.
keyPoints: Squared loss elicits the conditional mean; absolute loss elicits a conditional median.
MSE and RMSE rank the same model on one fixed evaluation set, but RMSE has target units.
Large residuals dominate MSE through squaring, while every residual contributes linearly to MAE.
Averaging over rows can overweight repeated entities; aggregation must follow the independent decision unit.
Metric selection should represent operational loss, tail risk and subgroup consequences.
lessons.description: Mean squared error and mean absolute error summarize regression residuals using different cost geometries. This chapter derives MSE, RMSE and MAE, proves that squared loss targets a conditional mean while absolute loss targets a conditional median, and explains convexity, gradients, subgradients, outlier influence and units. It covers weighted and grouped aggregation, multioutput targets, log-scale evaluation, inverse transforms, missing targets, heteroskedasticity, tail metrics, confidence intervals, baselines and asymmetric alternatives such as pinball loss. Worked examples show one outlier reversing model preference and explain why back-transforming a log forecast requires care. The lab implements weighted MSE, RMSE and MAE, compares with scikit-learn, verifies inequalities and demonstrates the mean-versus-median optimum. Production guidance fixes the evaluation contract, monitors residual slices and target delay, and prevents metric-definition drift. The goal is to choose an error measure that represents the actual prediction estimand and cost rather than declaring one metric universally robust. It also explains how paired comparisons keep competing models on the same evidence.
learningObjectives: Compute and interpret weighted MSE, RMSE and MAE on a declared target scale.
Derive their conditional mean and median population optima.
Diagnose outlier, grouping, transform and aggregation effects on model rankings.
Design a regression scorecard with baselines, uncertainty, tails and operational slices.
lessons.labGoal: Implement weighted MSE, RMSE and MAE, compare with scikit-learn, and verify their invariants and point optima.
followUpQuestions: Why does MSE target the mean?
Can RMSE be averaged across folds?
What if overprediction costs twice underprediction?

lessons.title: Precision, Recall & F1
lessons.interviewAnswer: Classification metrics start from the decision and the evaluation population. Accuracy is the fraction correct, but it hides which class is harmed and can look excellent under imbalance. A confusion matrix separates false positives and false negatives. Precision asks, among predicted positives, how many were positive; recall or sensitivity asks, among actual positives, how many were found; specificity measures rejection of negatives. F-beta combines precision and recall with a declared trade-off, while balanced accuracy and macro averaging prevent large classes from dominating. For probabilistic models I also evaluate log loss, Brier score and calibration because threshold metrics discard probability quality. I freeze label semantics, positive class, threshold, averaging rule, sample unit and abstention policy, then report uncertainty and operational slices. No single classification metric is universally sufficient.
keyPoints: The confusion matrix is the accounting identity behind thresholded classification metrics.
Precision depends on prevalence as well as model behavior; recall and specificity condition on actual class.
Micro, macro, weighted and per-class averages answer different population questions.
Threshold metrics evaluate a decision rule; proper probability scores evaluate the forecast before thresholding.
Undefined denominators, abstentions, repeated entities and delayed labels require explicit policies.
lessons.description: Classification metrics translate predictions into evidence about errors, probability quality and decision consequences. This chapter derives accuracy, precision, recall, specificity, negative predictive value, F-beta, balanced accuracy, Matthews correlation and multiclass averaging from the confusion matrix. It explains why prevalence and threshold alter predictive values, why accuracy can fail under imbalance, and how micro, macro, weighted and per-class reporting answer different questions. It separates hard-label evaluation from log loss, Brier score and calibration, covers top-k and multilabel settings, and treats abstention as an explicit outcome. Worked examples show a 99%-accurate useless classifier and a prevalence shift that changes precision without changing sensitivity or specificity. The lab implements binary counts and metrics, verifies them against scikit-learn, and checks invariants. Production guidance versions label definitions, positive-class orientation, thresholds, missing-label and abstention policies, evaluates independent entities and operational slices, and connects metrics to review capacity and error costs. Denominators and raw counts remain visible so small or undefined cells cannot masquerade as certainty.
learningObjectives: Derive binary classification metrics from confusion counts and explain their conditioning direction.
Select per-class, micro, macro and weighted summaries for a declared evaluation population.
Separate thresholded decision quality from ranking and probability-forecast quality.
Build a production scorecard that handles prevalence, abstention, uncertainty and operational cost.
lessons.labGoal: Implement confusion counts and core binary metrics, compare them with scikit-learn, and verify denominator and label invariants.
followUpQuestions: When is balanced accuracy useful?
How do you handle precision when there are no predicted positives?
Why can micro F1 equal accuracy?

lessons.title: ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC
lessons.interviewAnswer: ROC and precision-recall curves evaluate a ranking across thresholds, but they emphasize different consequences. ROC plots true-positive rate against false-positive rate; its area is the probability that a randomly chosen positive receives a higher score than a randomly chosen negative, with tie handling. PR plots precision against recall and directly exposes alert purity, so it is usually more informative when positives are rare and false-positive volume matters. ROC AUC is prevalence-invariant under fixed class-conditional score distributions, whereas precision and PR baselines change with prevalence. Average precision is a non-interpolated weighted mean of precisions over recall increments and is not identical to every trapezoidal PR area. Neither curve selects an operating threshold or proves calibration. I compare curves on the same untouched examples, add uncertainty over independent units, report partial or capacity-constrained regions, and choose a threshold using costs and constraints outside the final test set.
keyPoints: ROC summarizes TPR versus FPR; PR summarizes precision versus recall over score thresholds.
ROC AUC has a pairwise ranking interpretation but may hide large absolute false-positive volume.
The no-skill PR precision baseline is prevalence, so PR results do not transport unchanged across populations.
Average precision and trapezoidal PR AUC use different interpolation assumptions and should be named precisely.
Curves evaluate ranking, not probability calibration, business utility or a deployed threshold by themselves.
lessons.description: ROC and precision-recall analysis evaluates how a classifier ranks positives above negatives across possible thresholds. This chapter derives both curves from a sorted score list, explains their axes and baselines, and gives ROC AUC its pairwise probability interpretation. It shows why a seemingly tiny false-positive rate can overwhelm a rare-event system, why precision-recall curves expose alert purity, and why PR baselines move with prevalence. It distinguishes average precision from trapezoidal PR area, discusses ties, interpolation, sample weights, multiclass averaging, partial AUC and precision at a capacity limit. Worked examples calculate threshold points and translate rates into review counts. The lab builds curves from scratch, verifies AUC and average precision against scikit-learn, checks score-order invariance, and demonstrates the prevalence effect. Production guidance evaluates paired predictions on untouched cohorts, attaches cluster-aware uncertainty, focuses on feasible operating regions, checks calibration separately, and selects thresholds from costs or constraints without reusing final-test labels. Every reported point stays connected to its threshold, confusion counts and expected operational volume.
learningObjectives: Construct ROC and precision-recall points from ranked scores and threshold confusion counts.
Interpret ROC AUC, average precision, baselines and prevalence effects without overclaiming.
Compare models in an operationally feasible region using paired uncertainty and capacity constraints.
Separate ranking evaluation from calibration, threshold selection and downstream utility.
lessons.labGoal: Build ROC and precision-recall points from ranked scores, verify standard areas, and demonstrate invariance and prevalence behavior.
followUpQuestions: Why is ROC AUC invariant to a monotonic score transform?
When should partial AUC be used?
Can high AUC coexist with poor calibration?

lessons.title: Train/Validation/Test & Cross-validation
lessons.interviewAnswer: Cross-validation estimates how a complete training procedure generalizes by repeatedly fitting it on training folds and scoring held-out folds. The splitter must reproduce the deployment unit and direction: shuffled K-fold for approximately IID units, GroupKFold when entities repeat, blocked or rolling splits for future prediction, and stratification when class support is needed. Every learned step—including imputation, scaling, encoding, feature selection, resampling and calibration—must be fitted inside each training fold, normally through a pipeline. CV estimates a procedure, not one already-fitted model. Fold scores are correlated because training sets overlap, so their standard deviation is not a simple confidence interval. I use out-of-fold predictions for paired diagnostics, keep an untouched final test set when selection is extensive, and use nested CV when the same data drive hyperparameter or model search and unbiased performance estimation.
keyPoints: The resampling unit and temporal direction must match the future generalization claim.
All data-dependent transformations belong inside the fold-specific training pipeline.
Cross-validation evaluates a training procedure; the final model is refit on all development data afterward.
Fold scores are dependent and can hide example weighting differences; preserve out-of-fold predictions and fold sizes.
Model selection and performance estimation are distinct tasks; nested CV or a final test set separates them.
lessons.description: Cross-validation is a controlled simulation of training and deployment, not merely repeated random splitting. This chapter derives the out-of-fold estimate, distinguishes observation-weighted from fold-weighted aggregation, and explains the bias, variance and computational trade-offs of holdout, K-fold, repeated K-fold and leave-one-out evaluation. It selects splitters for IID observations, stratified classification, repeated entities, spatial groups and temporal forecasting, including why stratification can reduce observed fold variability. It shows how pipelines keep imputation, scaling, encoding, feature selection, resampling and calibration inside each training fold. Worked examples expose patient leakage and unequal fold weighting. The lab performs manual pipeline-based K-fold evaluation, verifies scikit-learn results and confirms that every row receives exactly one out-of-fold prediction. Production guidance versions split manifests and seeds, records fold-level artifacts and failures, compares paired predictions, separates model selection from estimation, and refits the chosen procedure on all eligible development data without touching the final test set. The emphasis is faithful rehearsal of the actual future novelty rather than maximizing a convenient resampling score.
learningObjectives: Choose a splitter whose held-out unit and temporal direction match deployment.
Construct leakage-safe fold pipelines and complete out-of-fold predictions.
Aggregate fold evidence with the correct observation, group or time weighting.
Separate tuning, comparison and final estimation using nested or held-out evaluation.
lessons.labGoal: Build leakage-safe K-fold evaluation with a preprocessing pipeline, verify library agreement, and construct complete out-of-fold predictions.
followUpQuestions: When should GroupKFold be used?
Why put scaling in a pipeline?
What is the difference between cross_val_score and cross_val_predict?

lessons.title: Data Leakage
lessons.interviewAnswer: Data leakage occurs when model training or evaluation uses information that would not be available for the same prediction in production, or when the validation boundary is contaminated. Target leakage includes post-outcome fields and features computed with future data. Train-test contamination includes fitting imputers, encoders, scalers, feature selectors or oversampling on all rows. Entity leakage places related rows in both sides; temporal leakage trains on the future or uses revised snapshots. Selection leakage arises when the test set repeatedly guides choices. I prevent leakage by defining a prediction timestamp and label horizon, documenting feature availability and lineage, splitting raw data by entity and time before learned transforms, fitting a complete pipeline inside each fold, using point-in-time joins, and reserving final evidence. I also run adversarial checks: remove suspicious features, shift cutoffs, inspect near-perfect proxies, and reproduce every feature from only the allowed historical snapshot.
keyPoints: Availability is defined at the prediction event, not by whether a column exists in today's warehouse.
Split raw independent units before fitting transformations, resampling, selection or calibration.
Point-in-time correct joins need event time, ingestion time, revision policy and label windows.
Repeated entities, duplicates and near-duplicates can contaminate validation without explicit target columns.
A test set ceases to be independent when repeated inspection changes modeling decisions.
lessons.description: Data leakage is any violation of the information or evaluation boundary that makes offline performance easier than deployment. This chapter distinguishes target, temporal, entity, duplicate, preprocessing, feature-selection, resampling and test-set selection leakage. It defines prediction time, feature availability, event time, ingestion time, label horizon and revision policy, then shows how point-in-time joins reconstruct what the system actually knew. It explains why splitting raw independent units must precede imputation, scaling, encoding, target statistics, feature selection, calibration and oversampling. Worked examples expose a post-outcome hospital field and a historical aggregate rebuilt with future transactions. The lab creates an explicit target proxy, demonstrates its inflated validation AUC, removes it through an availability allowlist and verifies split disjointness. Production guidance maintains feature lineage and cutoff manifests, scans duplicates and proxies, replays features from historical snapshots, restricts final-test access, monitors online parity and keeps rollback paths when suspicious drift or impossible offline-online gaps appear. Every release should carry evidence that its inputs were reproducible at their original prediction cutoffs.
learningObjectives: Classify target, temporal, entity, transformation and selection leakage from concrete pipelines.
Specify prediction-time availability and point-in-time join semantics for every feature.
Design raw-data splits and fold-local pipelines that preserve entity and temporal boundaries.
Audit suspicious performance using lineage, ablations, duplicates and historical replay.
lessons.labGoal: Create and detect a post-outcome target proxy, enforce an availability allowlist, and verify clean train-test boundaries.
followUpQuestions: Is normalization before splitting always serious leakage?
How do you detect duplicate leakage in images or text?
What is point-in-time correctness?

lessons.title: Class Imbalance
lessons.interviewAnswer: Class imbalance means class frequencies and error costs are uneven; it does not by itself make learning impossible. I first preserve the natural prevalence in validation and use precision-recall, per-class recall, calibrated probabilities, capacity metrics and expected cost instead of accuracy alone. During training I may use class or sample weights, minority oversampling, majority undersampling, focal-style losses or anomaly methods, but every resampling step stays inside the training fold. Weights change the optimization target and resampling changes the effective prior, so raw probabilities may need correction or calibration on natural-prevalence data. Threshold selection is a separate decision problem based on false-positive cost, missed-positive cost and capacity. I also check rare-positive uncertainty, duplicates, temporal drift and subgroup support. The goal is not a balanced training table; it is reliable performance and utility on the real deployment population.
keyPoints: Imbalance describes prevalence; the actual problem depends on overlap, label quality, sample size and error cost.
Keep validation and test data at deployment prevalence unless estimating a deliberately reweighted population.
Class weights and resampling affect training, while thresholding affects the deployed action; they are not interchangeable.
Oversampling must occur within training folds, and synthetic points must never use validation neighbors.
Probability calibration must be assessed after weighting or resampling on data with the intended prevalence.
lessons.description: Class imbalance is a mismatch in class frequency, not a license to optimize accuracy or balance every dataset mechanically. This chapter separates prevalence, sample size, class overlap, label noise and asymmetric cost; selects per-class, precision-recall, capacity and probability metrics; and quantifies why false-positive volume dominates rare-event systems. It compares class and sample weighting, random over- and undersampling, synthetic sampling, focal-style objectives, hard-negative mining and anomaly framing. It explains fold-local resampling, duplicate dependence, prior distortion, posterior correction and calibration on natural-prevalence data. Worked examples translate a 1% false-positive rate into thousands of alerts and derive balanced class weights. The lab calculates weights, fits weighted and unweighted logistic models, verifies the official formula and checks how weighting changes predictions without altering the evaluation cohort. Production guidance monitors prevalence, label delay, score distributions, queue capacity, rare-class uncertainty and slices while preserving cost-aware thresholds and rollback behavior. It treats data collection and label adjudication as first-class remedies when the rare class lacks genuine independent evidence.
learningObjectives: Diagnose whether imbalance, overlap, label quality or cost is the central failure mode.
Apply weighting and resampling inside training folds without corrupting evaluation prevalence.
Evaluate rare events using ranking, calibration, counts, cost and independent-unit uncertainty.
Correct or recalibrate scores when training interventions change the effective prior.
lessons.labGoal: Derive balanced class weights, fit weighted and unweighted classifiers, and verify the evaluation population remains untouched.
followUpQuestions: When is undersampling useful?
Why can class weights damage calibration?
How should rare-class uncertainty be reported?

lessons.title: Missing Values & Outliers
lessons.interviewAnswer: Missing values are generated by a process, not merely blank cells. I distinguish structural absence, measurement failure and unknown values, then reason about MCAR, MAR and MNAR assumptions relative to observed data. Dropping rows is defensible only when the target population and missingness mechanism make the resulting selection acceptable. Simple median or most-frequent imputation is a strong predictive baseline; indicators can preserve the fact that a value was missing; model-based or multiple imputation is useful when uncertainty in the missing values matters for inference. Every imputer is fitted inside training folds, and time-aware features use only historically available values. I compare native missing-value models with pipeline baselines, evaluate performance by missingness pattern and cohort, and monitor rates and upstream causes. Imputation does not recover truth: it supplies a modeling value under assumptions that must be versioned and stress-tested.
keyPoints: Separate structural absence, collection failure, censoring and semantically unknown categories before choosing a treatment.
MCAR, MAR and MNAR describe the missingness mechanism relative to variables and assumptions, not a property proven by a quick test.
Fit imputers and missingness-derived feature selection only on training folds.
Single imputation understates uncertainty for statistical inference; multiple imputation propagates between-imputation variation under its model.
Missingness rates and patterns are production data-quality signals even when the model accepts NaN natively.
lessons.description: Missing-value handling begins with the data-generating and collection process. This chapter distinguishes structural absence, unknown categories, sensor failure, censoring and delayed availability; defines MCAR, MAR and MNAR; and explains why these assumptions are rarely proven from observed data alone. It compares row or column deletion, constant, mean, median, mode, groupwise, nearest-neighbor, iterative and multiple imputation, missingness indicators and estimators with native missing-value support. It shows how single imputation changes variance and relationships, why target-aware imputation can leak, and how multiple imputation propagates uncertainty for inference. Worked examples expose selection bias from complete-case analysis and the predictive value of a measurement indicator. The lab implements training-only median imputation and indicators, verifies scikit-learn pipeline behavior and checks that validation extremes cannot alter fitted fills. Production guidance versions missing-value semantics and fallback rules, monitors rates and patterns by source and cohort, tests all-missing and new-category cases, and treats sudden missingness as an upstream incident rather than silently masking it.
learningObjectives: Classify missingness semantics and reason explicitly about MCAR, MAR and MNAR assumptions.
Choose deletion, imputation, indicators or native handling for predictive and inferential goals.
Build fold-local imputation pipelines and test leakage, edge cases and missingness patterns.
Monitor missing-data behavior as both a model input and a production data-quality signal.
lessons.labGoal: Implement training-only median imputation with indicators, verify pipeline parity, and prove validation extremes cannot change fitted values.
followUpQuestions: When is a missingness indicator useful?
Why fit median imputation inside CV?
When is multiple imputation preferable?

lessons.title: Feature Importance & Explainability
lessons.interviewAnswer: Feature importance is method-, model-, dataset- and metric-specific; it is not an intrinsic causal property of a column. Linear coefficients describe link-scale changes conditional on other features and depend on units. Tree impurity importance sums training split gains and can favor continuous or high-cardinality variables. Permutation importance measures held-out score degradation after breaking one feature's association with the outcome for a fixed fitted model, but correlated substitutes can make each look unimportant and unrealistic permutations can leave the data manifold. I start with validated model performance, compute held-out permutation importance with a declared scorer, group related features, inspect repeats and folds, and compare with coefficients or model-specific diagnostics. I use ablation and retraining when the question is whether a feature family is necessary. Explanations are descriptive of the fitted system, not causal effects, and sensitive features require governance even if reported importance is small.
keyPoints: Importance answers a specific question about a fitted model, data distribution and scoring rule.
Impurity gain is fast but training-based and biased toward features with many candidate splits.
Held-out permutation importance measures reliance under a feature-breaking intervention, not standalone predictive information.
Correlation, interactions, encodings and grouped feature families can redistribute or hide importance.
Use stability, ablation, domain review and causal evidence before making removal or policy decisions.
lessons.description: Feature importance is a family of model-inspection questions rather than one universal ranking. This chapter interprets standardized coefficients, tree impurity decrease, split and gain counts, held-out permutation, grouped permutation, drop-column retraining and ablation. It explains high-cardinality bias, training-versus-test importance, scorer dependence, correlation and substitute features, interactions, one-hot fragmentation and unrealistic permutations. It separates global average reliance from local and subgroup behavior and distinguishes predictive attribution from causal effect, fairness and data-collection value. Worked examples show duplicated signals hiding each other's permutation importance and a random high-cardinality feature attracting tree splits. The lab fits a random forest, compares impurity and repeated held-out permutation scores, and verifies that genuine signal outranks independent noise. Production guidance versions model, dataset, scorer, feature groups and random seeds, tracks stability across folds and cohorts, uses ablation before deleting expensive inputs, and treats explanation drift as diagnostic evidence rather than an automatic release gate. Every chart names its population, perturbation, metric and uncertainty so rankings cannot travel without their assumptions.
learningObjectives: Interpret coefficient, impurity, permutation and retraining importance as different estimands.
Diagnose cardinality, correlation, interaction, grouping and out-of-distribution perturbation failures.
Compute held-out repeated and grouped importance with appropriate metrics and uncertainty.
Use importance responsibly for debugging, feature cost, governance and hypothesis generation.
lessons.labGoal: Compare tree impurity and held-out permutation importance, verify repeat behavior, and identify signal over independent noise.
followUpQuestions: Why compute permutation importance on held-out data?
What is grouped permutation importance?
When use drop-column importance?

lessons.title: Neural Network Fundamentals
lessons.interviewAnswer: A neural network composes linear transformations with nonlinear activations. Training adjusts parameters to minimize a loss, while intermediate layers learn representations useful for the task.
keyPoints: Layers
Weights/biases
Activation
Loss/optimizer
lessons.description: Neural Network Fundamentals is a core topic in Deep Learning. Every DL interview expects you to explain a neural network from first principles, not just name PyTorch modules. This chapter turns the interview-level summary into a complete engineering and analytical treatment. The starting mental model is: A neural network repeatedly performs weighted combinations followed by nonlinear transformations. Training adjusts the weights so those transformations produce useful representations for the task. The formal and implementation discussion builds from Layers, Weights/biases, Activation, Loss/optimizer, while keeping the unit of data, objective, assumptions, and failure boundaries explicit. The original technical core is preserved: A feed-forward layer computes z=Wx+b and activation a=φ(z). Stacking linear layers without nonlinearities collapses to one linear transformation, so activations create expressive nonlinear functions. The final layer/loss depends on the task: logits plus cross-entropy for classification, continuous outputs with regression losses, etc. Parameters are learned by backpropagation and an optimizer over mini-batches. Rather than treating those statements as isolated facts, the chapter connects them to data preparation, evaluation design, numerical or systems behavior, and choices that change under scale or distribution shift. lessons.title: Case Study: Scientific 3D Reconstruction / Super-resolution
lessons.interviewAnswer: I frame scientific reconstruction or super-resolution as an inverse problem, not image beautification. A latent high-resolution field x is observed through a forward operator y=H(x)+noise that includes optics, sampling, blur, missing angles or detector effects. I start with the scientific quantity and an honest baseline—interpolation, regularized inversion or domain software—then split by specimen, acquisition session and instrument to prevent patch leakage. Evaluation separates data consistency H(x_hat)≈y, full-reference fidelity where truth exists, task validity and perceptual realism. A GAN or diffusion prior may produce plausible high frequencies that are scientifically false, so uncertainty, blinded expert review and downstream measurements are required. Deployment preserves raw data, model and calibration versions, out-of-distribution detection, deterministic fallback and reconstruction audit trails. I never claim recovered detail beyond evidence supported by the acquisition process.
keyPoints: Define the physical forward model and scientific decision before selecting a network.
Patch-level random splits leak specimen and acquisition signatures; split at the independent experimental unit.
Pixel, structural, perceptual, data-consistency and downstream scientific metrics answer different questions.
Perceptual realism is not factual or physical correctness; generative priors can hallucinate convincing structures.
Reproducible deployment versions calibration, preprocessing, model, uncertainty, raw inputs and fallback.
lessons.description: Scientific 3D reconstruction and super-resolution are inverse problems in which incomplete or degraded measurements are mapped to a higher-resolution latent field. This case study begins with the acquisition operator, point-spread function, sampling geometry, noise and calibration, then defines the scientific measurement or decision that reconstruction must support. It builds baselines from interpolation and regularized inversion before learned residual, adversarial or unpaired approaches. Dataset design covers specimen, patient, site, session and instrument grouping, patch extraction after splitting, synthetic degradation mismatch and paired versus unpaired supervision. Evaluation separates MSE and PSNR, SSIM, perceptual preference, forward-model consistency, morphology, counts and blinded domain review. It highlights the perception–distortion trade-off and the distinction between plausible realism and factual physical correctness. The lab simulates blur and downsampling, compares nearest and regularized reconstructions, verifies observation consistency and shows that an unconstrained sharpened result can worsen physical agreement. Production design versions raw measurements, calibration, preprocessing and model; computes uncertainty and OOD signals; uses canaries, fallbacks and audit artifacts; and monitors instrument drift and downstream bias. The chapter concludes with a defense framework covering alternatives, negative results, limitations and claims that remain scientifically warranted.
learningObjectives: Model reconstruction through an acquisition operator, noise and calibration rather than treating it as generic image translation.
Create specimen- and acquisition-level splits that prevent patch and instrument leakage.
Evaluate pixel fidelity, structure, data consistency, uncertainty and downstream scientific validity separately.
Design an auditable deployment that distinguishes perceptual realism from supported physical detail.

lessons.title: Case Study: Graph-based Matching & Recommendation
lessons.interviewAnswer: For graph-based matching, I first define node and edge semantics, prediction time and the constrained decision. In reviewer assignment, paper and reviewer nodes have text and profile features; historical bids, authorship, expertise and prior assignments form typed edges, but future decisions and conflicts must not leak into training. I establish lexical or embedding similarity and popularity baselines before a GNN. Neighborhood aggregation is justified only if graph relations carry incremental signal and new-node induction is handled. Offline link metrics are insufficient: the assignment optimizer must respect conflicts, capacity, coverage and fairness. I evaluate chronologically with unseen papers and reviewers, report candidate recall before ranking quality, calibration and constrained assignment utility, then shadow against human decisions. Production versions the graph snapshot, features, conflict policy, model and optimizer; supports abstention, explanations, audit, manual override and rollback.
keyPoints: Graph construction and temporal edge availability define the learning problem and its leakage risks.
Strong content and heuristic baselines must precede graph complexity.
Candidate generation, edge scoring and constrained assignment are separate stages with separate metrics.
A high link-prediction score can still produce infeasible, unfair or low-coverage assignments.
Sensitive relationships, conflicts, human override and explanation require governance and audit.
lessons.description: Graph-based matching and recommendation combine relational representation learning with constrained decisions. This case study defines a heterogeneous, time-indexed graph of papers, reviewers, topics, organizations, interactions and conflicts, then establishes content, popularity and collaborative baselines. It develops neighborhood aggregation and inductive GraphSAGE-style representations, negative sampling, cold start, temporal leakage and oversmoothing. Candidate retrieval, edge scoring and the final assignment optimizer are treated as independent components: the optimizer enforces capacity, conflicts, minimum coverage, load balance and optional diversity constraints. Evaluation includes candidate recall, ranking quality, calibration, feasible assignment utility, unmatched entities, exposure and subgroup behavior on chronological unseen-node splits. The lab builds content and graph scores for a toy bipartite problem, solves a capacity-constrained assignment with SciPy and verifies conflict, capacity and coverage invariants. Production design versions graph snapshots and edge-time policy, prevents forbidden relationships from training or serving, caches embeddings with freshness, monitors degree and exposure drift, explains scores, supports human override and rolls back model and optimizer separately. The chapter also discusses privacy, popularity feedback, strategic bidding and when simpler content matching is safer than a GNN.
