lessons.title: Case Study: Real-time Streaming Application
lessons.interviewAnswer: I design a streaming application from event semantics and failure contracts. Each event has a stable ID, key, event time, schema version and source position. I distinguish event time from processing time, define windows and a watermark or lateness policy, and specify whether late data updates, retracts, side-outputs or drops. Partition keys preserve needed ordering while avoiding hot shards. State is bounded by window and retention, checkpointed consistently, and sinks are idempotent or transactional; 'exactly once' means each event affects the final result once across the entire source–state–sink path, not that the broker never redelivers. I test duplicates, out-of-order arrivals, crashes before and after checkpoints, schema changes and backpressure. Production monitors consumer lag, watermark lag, late rate, state size, checkpoint health, output reconciliation and replay, with dead letters, backfill, versioned savepoints and rollback.
keyPoints: Event time, processing time, watermarks and allowed lateness are product semantics, not only framework configuration.
Stable IDs and idempotent or transactional sinks are required to tolerate replay without duplicate effects.
Partitioning chooses ordering and parallelism while exposing skew and hot-key risks.
Exactly-once state consistency does not automatically provide end-to-end exactly-once external effects.
Replay, schema evolution, reconciliation, backpressure, savepoints and rollback must be designed before launch.
lessons.description: A real-time streaming application processes unbounded, out-of-order and replayed events while maintaining state and producing timely effects. This case study begins with an event contract containing identity, key, event time, ingestion time, schema and source metadata. It compares event, processing and ingestion time; defines tumbling, sliding and session windows; and explains watermarks, idleness, allowed lateness, updates and retractions. Partitioning is tied to ordering, parallelism and hot keys. Stateful operators, checkpoints, savepoints and recovery are separated from broker delivery and external sink guarantees. At-least-once, at-most-once and exactly-once claims are traced end to end, including idempotency, transactions, two-phase commit and side effects that cannot join a transaction. The lab implements deterministic event-time windows, deduplication and late-event classification and verifies replay invariance. Production design covers schema compatibility, backpressure, consumer and watermark lag, state TTL, checkpoint tuning, dead letters, replay, batch reconciliation, backfills, privacy, deployment and rollback. Failure drills include worker and broker restart, poison events, skew, slow sinks and schema rollout. The final architecture is evaluated by correctness and recovery under disorder, not only steady-state latency.
learningObjectives: Define event identity, key, time, schema, lateness and correction semantics for a real product.
Trace ordering, state, checkpoint and sink guarantees through the end-to-end pipeline.
Design replay-invariant outputs and tests for duplicates, disorder, crashes, skew and schema change.
Operate the stream with lag, watermark, state, checkpoint, reconciliation, backfill and rollback controls.
lessons.labGoal: Implement deterministic event-time windows with deduplication and verify replay and order invariance plus late-event accounting.

lessons.title: Case Study: LLM Copilot with Tools + RAG
lessons.interviewAnswer: I design an LLM copilot as a permissioned workflow, not a chatbot with broad tools. I define user tasks, knowledge freshness, allowed actions and harm boundaries. Retrieval and generation are evaluated separately: ingestion, chunking and access filtering must place authoritative evidence in context; the model must cite and stay within that evidence. Tools have narrow typed schemas, server-side authorization, validation, idempotency and approval for consequential writes—the model can request an action but never grants itself permission. The orchestrator limits steps, time, tokens and cost, handles retries and preserves tool-call lineage. I test answer correctness, citation entailment, retrieval recall, tool choice, argument validity, side-effect safety, refusal and prompt injection using trace-level evals. Production pins model and prompt versions, redacts sensitive logs, monitors latency and cost, canaries changes, and offers read-only or search fallback and kill switches.
keyPoints: Retrieval accuracy, generation groundedness and tool execution correctness are distinct quality layers.
Tool availability is not authorization; every call is validated and permissioned on the server.
Retrieved content and tool outputs are untrusted data that can contain prompt injection or stale instructions.
Trace-level evaluation must cover routing, arguments, citations, side effects, refusal, latency and cost.
Version models, prompts, indexes, tools and policies independently with canaries, audit and rollback.
lessons.description: An LLM copilot with retrieval and tools is a compound system whose language model operates within evidence, authorization and workflow boundaries. This case study defines user jobs, allowed knowledge and action risk before selecting models or frameworks. It designs ingestion with document provenance, versions, access-control metadata, chunking and deletion; hybrid retrieval and reranking; context assembly and citation mapping; and answer generation that can abstain when evidence is insufficient. Tool calling is implemented through narrow schemas, application-side execution, server-side authentication and authorization, argument validation, idempotency and user approval. The chapter treats retrieved text and tool output as untrusted data, covering prompt injection, exfiltration, confused-deputy attacks and least privilege. Evaluation separates retrieval recall, answer correctness, citation entailment, tool routing, arguments, side effects, refusal, latency and cost, then recombines them in trace-level task suites. The lab implements a small access-filtered TF-IDF retriever and permissioned tool dispatcher and verifies that unauthorized or injected actions cannot execute. Production guidance versions model, prompt, index, document corpus, tool and policy; logs redacted traces; rate-limits loops; canaries changes; monitors drift and failures; and supplies read-only fallback, escalation and kill switches. Current official OpenAI guidance is used for Responses API function calling and file search concepts without hard-coding one model alias.

Implement narrow tool contracts with server-side authorization, validation, idempotency and approval.

lessons.title: Time-Series Splits & Backtesting
lessons.interviewAnswer: Time-series evaluation must simulate what was knowable at each forecast origin. I never randomly shuffle future rows into training. I define the operational origin schedule, forecast horizon, data latency, update cadence and retraining policy, then use expanding or rolling windows whose training timestamps and feature event times precede each origin. A gap or embargo is needed when labels, rolling windows or delayed features overlap the validation period. Multi-step forecasts are evaluated by horizon because one-step recursive backtests hide error accumulation. Every transformation, lag, model selection and calibration step is refit within each training window. I compare against naive, seasonal-naive and current-production baselines using the same origins, aggregate across series and time according to business exposure, and preserve paired errors. The final backtest includes realistic missing releases, revisions, cold starts, outages and computation cutoffs; one convenient historical split is not sufficient evidence.
keyPoints: Forecast origins, horizons and information-release times define the evaluation boundary.
Expanding windows mimic accumulating history; rolling windows mimic forgetting or fixed training budgets.
A gap prevents overlapping labels, windows or delayed availability from crossing the split.
All preprocessing, feature creation and selection must be origin-local and point-in-time correct.
Report horizon, series and regime performance with paired baselines and realistic production constraints.
lessons.description: Time-series splitting and backtesting recreate historical forecast decisions under the information that existed at each origin. This chapter distinguishes simple holdout, expanding-window, rolling-window, blocked and prequential evaluation; defines origins, horizons, gaps, embargoes, label maturity and release calendars; and explains why random K-fold and globally computed lags leak. It covers direct, recursive and multi-output horizons, rolling feature state, panel series, cold starts, nested temporal tuning, refit cadence and fixed-versus-updated model comparisons. It develops horizon- and series-aware aggregation, paired uncertainty, regime slices and stress windows while requiring seasonal-naive and production baselines. Worked examples expose overlapping-label leakage and a revised macroeconomic feature that did not exist at forecast time. The lab implements expanding splits with a gap, verifies scikit-learn's TimeSeriesSplit boundaries and compares a rolling-mean forecast against a last-value baseline across identical origins. Production guidance persists origin manifests, data vintages, feature cutoffs and model versions and treats replay parity as a release gate.

lessons.title: Stationarity, ACF & PACF
lessons.interviewAnswer: Weak stationarity means constant mean and variance and autocovariance depending only on lag, not calendar time. Many forecasting models need a stable transformed process or stable residuals rather than a stationary raw business series. I plot the series and rolling regimes, remove known trend or seasonality, and difference only when persistence diagnostics and domain logic justify it. The ACF at lag k measures correlation between y_t and y_{t-k}; the PACF measures the incremental linear association after intermediate lags. For an AR(p), PACF tends to cut off after p while ACF decays; for an MA(q), ACF tends to cut off after q, but finite samples, seasonality and mixed models blur these heuristics. ADF and KPSS use opposite nulls and are sensitive to deterministic terms, breaks and sample size. I treat tests as supporting evidence, avoid overdifferencing, and validate model residuals and forecast performance on rolling origins.
keyPoints: Stationarity is a property of a stochastic process and representation, not a guarantee from one flat-looking plot.
Trend, seasonality, changing variance and structural breaks can create persistent sample autocorrelation.
ACF describes lag correlation; PACF isolates incremental linear lag association conditional on shorter lags.
Differencing can remove stochastic trend but can also over-difference, amplify noise and erase long-run information.
Unit-root tests depend on deterministic terms and have limited power; combine them with plots, domain knowledge and backtests.
lessons.description: Stationarity, autocorrelation and partial autocorrelation provide the core diagnostic language for linear time-series dependence. This chapter defines strict and weak stationarity, distinguishes deterministic trend from unit-root stochastic trend, and analyzes changing variance, seasonality and structural breaks. It derives the ACF and PACF, explains canonical AR and MA cutoff-versus-decay patterns, seasonal spikes, confidence bands and the limits of data-driven order selection. It develops first, seasonal and fractional differencing intuition, variance-stabilizing transforms, overdifferencing symptoms and cointegration warnings. It compares ADF and KPSS null hypotheses and shows how deterministic terms and breaks affect conclusions. Worked examples derive the AR(1) ACF and expose a trending series with spurious persistence. The lab simulates stationary AR(1) and random-walk processes, verifies sample ACF behavior against statsmodels and checks contrasting ADF evidence. Production guidance estimates diagnostics within training windows, monitors residual autocorrelation and regime shifts and chooses transformations by rolling forecast performance rather than a single test.

Compute and interpret ACF and PACF for AR, MA and seasonal dependence.

lessons.title: Forecasting Metrics & Baselines
lessons.interviewAnswer: Forecast metrics must match the decision, scale, horizon and forecast object. I start with chronological forecast errors e_{s,o,h}=y_{s,o+h}-yhat_{s,o,h} from identical origins. MAE targets the conditional median and is interpretable in target units; RMSE targets the conditional mean and emphasizes large errors. MAPE is undefined or unstable near zero and asymmetric, so I usually prefer MASE or RMSSE for cross-series comparison, using a training-only naive or seasonal-naive scale. WAPE is an aggregate ratio, not an average item percentage, and can hide where error occurs. I report signed bias, horizon and series slices, baseline skill and business-weighted cost. For quantiles or distributions I use proper scores such as pinball loss, interval score or CRPS plus empirical coverage and sharpness. I never choose a model from one pooled number: I preserve paired errors, quantify uncertainty with temporal blocks or independent series, and inspect high-impact regimes.
keyPoints: Metric choice determines the statistical functional being estimated: mean, median, quantile or full distribution.
Scale-free metrics still encode a denominator and weighting policy; compute scaling terms from training history only.
MAPE and sMAPE are unreliable around zero and can reward systematically low forecasts.
Evaluate identical origins by horizon, series and regime before applying declared business weights.
Probabilistic forecasts require proper scoring rules together with calibration and sharpness diagnostics.
lessons.description: Forecasting metrics translate forecast errors into model-selection and operating decisions. Worked examples show ranking reversal and percentage-error instability. The lab implements a forecast scorecard, verifies core values against scikit-learn, and demonstrates why MAPE explodes near zero while MASE remains interpretable. Production guidance versions metric definitions, denominators and cohorts, delays scoring until labels mature, and monitors bias, negative skill and interval miscalibration by operational slice.

lessons.title: Causal Inference vs Prediction
lessons.interviewAnswer: Prediction estimates outcomes or labels under the observed data-generating process; causal inference estimates contrasts between well-defined interventions. A model can predict treatment recipients have worse outcomes because sicker people receive treatment even when treatment helps. I begin with a target trial or causal question: population, treatment strategies, assignment, time zero, follow-up, outcome, estimand and analysis. Potential outcomes define effects such as E[Y(1)-Y(0)], while a DAG makes assumptions about confounding, mediation, selection and timing explicit. Identification asks whether the estimand is expressible from observed data under consistency, exchangeability, positivity and interference assumptions; estimation then fits that observed-data functional. Flexible ML improves nuisance prediction but cannot repair an unidentified effect. I report assumptions, overlap, sensitivity, uncertainty, diagnostics and the population to which the result transports, never causal language from predictive accuracy alone.
keyPoints: Prediction concerns observed conditional distributions; causal inference concerns outcomes under interventions.
Define population, treatment versions, time zero, outcome horizon and estimand before choosing an estimator.
Identification assumptions connect unobserved counterfactual contrasts to observed-data quantities.
High predictive accuracy does not establish exchangeability, positivity, consistency or absence of interference.
Causal estimates require design diagnostics, sensitivity analysis and a stated target population, not only model metrics.
lessons.description: Causal inference and prediction solve different statistical problems. This chapter contrasts forecasts under the observed policy with outcomes under explicit interventions and builds a workflow from target question to estimand, identification, estimation and sensitivity analysis. It introduces potential outcomes, average treatment effects, consistency, exchangeability, positivity, interference and causal DAGs; distinguishes total, direct, mediated, intention-to-treat and per-protocol questions; and uses target-trial emulation to align eligibility, assignment, time zero and follow-up. It explains why predictive importance, coefficients and high accuracy do not identify effects, while randomized and quasi-experimental designs can identify effects without maximizing prediction. Worked examples expose confounding by indication and treatment-policy feedback. The lab simulates a beneficial treatment preferentially assigned to high-risk units, shows the naive association has the wrong sign, and recovers the effect with covariate adjustment under the simulated assumptions. Production guidance versions causal questions and cohorts, monitors overlap and treatment policy, reports sensitivity and uncertainty, and prevents decision systems from retraining on their own interventions without evaluation design.

lessons.title: DAGs, Confounders & Colliders
lessons.interviewAnswer: A causal DAG is a directed acyclic graph whose arrows encode direct causal relationships under a chosen level of abstraction. It is not learned from correlations alone; it records domain assumptions and lets us reason about open paths. A confounder is a common cause of treatment and outcome, creating a backdoor path that must be blocked. A mediator lies on the causal path and adjusting for it changes a total-effect question. A collider is a common effect; conditioning on it or its descendants can open a previously blocked path and create association. I define treatment, outcome, time order and target effect, draw all plausible common causes including unmeasured ones, apply d-separation or the backdoor criterion, and avoid descendants of treatment for total effects. I compare defensible adjustment sets, use negative controls or sensitivity analysis, and never treat an algorithmically discovered graph as identified truth without interventions or strong assumptions.
keyPoints: DAG arrows express causal assumptions, not regression coefficients or mere temporal correlation.
Confounders open noncausal backdoor paths; mediators carry effects; colliders block paths until conditioned on.
d-separation is a graphical rule for conditional independence implied by the assumed graph.
An adjustment set is effect- and graph-specific; adding variables can create rather than remove bias.
Unmeasured nodes belong in the graph because they determine identification even when absent from the dataset.
lessons.description: Directed acyclic graphs turn causal assumptions into a precise map for identification and bias analysis. This chapter defines nodes, arrows, paths, ancestors, descendants, forks, chains and colliders; derives d-separation; and explains why confounding, mediation and selection depend on graph position rather than variable names. It applies the backdoor criterion, distinguishes total from direct effects, analyzes M-bias, proxy adjustment, measurement error and selection on descendants, and explains why unmeasured causes must appear even when they cannot enter a model. It also covers Markov equivalence and the assumptions behind causal discovery. Worked examples show confounder adjustment removing bias and collider adjustment creating it. The lab simulates both structures and verifies their opposite regression consequences. Production guidance versions graphs, node semantics, time availability and adjustment sets, reviews new features for post-treatment status, maintains negative-control and sensitivity evidence, and treats every graph revision as a change to the causal claim rather than a cosmetic diagram update.
learningObjectives: Classify causal paths, forks, chains and colliders and apply d-separation correctly.

lessons.title: Profiling & Benchmarking ML Systems

lessons.title: Pruning & Knowledge Distillation
lessons.interviewAnswer: Pruning removes low-value parameters or structure; distillation trains a smaller student to mimic a larger teacher. Both can reduce serving cost, but structured pruning usually maps to hardware better than arbitrary sparsity, and distillation quality depends on the teacher targets and task.

teacher/student
soft targets
hardware-aware speedup
lessons.description: Pruning & Knowledge Distillation is a core topic in AI / ML Performance & Scaling. Parameter count is not the same as real latency. Compression methods matter only if the runtime can exploit them. This chapter turns the interview-level summary into a complete engineering and analytical treatment. The starting mental model is: Pruning asks “what can I remove?” Distillation asks “can a smaller model learn the useful behavior of the bigger one?”. The formal and implementation discussion builds from unstructured vs structured pruning, teacher/student, soft targets, hardware-aware speedup, while keeping the unit of data, objective, assumptions, and failure boundaries explicit. lessons.title: Big-O Time & Space Complexity
lessons.interviewAnswer: Big-O gives an asymptotic upper bound on how resource use grows with an input-size variable under a stated computation model. Big-Theta is a tight bound and Big-Omega a lower bound. I separately state worst, expected, or amortized behavior and analyze both time and auxiliary space. Complexity removes constants and lower-order terms, so it is ideal for scalability comparisons but must be combined with representative profiling, memory traffic, and real input sizes for an engineering decision.
keyPoints: Define the size variable
State bound and case
Count dominant repeated work
Analyze auxiliary and output space
Measure constants at real scale
lessons.description: Complexity analysis predicts how an algorithm's resource demand grows as a chosen input parameter grows. It is a mathematical model, not a stopwatch result and not a complete performance verdict. This chapter develops Big-O, Big-Omega, and Big-Theta from explicit bounds; separates best, worst, expected, and amortized analysis; and shows how to count loops, recursion, sorting, hashing, and memory. You will learn to choose the correct size variable, account for input representation and output size, recognize hidden work in library calls, and compare algorithms under a stated machine model. A worked deduplication example contrasts a quadratic repeated scan with an expected-linear hash-based pass while keeping hashing assumptions visible. The engineering sections connect asymptotic reasoning to cache behavior, allocation, vectorization, network I/O, tail latency, and profiling. The objective is not to chant a complexity table. It is to produce a defensible growth model, identify the term that will dominate at relevant scale, validate that model with representative measurements, and know when constant factors, data distribution, or a different bottleneck changes the operational choice.
learningObjectives: Derive asymptotic time and auxiliary-space bounds from loops, recurrences, and composed operations.
Distinguish upper, lower, tight, worst-case, expected, and amortized claims without mixing their assumptions.
Relate an asymptotic model to profiling evidence, memory limits, latency objectives, and production input distributions.

lessons.title: Hash Tables, Sets & Dictionaries
lessons.interviewAnswer: A hash table maps a key's hash into table locations and resolves collisions by chaining or probing. With a suitable hash function and controlled load factor, lookup, insertion, and deletion are expected O(1), while worst case can be O(n) and resizing makes individual operations expensive. Equal keys must have equal stable hashes, so mutable equality-relevant state cannot change while a key is stored. Sets retain keys; dictionaries associate values. Production use also needs memory, eviction, normalization, concurrency, and adversarial-input policies.
keyPoints: Hash narrows the search
Collisions are inevitable
Equal implies equal hash
Load factor drives resizing
Bound state and key lifetime
lessons.description: A hash table implements a dynamic set or mapping by converting a key into an array location and resolving collisions among keys that land together. This chapter moves from a direct-address table to hashing, then explains hash/equality contracts, load factor, separate chaining, open addressing, resizing, expected versus worst-case cost, iteration semantics, and security concerns. It connects the abstract structure to Python dictionaries and sets without claiming that every implementation detail is a language guarantee. You will build a small chained table, use standard mappings for counting and deduplication, and verify collision, update, deletion, resizing, and duplicate behavior. The design sections extend beyond syntax to caches, joins, idempotency stores, and streaming deduplication, where lifetime and cardinality can matter more than lookup speed. By the end, you should be able to justify a hash table over an ordered structure, state what expected O(1) assumes, recognize an invalid mutable key, estimate memory and resize effects, and design bounds, normalization, concurrency, and observability for a production mapping.

Apply the equality-and-hash contract and distinguish language guarantees from implementation details.

lessons.title: Stacks, Queues & Heaps
lessons.interviewAnswer: A stack is last-in-first-out and supports push/pop at one end; a FIFO queue removes the earliest item; a deque supports efficient operations at both ends; and a heap-backed priority queue removes the smallest or largest priority. A binary heap is a partial order: the root is extreme, but the whole array is not sorted. Peek is O(1), push and pop are O(log n), and heap construction is O(n). In production, also define capacity, tie-breaking, concurrency, starvation, and overload behavior.
keyPoints: Removal rule selects the ADT
Deque for both ends
Heap maintains a partial order
Top-k uses bounded heap state
Queues require overload policy
lessons.description: Stacks, queues, deques, and heaps are small interfaces that encode different ordering policies. A stack exposes the most recently added item, a queue exposes the earliest waiting item, a deque supports both ends, and a priority queue exposes the item with the most urgent priority rather than the oldest arrival. This chapter connects those abstract data types to array and linked representations, Python lists and `collections.deque`, binary heap invariants, top-k streaming, stable tie-breaking, lazy deletion, and bounded backpressure. You will trace breadth-first and depth-first frontiers, build a min-heap from first principles, and use `heapq` without confusing a partial heap order with a sorted sequence. The systems section covers scheduler fairness, stale priority entries, queue overload, starvation, and metrics such as depth and wait time. The central skill is choosing a structure from the removal rule and required operations, then proving the invariant and lifecycle. Complexity tables matter, but correctness also depends on what happens when the structure is empty, full, concurrently mutated, or fed faster than consumers can drain it.

lessons.title: Trees, Graph Traversal, BFS & DFS
lessons.interviewAnswer: Represent a sparse graph with adjacency lists so storage is O(V+E). BFS uses a FIFO queue and explores by increasing edge distance, which gives shortest paths in an unweighted graph. DFS uses recursion or an explicit stack, explores one branch deeply, and supports connectivity, cycle detection, and topological ordering. Mark vertices discovered when they enter the frontier to avoid duplicate work. A full traversal is O(V+E) with adjacency lists; weighted shortest paths require another algorithm.
keyPoints: State graph semantics first
Adjacency lists suit sparse graphs
BFS gives unweighted distance
DFS exposes structure
Discovery state prevents repeated frontier work
lessons.description: Trees and graphs represent relationships, while traversal algorithms turn those relationships into an ordered exploration. This chapter defines vertices, edges, directedness, weights, paths, cycles, connected components, rooted trees, and common adjacency representations. It derives breadth-first search (BFS) and depth-first search (DFS), explains why BFS finds minimum-edge paths in an unweighted graph, and shows how DFS supports cycle detection and topological ordering in directed acyclic graphs. You will learn when to mark a vertex discovered, how parent and color state reconstruct results, why recursive DFS can overflow the call stack, and why a visited set does not automatically solve every graph problem. A worked dependency example performs topological validation and reports a cycle instead of returning a misleading order. Production sections cover graph size, high-degree vertices, duplicate edges, identity normalization, partial data, deterministic output, traversal limits, and graph stores. lessons.title: Sorting, Binary Search & Selection
lessons.interviewAnswer: Comparison sorting generally requires Omega(n log n) comparisons in the worst case. Stable sorting preserves the input order of equal keys, which matters for multi-key workflows. Binary search reduces boundary lookup in a sorted or otherwise monotonic domain to O(log n), but the invariant and duplicate policy must be explicit; insertion into a Python list remains O(n). For top-k or kth selection, avoid a full sort when a heap or partition algorithm meets the contract. Production design also considers memory, I/O, determinism, missing values, and concurrent mutation.
keyPoints: Order contract before algorithm
Stable ties preserve prior order
Binary search finds a boundary
Search O(log n), insertion O(n)
Partial answers can avoid full sort
lessons.description: Sorting converts an unordered collection into an order that supports merging, grouping, range queries, deterministic output, and binary search. Binary search is broader than exact lookup: it finds a boundary in a monotonic predicate, provided the invariant and interval convention are correct. Selection algorithms and bounded heaps can answer kth-element or top-k questions without fully sorting all input. This chapter derives comparison-sort limits, contrasts stable and unstable algorithms, explains Python's key-based stable sorting, traces lower-bound binary search with duplicates, and distinguishes O(log n) search from O(n) insertion into an array. It also covers partial selection, external sorting, non-comparison sorting assumptions, floating-point and missing-value order, and concurrent mutation. You will implement stable merge sort and a left-bound search, use `sorted`, `bisect`, and `heapq`, and verify permutation, ordering, stability, and boundary properties. The engineering goal is to choose the least work that satisfies the actual output contract while making ordering, tie, key, memory, and determinism semantics explicit.

lessons.title: Sampling & Streaming Algorithms
lessons.interviewAnswer: A streaming algorithm updates a bounded summary in one or few passes rather than storing all items. Reservoir sampling keeps k uniform positions from a stream of unknown length by retaining item t with probability k/t and replacing a random reservoir position. Count-min sketch uses multiple hashed counter rows; query returns the minimum counter, so it never underestimates nonnegative insertion-only frequency but can overestimate through collisions. These guarantees depend on randomness, hash, update, and window assumptions, and production needs replay-safe checkpoints and accuracy monitoring.
keyPoints: Bounded state changes the problem
Reservoir gives uniform positions
Sketches expose explicit error
Merge only compatible summaries
Window, replay, and identity are semantics
lessons.description: Streaming algorithms process items in one or a few passes while keeping state far smaller than the complete history. They are necessary when input is unbounded, arrives faster than storage queries can respond, or is simply too large to materialize. This chapter begins with exact one-pass aggregates, then derives reservoir sampling for a uniform fixed-size sample from an unknown-length stream. It explains how approximate sketches trade memory for controlled error, using count-min sketch as the main example and distinguishing one-sided frequency overestimation from unbiased sampling. You will learn how mergeability supports partitioned processing, why randomness and hash independence assumptions must be stated, how windows change the problem, and why a compact structure is not automatically correct under deletions or concept drift. A worked stream monitor maintains exact totals, a reservoir, and approximate heavy-hitter counts while preserving checkpointable state. Production sections cover event identity, ordering, late data, replay, deduplication, seed/version management, overflow, adversarial keys, accuracy audits, and fallback. The goal is to choose an explicit error and retention contract, not to use approximation merely because it sounds scalable.
learningObjectives: Derive reservoir sampling's inclusion probability and implement a reproducible fixed-size sample from an unknown-length stream.
Explain count-min sketch update, query, overestimation, width/depth trade-offs, and merge requirements.

lessons.labGoal: Build reservoir sampling and count-min sketch, then verify size, reproducibility, no-underestimation, merge compatibility, and approximate uniformity.
followUpQuestions: Why does reservoir sampling keep every position with probability k/n?
Why does count-min use the minimum counter?
Can exact distinct count use bounded memory for an unbounded universe?

lessons.title: A Systematic EDA Workflow
lessons.interviewAnswer: A systematic EDA starts with the business question, target population, unit/grain, time window, and source lineage. Then validate schema, keys, row counts, joins, duplicates, missingness, ranges, and reconciliation totals. Inspect univariate distributions, time patterns, relationships and subgroups on raw and meaningful transformed scales, while checking leakage and collection artifacts. Log observations and hypotheses separately, avoid causal or confirmatory claims from exploration, and turn the result into reproducible code, data-quality assertions, and a documented validation plan.
keyPoints: Question and grain come before plots
Data contracts and reconciliation precede statistical summaries
Exploration is multiplicity-rich and hypothesis-generating
Time, subgroup, and collection processes can dominate patterns
A reproducible audit is a deliverable, not a disposable notebook
lessons.description: Exploratory data analysis is a disciplined investigation of a dataset's provenance, structure, quality, distributions, relationships, time behavior, and fitness for a specific decision. It is not a hunt for attractive plots or significant correlations. This chapter builds a reproducible workflow from problem framing and grain through schema, joins, missingness, duplicates, ranges, univariate and multivariate views, target leakage, temporal splits, hypothesis logging, and handoff to confirmatory analysis. You will learn to distinguish discovery from validation, use invariants and reconciliation totals, inspect both raw and transformed scales, detect subpopulation and collection effects, and turn observations into testable follow-ups rather than causal claims. The worked example audits an orders-and-customers dataset whose duplicated join silently changes the business population. The lab builds a dependency-light profiling report, compares it with pandas, and verifies row, uniqueness, missingness, and range contracts. Production guidance covers snapshots, lineage, privacy, compute budgets, notebooks versus pipelines, review, monitoring, and rollback. The aim is an EDA artifact another analyst can reproduce, challenge, and safely build upon.
learningObjectives: Frame EDA around a target population, estimand or decision, unit of analysis, and data-generating process.
Audit schema, grain, keys, joins, missingness, duplicates, ranges, distributions, dependence, and time before modeling.
Separate exploratory hypotheses from confirmatory evidence and prevent leakage, selection, and multiplicity from contaminating conclusions.
Produce a reproducible EDA report with invariants, lineage, limitations, and explicit next actions.
lessons.labGoal: Build a small reproducible table profiler, compare key summaries with pandas, and verify grain, missingness, range, and category contracts.
followUpQuestions: What is the first thing you check in a new dataset?
How do you prevent EDA from becoming p-hacking?
What should leave the notebook?

lessons.title: Distributions, Skewness & Outliers
lessons.interviewAnswer: I inspect distributions with quantiles, robust and classical summaries, histograms plus ECDFs, and relevant transformations, conditioned on time and groups. An outlier is unusual under a reference model; it may be an error, a valid rare event, a new regime, a leverage point, or the case we most care about. I validate source units and lineage, use domain bounds and robust diagnostics, inspect influence on conclusions, and report sensitivity with and without justified corrections. I never delete points solely because a z-score or IQR rule flags them.
keyPoints: Shape and support matter beyond mean and variance
Plot tuning can create or hide apparent structure
Outlier status depends on reference and context
Leverage and influence are model-relative
Treatment decisions require lineage, domain knowledge, and sensitivity
lessons.description: Distribution analysis describes where values concentrate, how they vary, whether they are bounded, skewed, heavy-tailed, multimodal, discrete, zero-inflated, censored, or contaminated, and how those features change across populations and time. Outliers are observations unusual relative to a stated reference—not automatically errors to delete. This chapter compares mean/SD with median/IQR/MAD, histograms with ECDFs and KDEs, raw with transformed scales, z-scores with robust rules, and univariate with multivariate or contextual anomalies. You will learn to distinguish data errors, rare valid cases, regime shifts, leverage points, influential observations, and extreme values created by aggregation or selection; to use tail diagnostics and domain bounds; and to analyze results with and without consequential points. The worked example separates a currency-unit error from valid high-value orders. The lab implements robust summaries and IQR/MAD flags, verifies affine behavior, and compares with NumPy/pandas. Production guidance covers raw-value preservation, winsorization contracts, robust models, alerting, privacy, drift, and rollback.
learningObjectives: Characterize center, spread, shape, tails, support, modality, discreteness, and conditional distribution shifts.
Choose robust and classical summaries according to contamination, skewness, and decision loss.
Classify unusual observations as errors, valid rare cases, contextual anomalies, leverage, or influence before treatment.
Design sensitivity analyses and production controls that preserve evidence while limiting operational harm from extremes.
lessons.labGoal: Compute classical and robust distribution summaries, flag—not delete—unusual values, and verify translation/scale behavior against NumPy.

visualSummaries.title: Body and tail on one conceptual ECDF

followUpQuestions: Is an outlier necessarily bad data?
When prefer median to mean?
How do you assess whether a point is influential?

lessons.title: Missingness: MCAR, MAR & MNAR
lessons.interviewAnswer: Let R indicate whether a value is observed. MCAR means R is independent of observed and missing values; MAR means missingness may depend on observed data but not the missing value after conditioning; MNAR means it still depends on the unseen value or unobserved causes. These are assumptions about the data-generating process and MNAR versus MAR is generally not testable from observed data alone. I preserve missingness masks and reason codes, analyze patterns by time/source/covariates, choose design-consistent weighting or multiple imputation, prevent leakage, propagate uncertainty, and run MNAR sensitivity analyses.
keyPoints: Missingness is data with a mechanism and provenance
MAR is conditional, not 'random-looking'
Observed data cannot generally distinguish MAR from MNAR
Imputation model and analysis model must be congenial
Production missingness can shift and become informative
lessons.description: Missing data are generated by a process. MCAR, MAR, and MNAR describe conditional relationships between missingness indicators and data, not visual patterns a dataset can prove from observed cells alone. This chapter defines unit versus item nonresponse, structural versus censored missingness, Rubin's mechanisms, ignorability conditions, complete-case analysis, indicator methods, single and multiple imputation, inverse-probability weighting, likelihood-based estimation, and sensitivity analysis. You will learn why filling every null is not a solution, why outcome imputation must respect train/test and temporal boundaries, how missingness indicators can be predictive yet unstable, and why uncertainty from imputation must be propagated rather than treating guessed values as observed. The worked example contrasts lab tests ordered by severity with device-sensor outages. The lab simulates MCAR and outcome-related missingness, quantifies complete-case bias, applies a valid observed-covariate adjustment, and verifies assumptions. Production guidance covers reason codes, masks, imputation artifacts, monitoring, privacy, model serving, and rollback. The emphasis is defensible inference, not cosmetically complete tables.
learningObjectives: Define MCAR, MAR, and MNAR using missingness indicators and observed/unobserved data.
Distinguish structural absence, censoring, item nonresponse, unit nonresponse, and pipeline failures before choosing treatment.
Select complete-case, weighting, likelihood, or multiple-imputation methods with explicit assumptions and uncertainty propagation.
Design missingness diagnostics, sensitivity analyses, and production monitoring without leaking future or target information.
lessons.labGoal: Simulate MCAR and covariate-dependent missingness, quantify complete-case bias, and verify an observed-stratum adjustment under its assumptions.
followUpQuestions: Can you test whether data are MNAR?
When is a missing indicator useful?
Why use multiple rather than single imputation?

lessons.title: Choosing the Right Statistical Visualization
lessons.interviewAnswer: I start with the question: compare magnitude, see change over ordered time, inspect a distribution, relate variables, show composition, or locate geography. Then I map the most important quantitative comparison to aligned position or length; use lines only for ordered continuity, scatterplots for paired numeric observations, histograms/ECDFs for distributions, bars for category magnitudes, and small multiples for groups. I state aggregation and uncertainty, use honest scales and accessible redundant encodings, limit color, label units and denominators, and test the chart against raw data and audience decisions.
keyPoints: Task and data semantics determine the chart
Position and length support precise comparison
Aggregation and connection make statistical claims
Scales, baselines, and color carry meaning
Accessibility and uncertainty belong in the specification
lessons.description: Statistical visualization maps data fields and uncertainty to visual channels—position, length, angle, area, color, shape, texture, and facets—so a specific comparison becomes perceptually accessible. The best chart follows the analytical task, variable type, data grain, and audience; it is not chosen from a gallery by aesthetics. This chapter develops a task-first selection framework for distributions, trends, relationships, rankings, parts-to-whole, flows, geospatial patterns, and uncertainty. It explains perceptual accuracy, scales and transforms, overplotting, aggregation, small multiples, color semantics, accessibility, annotations, interactivity, and the distinction between raw observations, estimates, and model outputs. You will learn why bars need meaningful baselines, why line connections imply order, why area and angle comparisons are difficult, and how uncertainty must be encoded and labeled. The worked example redesigns a crowded multi-metric executive chart. The lab builds a declarative chart-spec validator and verifies task/type constraints alongside a matplotlib implementation. Production guidance covers semantic chart contracts, responsive design, accessible alternatives, testing, rendering, data freshness, privacy, and rollback.
learningObjectives: Choose a chart from the analytical task, field type, grain, ordering, and uncertainty rather than decoration.
Map high-priority comparisons to perceptually accurate channels and use facets or aggregation without hiding structure.
Select scales, baselines, color systems, labels, and accessibility features that preserve data meaning.
Design and test chart specifications as versioned semantic interfaces backed by data and metric contracts.
lessons.labGoal: Build a semantic chart-spec validator, reject misleading field/mark combinations, and render a verified bar chart with matplotlib.
followUpQuestions: When should a bar chart start at zero?
How do you show many overlapping points?
What should an uncertainty band say?

lessons.title: Misleading Charts & Visualization Pitfalls
lessons.interviewAnswer: I audit a chart at four layers: data and population; transformation, aggregation, denominator and filters; visual encoding, scale and baseline; and annotation/context. Common traps are truncated bar axes, 3D or area distortion, dual axes, cherry-picked windows, unequal time spacing, changing denominators, misleading bins/colors, overplotting, omitted uncertainty, and causal wording. I reconstruct the underlying table, compare alternate honest views, quantify how the claim changes, and add semantic tests so the correction is reproducible.
keyPoints: A chart inherits every upstream data and metric assumption
Visual geometry can amplify or suppress differences
Selection of windows, bins, groups, and annotations is analytical flexibility
Uncertainty and denominators are essential context
Semantic review complements pixel snapshots
lessons.description: Misleading visualization can arise from incorrect data, dishonest transformations, perceptual distortion, omitted context, or interaction defaults that selectively reveal a story. This chapter analyzes truncated baselines, distorted area and 3D perspective, dual axes, unequal time spacing, cumulative-versus-period confusion, cherry-picked windows, inappropriate smoothing, bin and color manipulation, denominator changes, map-area bias, missing uncertainty, overplotting, and deceptive annotation. You will learn to audit a chart by reconstructing its data transformation, scale, baseline, aggregation, filters, and encoding; distinguish intentional deception from harmful defaults; and design automated semantic checks alongside human review. The worked example deconstructs a dashboard where a truncated axis and changing denominator exaggerate a retention improvement. The lab implements chart-integrity checks for baselines, time order, denominator consistency, and proportional areas, then verifies them against deliberately bad specs. Production guidance covers metric lineage, query review, accessible exports, snapshot testing, issue severity, monitoring, and correction/rollback communication. Every published view should remain reconstructable from its data and specification.
learningObjectives: Trace a visual claim back through filters, aggregation, denominators, transformations, scales, and source data.
Recognize perceptual distortions from baselines, area/volume, dual axes, color, bins, smoothing, and map geometry.
Detect selection and context failures involving time windows, missing groups, uncertainty, and annotation.
Implement semantic visualization checks and correction workflows without assuming every misleading chart is malicious.
lessons.labGoal: Implement semantic integrity checks for baselines, time order, denominator stability, and area encoding, then verify detection on bad chart specs.
followUpQuestions: Are truncated axes always wrong?
Why are dual axes risky?
How do you automate chart integrity?

lessons.title: GroupBy, Pivot & Cohort Analysis
lessons.interviewAnswer: GroupBy is split–apply–combine: partition rows by keys, compute an operation per group, and return an output whose grain depends on aggregation, transformation, or filtering. I declare the output grain, null/category behavior, and additive components, then reconcile to source totals. Pivot reshapes a unique key combination; duplicates require an explicit aggregation, not accidental first value. For cohorts, assign each entity once, compute period age consistently, deduplicate entity-period activity, keep denominators tied to the original eligible cohort, and mark recent right-censored cells as unavailable rather than zero.
keyPoints: Every grouped result has a grain and key contract
Ratios should aggregate numerator and denominator
Pivot duplicates require an explicit rule
Cohort and calendar time are distinct axes
Censoring and late data define which retention cells are observable
lessons.description: GroupBy and pivot operations transform event-level rows into metrics at a declared output grain. Cohort analysis adds two time axes—when an entity entered and how long it has progressed—so lifecycle behavior is separated from calendar conditions. This chapter develops split–apply–combine semantics, aggregation versus transformation, multi-key grouping, observed versus unobserved categories, null-key handling, weighted rates, ratios of sums, pivot uniqueness, margins, cohort assignment, age calculation, right censoring, retention denominators, and reconciliation. You will learn why average of averages is usually wrong, why groupby can silently drop null keys, how duplicate entity-period rows inflate retention, and why incomplete recent cohorts must not be compared with mature cohorts. The worked example builds a monthly signup-retention matrix and diagnoses a denominator bug. The lab implements grouping and cohort retention from first principles, compares with pandas, and verifies totals, grain, and monotonic eligibility. Production guidance covers semantic models, incremental recomputation, late events, time zones, sparse output, privacy, monitoring, and rollback.
learningObjectives: Declare input and output grain for groupby, aggregation, transformation, and pivot operations.
Compute weighted rates and ratios from additive components without averaging subgroup averages incorrectly.
Construct cohort and age indices with stable entity assignment, mature denominators, and late-event handling.
Verify grouped outputs through reconciliation, uniqueness, category/null semantics, and incremental consistency.
lessons.labGoal: Build grouped rate and cohort retention logic from first principles, compare with pandas, and verify grain, reconciliation, distinctness, and maturity bounds.
followUpQuestions: What is the difference between aggregate and transform?
Why is average of averages wrong?
How do late events affect cohorts?

lessons.title: Sampling Distributions & Standard Error
lessons.interviewAnswer: A sampling distribution describes how a statistic would vary over repeated samples from the same data-generating process and design. Its standard deviation is the statistic's standard error. For an independent sample mean with finite variance, SE is sigma divided by square root n, estimated by s divided by square root n. That is different from the standard deviation of individual observations. The formula changes under clustering, time dependence, unequal weights, or finite-population sampling, and a small SE says nothing about selection bias.
keyPoints: Random data make estimators random before sampling
Standard error measures estimator variability, not raw spread
Independence and design determine effective information
Bias and variance are separate failure modes
Simulation can audit analytic uncertainty formulas
lessons.description: A sampling distribution is the probability distribution of a statistic over repeated samples generated by the same population and sampling design. It is the bridge from observed data to uncertainty about an estimator. This chapter separates the population distribution, the empirical distribution of one sample, and the sampling distribution of an estimator; derives the standard error of a mean; explains why standard deviation and standard error answer different questions; and shows how dependence, unequal weights, clustering, and finite populations change the calculation. You will learn when a central-limit approximation is credible, why an unbiased estimator can still be too noisy to use, and why a low standard error cannot repair selection bias. The worked example and lab simulate repeated samples so that sampling variability is visible rather than merely asserted. Production guidance covers unit-of-analysis mistakes, correlated observations, design-aware uncertainty, reproducible simulation, and monitoring effective sample size. The goal is to make every later interval, test, and power calculation rest on a clear data-generating and sampling model.
learningObjectives: Distinguish a population distribution, a sample distribution, and an estimator's sampling distribution.
Derive and interpret standard error for independent means and recognize when the square-root-n rule fails.
Diagnose how bias, dependence, weighting, clustering, and finite-population sampling affect uncertainty.
Estimate sampling uncertainty analytically or by simulation and verify the result against repeated samples.
lessons.labGoal: Simulate a sampling distribution, verify the analytic SE, and show how cluster dependence invalidates a row-level iid calculation.
followUpQuestions: Why is standard error usually smaller than standard deviation?
Can an estimator have zero standard error and still be wrong?
How would you estimate SE when no closed form is available?

lessons.title: Bootstrap & Resampling
lessons.interviewAnswer: The nonparametric bootstrap treats the empirical distribution as an estimate of the population: draw many size-n samples with replacement, recompute the entire estimator, and use the resulting distribution for standard errors or intervals. It works when the observed sample represents the repetition mechanism and the estimator is sufficiently regular. Resample the independent unit—pairs, users, clusters, or time blocks—not blindly rows. Bootstrap cannot repair selection bias, absent rare classes, or a fundamentally misspecified pipeline, and interval choice and Monte Carlo error must be reported.
keyPoints: Resampling approximates repeated sampling from an estimated population
Replacement preserves iid draws from the empirical distribution
The estimator must be recomputed end to end
Dependence determines the resampling unit
Coverage must be checked rather than assumed
lessons.description: The bootstrap estimates an estimator's sampling behavior by repeatedly sampling with replacement from the empirical distribution and recomputing the complete statistic. It is powerful because it can approximate standard errors, bias, and confidence intervals when analytic derivations are inconvenient, but it is not assumption-free. This chapter develops the plug-in principle, explains why replacement matters, distinguishes ordinary, paired, stratified, cluster, block, parametric, and residual bootstraps, and compares percentile, basic, normal, and bias-corrected accelerated intervals. You will learn when the empirical distribution is a reasonable stand-in for the population, why rare events and nonsmooth statistics cause instability, and why resampling rows breaks dependence. The worked example estimates a difference in medians while preserving treatment groups. The lab implements a bootstrap distribution from first principles, compares it with SciPy's current API, verifies reproducibility and interval behavior, and demonstrates the effect of sample size. Production guidance covers resampling grain, pipeline refitting, Monte Carlo error, seeds, compute budgets, privacy, and coverage audits.
learningObjectives: Explain the empirical plug-in principle and why bootstrap resamples have the original sample size with replacement.
Choose a resampling scheme that preserves pairing, groups, clusters, time dependence, weights, and model-fitting steps.
Compare common bootstrap interval constructions and diagnose skewness, bias, discreteness, and boundary failure.
Implement reproducible bootstrap uncertainty and verify it against simulation or an official library.
lessons.labGoal: Build a bootstrap confidence interval for a median, compare with SciPy BCa output, and verify reproducibility and narrowing with more data.
followUpQuestions: Why sample with replacement?
What does increasing B accomplish?
When would you use a block bootstrap?

lessons.title: Permutation & Randomization Tests
lessons.interviewAnswer: A permutation test compares an observed statistic with values obtained by shuffling in a way justified under the null. In a randomized experiment, reassign labels according to the actual assignment mechanism; in observational data, a label shuffle additionally requires exchangeability. Preserve pairs, blocks, clusters, and treatment counts. Exact enumeration is possible for small designs; otherwise sample permutations and use a correction such as (b+1)/(B+1). The p-value is valid for the specified statistic, null, design, and extremeness rule—not because permutation is automatically nonparametric.
keyPoints: Randomization mechanism can supply the null distribution
Exchangeability is a substantive assumption
Pairs, blocks, and clusters constrain valid transformations
The statistic determines sensitivity and two-sided ordering
Monte Carlo p-values have simulation uncertainty
lessons.description: Permutation and randomization tests build a reference distribution by applying transformations that are valid under a null hypothesis—often reallocating treatment labels or swapping paired signs—and comparing the observed statistic with that distribution. Their strength is transparent design-based calibration with few distributional assumptions; their danger is the casual belief that any labels may be shuffled. This chapter distinguishes Fisher randomization inference from observational permutation tests, defines exchangeability, shows exact and Monte Carlo tail calculations, handles paired and blocked designs, and explains studentization, ties, two-sided definitions, and the plus-one correction for sampled permutations. You will learn how interference, clustering, covariate-adaptive assignment, unequal variances, and data-dependent statistic selection invalidate naive shuffles. The worked example uses a randomized conversion experiment with a difference-in-means statistic. The lab enumerates a small exact test, compares it with SciPy, and verifies symmetry and p-value bounds. Production guidance covers assignment reconstruction, reproducible RNG, batch computation, audit logs, precision, and sequential use.
learningObjectives: Identify the exact transformation group justified by random assignment or exchangeability under the null.
Construct exact and Monte Carlo permutation distributions for independent, paired, blocked, and clustered designs.
Choose and predefine a statistic and two-sided extremeness rule appropriate to the alternative.
Diagnose invalid shuffles caused by dependence, unequal assignment, interference, or post-selection.
lessons.labGoal: Enumerate an exact two-sample permutation test, verify its tail calculation against SciPy, and preserve fixed group sizes.
followUpQuestions: What is exchangeability?
When is a permutation test exact?
Why studentize a permutation statistic?

lessons.title: Multiple Testing & False Discovery Rate
lessons.interviewAnswer: With m tests, individual alpha does not control the overall error. Bonferroni and Holm control the probability of at least one false rejection in a defined family; BH controls the expected false discovery proportion under its conditions and is usually more powerful when many discoveries are acceptable. For BH, sort p-values, find the largest k with p_(k)<=kq/m, and reject through k. Define the family before seeing results, account for dependence and selection, report adjusted values and effect sizes, and do not call FDR the probability each discovery is false.
keyPoints: Multiplicity begins with a declared family
FWER controls any false rejection; FDR controls expected false proportion
Holm dominates simple Bonferroni while retaining strong FWER control
BH is a step-up rule with dependence conditions
Adjustment does not repair biased tests or post-selection
lessons.description: Testing many hypotheses creates many opportunities for false discoveries. Multiplicity is not solved by interpreting each p-value in isolation; the analyst must define a family, choose an error criterion, and apply a procedure whose dependence assumptions and selection process match the problem. This chapter derives why unadjusted family-wise error grows, contrasts family-wise error rate with false discovery rate, explains Bonferroni, Holm, Benjamini–Hochberg, and Benjamini–Yekutieli ideas, and distinguishes adjusted p-values from local false-discovery probabilities. You will learn how hierarchical testing, gatekeeping, preregistration, holdout confirmation, and selective inference control different risks; why correlated tests complicate guarantees; and why adding hypotheses after looking changes the family. The worked example applies BH to ten feature metrics and interprets the rejection threshold. The lab implements Holm and BH from scratch, verifies monotonic adjusted values against SciPy, and checks invariants. Production guidance covers metric-family governance, lineage, online testing, dashboards, reproducibility, and audit of all attempted analyses.
learningObjectives: Quantify how repeated testing inflates the chance and number of false positives.
Choose between FWER and FDR according to the cost and volume of false discoveries.
Implement Bonferroni/Holm and Benjamini–Hochberg procedures with valid ordering and monotonicity.
Define hypothesis families and diagnose dependence, selection, and reporting practices that invalidate nominal control.
lessons.labGoal: Implement Holm FWER and BH FDR adjusted p-values, verify monotonicity, and compare BH output with SciPy.
followUpQuestions: When prefer FWER over FDR?
Why is Holm generally preferable to plain Bonferroni?
Does BH work under correlated tests?

lessons.title: Effect Size vs Statistical Significance
lessons.interviewAnswer: Effect size is the magnitude of the estimand—such as a 1.2 percentage-point lift, relative risk, mean difference, correlation, or standardized mean difference. A p-value combines magnitude with uncertainty and sample size, so a tiny effect can be significant in a huge sample and a useful effect nonsignificant in a small one. Report the effect in domain units first, its interval, baseline risk, and a predefined minimum worthwhile effect. Standardized measures aid comparison but depend on the chosen standard deviation and population.
keyPoints: Magnitude and evidence are separate
Domain units usually lead communication
Relative measures require baseline risk
Standardized effects depend on reference variability
Practical thresholds should be set before results
lessons.description: Effect size describes the magnitude of a difference or association; statistical significance describes how incompatible data are with a null model relative to sampling uncertainty. They answer different questions. This chapter covers raw effects, relative effects, standardized mean differences, correlations, odds and risk ratios, number needed to treat, and model-performance changes. It explains why standardization aids comparison but can hide domain meaning, how small-sample bias corrections such as Hedges' g work, and why odds ratios are often misread as risk ratios. You will learn to define a smallest effect of practical interest, pair estimates with uncertainty, distinguish clinical or business importance from detectability, and avoid interpreting noisy subgroup effect sizes without shrinkage. The worked example compares an accurately estimated tiny conversion lift with a larger uncertain one. The lab implements Cohen's d and Hedges' g, verifies scale/translation invariance, and checks against the raw mean difference. Production guidance covers estimand contracts, metric units, heterogeneous effects, decision curves, monitoring, and communication.
learningObjectives: Select raw, relative, standardized, or probability-scale effect measures that match the decision and outcome type.
Explain why p-values depend on effect magnitude, noise, sample size, and design while effect size is not significance.
Compute standardized mean differences with appropriate pooled variance and small-sample correction.
Interpret effects against predefined practical thresholds and report uncertainty, baseline risk, and heterogeneity.
lessons.labGoal: Compute Cohen's d and Hedges' g, verify translation/scale invariance, and keep the raw effect beside the standardized result.
followUpQuestions: Why can a tiny effect have a tiny p-value?
When prefer raw over standardized effect?
Why can odds ratio exaggerate intuition for common outcomes?

lessons.title: ANOVA & Comparing Multiple Groups
lessons.interviewAnswer: One-way ANOVA tests H0 that all group means are equal by comparing between-group mean square with within-group mean square. F=MS_between/MS_within, with k-1 and N-k degrees of freedom under the classical independent normal equal-variance model. A significant F says at least one mean differs; it does not identify which. Inspect residuals and design, use Welch ANOVA for unequal variances when appropriate, then apply prespecified contrasts or multiplicity-adjusted post-hoc tests and report effect sizes and intervals.
keyPoints: ANOVA partitions variability around the grand mean
The F statistic compares explained with residual variation
Omnibus rejection does not identify pairs
Residual independence and variance structure matter
Contrasts and post-hoc tests need multiplicity discipline
lessons.description: Analysis of variance tests whether group means exhibit more between-group variation than expected from within-group variation under a specified model. It avoids the uncontrolled multiplicity of running every pairwise t-test, but a significant omnibus F test says only that not all means are equal. This chapter derives the sums-of-squares decomposition and F ratio, explains degrees of freedom, effect sizes, diagnostics, planned contrasts, post-hoc comparisons, Welch ANOVA, nonparametric alternatives, and extensions to factorial and repeated-measures designs. You will learn why normality concerns residuals rather than raw outcomes, why independence is usually more important than mild normality, and why unequal variance with unbalanced groups can distort classical ANOVA. The worked example decomposes three campaign groups and follows the omnibus test with corrected comparisons. The lab computes one-way ANOVA from first principles, verifies decomposition and translation invariance, and compares with SciPy. Production guidance covers experimental units, contrast registries, assumptions, multiplicity, drift, and reporting estimates rather than only an F statistic.
learningObjectives: Derive between-, within-, and total sums of squares and explain the F ratio as signal relative to noise.
Interpret an omnibus rejection without claiming every group differs from every other group.
Choose classical, Welch, robust, permutation, or rank-based alternatives according to design and residual behavior.
Plan contrasts and adjust post-hoc comparisons while reporting group estimates, intervals, and effect sizes.
lessons.labGoal: Compute one-way ANOVA from first principles, verify the sums-of-squares identity and translation invariance, and compare F with SciPy.
followUpQuestions: Why not just run pairwise t-tests?
What does significant ANOVA tell you?
When use Welch ANOVA?

lessons.title: Chi-square Tests for Categorical Data
lessons.interviewAnswer: Pearson's chi-square statistic sums (observed-expected)^2/expected across categorical cells. For an r-by-c independence table, expected count is row total times column total divided by grand total and df=(r-1)(c-1), assuming independent units and adequate asymptotic counts. A significant result says the variables are associated, not which cells differ or that one causes the other. Inspect standardized residuals, report an effect size such as Cramér's V, adjust post-hoc analyses, and use exact or Monte Carlo methods for sparse tables.
keyPoints: Expected counts come from the null and fixed margins
Each cell contributes a squared standardized discrepancy
Degrees of freedom reflect marginal constraints
Sparse or dependent data break the usual reference
Association magnitude and cell pattern follow the omnibus test
lessons.description: Chi-square methods compare observed categorical counts with counts expected under a null model. The goodness-of-fit test asks whether one categorical distribution matches specified probabilities; the independence or homogeneity test asks whether two categorical variables are associated or whether group distributions agree. This chapter derives Pearson's statistic from standardized cell residuals, explains degrees of freedom and expected-count calculation, connects the contingency-table test with likelihood-ratio and log-linear models, and distinguishes association from causation. You will learn why tests operate on counts rather than percentages, when asymptotic calibration is unreliable, how sparse tables and structural zeros require exact, Monte Carlo, or category-restructuring approaches, and why a significant table needs cell-level residuals and effect sizes such as Cramér's V. The worked example analyzes channel by conversion status and identifies which cells drive the result. The lab computes expected counts and Pearson's statistic from first principles, verifies marginal preservation and decomposition, and compares with SciPy. Production guidance covers category contracts, rare-level handling, weighting, multiplicity, privacy, and drift.
learningObjectives: Distinguish chi-square goodness-of-fit, independence, and homogeneity questions and formulate their null models.
Compute expected counts, Pearson cell contributions, the total statistic, and correct degrees of freedom.
Diagnose sparse counts, structural zeros, dependence, sampling weights, and post-hoc cell inspection.
Report residual patterns and association magnitude without interpreting association as causation.
lessons.labGoal: Compute a Pearson independence test from scratch, verify expected margins and cell decomposition, and compare with SciPy.
followUpQuestions: How are expected counts computed for independence?
What if expected counts are small?
Does significant chi-square imply a strong relationship?

lessons.title: Power, Minimum Detectable Effect & Sample Size
lessons.interviewAnswer: Power is P(reject H0|a specified alternative is true), equal to 1-beta for a fixed design and test. Sample size grows with variance, stricter alpha, higher target power, and smaller effect—often approximately inverse-square in the detectable effect. Plan using the smallest effect worth acting on, realistic baseline/variance, independent unit, allocation, attrition, clustering, multiplicity, and stopping rule. MDE is what a design can reliably detect, not necessarily what matters. Do not use observed post-hoc power as new evidence; report the effect interval.
keyPoints: Power is a curve over alternatives, not one universal number
Effect threshold and variance drive sample size
Independent information matters more than row count
Design corrections must be included before launch
Simulation audits formulas for real metrics and pipelines
lessons.description: Statistical power is the probability that a prespecified procedure rejects its null under a particular alternative. Sample-size planning connects that operating characteristic to a meaningful effect, variance, alpha, allocation, design, attrition, and decision horizon. This chapter derives normal-mean scaling, distinguishes minimum detectable effect from minimum worthwhile effect, explains one- versus two-sided tests, unequal allocation, clustering, multiple testing, sequential designs, and simulation-based power for complex estimators. You will learn why post-hoc observed power adds little beyond the p-value, why plugging optimistic variance or conversion assumptions understates required sample size, and why increasing rows does not overcome correlation or bias. The worked example plans a two-arm conversion experiment in absolute percentage points and inflates for attrition and design effect. The lab implements an approximate two-sample proportion calculation, verifies monotonic relationships, and compares a t-test case with statsmodels. Production guidance covers preregistered assumptions, traffic forecasts, guardrails, simulation, re-estimation without unblinding effects, monitoring, and stopping behavior.
learningObjectives: Define power as a function of a specific alternative, procedure, design, and sample size.
Distinguish minimum detectable, minimum worthwhile, and observed effects in planning and interpretation.
Compute approximate sample sizes and adjust for allocation, clustering, attrition, multiplicity, and sequential monitoring.
Use simulation to validate analytic power for complex metrics and avoid post-hoc observed-power misuse.
lessons.labGoal: Compute approximate two-proportion sample size, verify monotonic design relationships, and compare an independent t-test case with statsmodels.
followUpQuestions: What happens to n if the target effect is halved?
Is 80% power always correct?
Why avoid observed post-hoc power?

lessons.title: Bayesian Updating: Prior, Likelihood & Posterior
lessons.interviewAnswer: Bayesian updating is posterior proportional to likelihood times prior: p(theta|y)=p(y|theta)p(theta)/p(y). The prior encodes assumptions before the current data, the likelihood is the data model, the evidence normalizes, and the posterior represents uncertainty conditional on both. Prediction integrates p(y_new|theta) over the posterior. Independent data batches can be updated sequentially, but duplicated or dependent evidence cannot be multiplied as if independent. Always check prior predictive implications, posterior sensitivity, model fit, and decision loss.
keyPoints: Bayes reverses conditioning through a generative model
The evidence normalizes and supports model comparison
Posterior uncertainty is conditional on model and prior
Prediction integrates rather than plugs in one parameter
Sequential updating requires correct conditional independence
lessons.description: Bayesian updating combines a prior distribution with a likelihood to produce a posterior distribution and then integrates that posterior to make predictions and decisions. The algebra is short, but responsible use requires clarity about what is conditioned on, how priors are chosen, which likelihood generated the data, and what uncertainty remains. This chapter develops Bayes' rule in odds and density form, separates prior predictive, posterior, posterior predictive, evidence, and likelihood, and explains sequential updating, exchangeability, sensitivity, and calibration. You will learn why the normalizing constant matters for model comparison but can be avoided by many samplers, why a posterior can be sharply wrong under misspecification, and how decision losses convert beliefs into actions. The worked example updates a Beta prior with conversion observations and computes the predictive chance of future successes. The lab implements a grid posterior from first principles, verifies it against the analytic Beta posterior, and checks normalization and sequential coherence. Production guidance covers prior governance, data lineage, numerical stability, monitoring, privacy, and rollback.
learningObjectives: Apply Bayes' rule in probability, odds, and density form while keeping conditioning directions correct.
Distinguish prior, likelihood, evidence, posterior, and posterior predictive distributions.
Perform coherent sequential updates and diagnose when order, dependence, or data reuse breaks the calculation.
Evaluate prior sensitivity, model misspecification, predictive calibration, and decision consequences before deployment.
lessons.labGoal: Build a grid posterior for a Bernoulli rate, verify it against the analytic Beta posterior, and test normalization and sequential coherence.
followUpQuestions: Why is the evidence often ignored in MCMC?
Does the prior always vanish with enough data?
What is the difference between posterior and posterior predictive?

lessons.title: Conjugate Priors
lessons.interviewAnswer: A prior is conjugate when the posterior stays in the same family after multiplying by a likelihood. Beta with Bernoulli/Binomial updates successes and failures; Gamma with Poisson updates shape by total counts and rate by exposure; Normal with known-variance Normal likelihood combines means by precision. Conjugacy gives exact, fast, sequential updates and useful test fixtures, but the likelihood and prior still need to fit the domain. Check rate-versus-scale conventions, predictive calibration, and whether drift or hierarchy requires a richer model.
keyPoints: Conjugacy is algebraic closure under updating
Sufficient statistics compress the evidence
Hyperparameters depend on parameterization conventions
Predictive distributions integrate parameter uncertainty
Computational convenience never replaces model criticism
lessons.description: A conjugate prior produces a posterior in the same distribution family as the prior for a chosen likelihood. Conjugacy turns Bayesian updating into hyperparameter arithmetic, making it valuable for intuition, streaming updates, exact benchmarks, and low-latency systems. It does not make a prior objectively correct or every model realistic. This chapter derives Beta–Binomial/Bernoulli, Gamma–Poisson, and Normal–Normal updates, interprets pseudo-counts and precision weighting carefully, and explains posterior predictive distributions, exponential-family structure, improper limits, and when conjugacy becomes a modeling trap. You will learn how parameterization conventions change formulas, why sufficient statistics enable constant-memory updates, how prior strength differs from sample size under heterogeneous data, and when mixtures or hierarchical priors preserve flexibility.
