The worked examples cover conversion and event-rate estimation. The lab implements Beta–Binomial and Gamma–Poisson updates, checks batch-order invariance, and verifies moments against SciPy. Production guidance covers parameterization tests, numerical bounds, nonstationarity, prior versioning, predictive calibration, and analytic fallbacks.
learningObjectives: Derive posterior hyperparameter updates for common conjugate likelihood–prior pairs.
Interpret hyperparameters through sufficient statistics without overclaiming literal prior sample size.
Compute posterior predictive distributions and distinguish them from plug-in likelihood predictions.
Recognize parameterization, support, misspecification, and nonstationarity cases where conjugacy should not drive model choice.
lessons.labGoal: Implement Beta–Bernoulli and Gamma–Poisson conjugate updates, verify batch-order invariance, and compare posterior moments with SciPy.
followUpQuestions: Why are conjugate updates easy to stream?
What is the predictive distribution for Beta–Bernoulli?
When should you leave conjugacy?

lessons.title: Credible Intervals vs Confidence Intervals
lessons.interviewAnswer: A 95% credible interval has 95% posterior probability for the parameter conditional on the model, prior, and observed data. A 95% confidence interval comes from a procedure that covers the fixed true parameter in 95% of repeated samples under its assumptions. The observed frequentist interval does not assign 95% probability to the parameter. Credible intervals may be equal-tailed or highest-density and depend on priors; confidence constructions differ too. Report the framework, estimand, method, assumptions, and practical thresholds, and evaluate both posterior sensitivity and repeated-sample calibration when useful.
keyPoints: Credible probability is conditional on model, prior, and data
Confidence is a property of a repeated-sampling procedure
Equal-tailed and highest-density sets answer different geometric summaries
Prediction includes observation noise beyond parameter uncertainty
Numerical similarity does not erase interpretive differences
lessons.description: Bayesian credible intervals and frequentist confidence intervals can have similar numerical endpoints while making different probability statements. A credible interval contains a specified posterior probability under a prior and likelihood. A confidence interval is generated by a procedure with stated repeated-sample coverage under a sampling model. This chapter builds both from the same binomial example, compares equal-tailed and highest-density credible sets, explains parameter transformations, nuisance parameters, posterior predictive intervals, and the circumstances in which Bayesian and frequentist intervals approximately agree. You will learn why neither framework is assumption-free, why optional stopping and selection require framework-specific care, how prior sensitivity affects sparse-data credible intervals, and why a 95% posterior interval is not automatically calibrated across repeated real datasets. The worked example contrasts a Beta posterior interval with Wilson confidence coverage. The lab computes equal-tailed posterior intervals, simulates frequentist coverage, and verifies transformation behavior. Production guidance covers naming, metadata, calibration, priors, sequential policies, decision thresholds, privacy, and communication.
learningObjectives: State the probability interpretation of credible and confidence intervals without mixing frameworks.
Construct equal-tailed and highest-density credible sets and contrast them with score or likelihood-based confidence intervals.
Distinguish parameter uncertainty from posterior predictive uncertainty and transform intervals coherently.
Evaluate prior sensitivity, frequentist coverage, calibration, selection, and stopping for deployed interval procedures.
lessons.labGoal: Compute a Beta credible interval, simulate its fixed-parameter coverage, and compare with a Wilson confidence interval.
followUpQuestions: Can a credible interval have 95% frequentist coverage?
Why might equal-tailed and highest-density intervals differ?
Which interval should a dashboard show?

lessons.title: MCMC & Posterior Sampling
lessons.interviewAnswer: MCMC constructs a Markov chain with the posterior as its stationary distribution, then estimates posterior expectations from retained dependent draws. Metropolis–Hastings accepts a proposal with the target-density and proposal-ratio correction; HMC uses gradients to propose distant moves and NUTS adapts trajectory length. Run multiple dispersed chains, separate warmup, and check rank-normalized split R-hat, bulk and tail ESS, Monte Carlo SE, trace plots, divergences, treedepth, and model-specific calibration. A high acceptance rate or long chain alone does not prove convergence, and thinning rarely fixes autocorrelation.
keyPoints: Stationarity does not guarantee finite-chain exploration
Dependent draws reduce effective information
Multiple diagnostics target different failures
Geometry and parameterization dominate sampler performance
Computation must be validated against known and simulated truth
lessons.description: Markov chain Monte Carlo approximates posterior expectations by constructing dependent draws whose stationary distribution is the target posterior. The central promise is asymptotic, while every real analysis uses finite chains that can fail to explore relevant modes or geometry. This chapter develops Metropolis–Hastings, Gibbs sampling, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, and the No-U-Turn Sampler; distinguishes warmup from retained sampling; and explains detailed balance, autocorrelation, effective sample size, Monte Carlo standard error, rank-normalized split R-hat, divergences, treedepth, energy diagnostics, and multimodality. You will learn why acceptance rate alone is not convergence, why thinning usually discards information, how centered versus noncentered parameterizations change hierarchical geometry, and how to validate an implementation against conjugate truth and simulation-based calibration. The worked example samples a one-dimensional Beta posterior, then contrasts its easy geometry with a funnel. The lab builds random-walk Metropolis, compares posterior moments with SciPy, and checks multiple-chain mixing. Production guidance covers deterministic seeds, chain parallelism, diagnostics gates, compute budgets, artifact storage, privacy, and safe failure behavior.
learningObjectives: Explain how a Markov transition kernel can leave a posterior invariant and why retained draws are dependent.
Implement Metropolis–Hastings and relate proposal scale to exploration, acceptance, and autocorrelation.
Interpret R-hat, bulk/tail ESS, Monte Carlo SE, divergences, treedepth, and trace diagnostics jointly.
Diagnose multimodality, funnels, constraints, initialization, and parameterization failures before using posterior summaries.
lessons.labGoal: Build random-walk Metropolis for a Beta target, verify moments and multiple-chain agreement, and quantify acceptance versus autocorrelation.
followUpQuestions: Why retain repeated states after rejection?
What is the difference between posterior SD and MCSE?
Why does noncentering help hierarchical models?

lessons.title: Hierarchical / Multilevel Models
lessons.interviewAnswer: A hierarchical model assumes group parameters come from a shared population distribution, then learns both group effects and population hyperparameters. It partially pools: a group estimate is pulled toward the population mean in proportion to its uncertainty, so small noisy groups shrink more than large precise groups. This improves average estimation and handles multiplicity, but relies on exchangeability and a credible group distribution. Check hyperpriors, centered versus noncentered geometry, outliers, group count, fairness, and prediction for new groups.
keyPoints: Partial pooling learns relatedness instead of choosing all-or-nothing pooling
Shrinkage strength follows relative within- and between-group precision
Exchangeability is a modeling claim
Hyperpriors regularize weakly identified group variation
New-group prediction integrates the population distribution
lessons.description: Hierarchical Bayesian models represent related groups with group-specific parameters drawn from a population distribution whose hyperparameters are learned from all groups. The result is partial pooling: noisy groups shrink more toward the population pattern, while well-observed groups retain more local information. This chapter contrasts no pooling, complete pooling, and partial pooling; derives Normal–Normal shrinkage; explains exchangeability, hyperpriors, varying intercepts and slopes, cross-level interactions, centered and noncentered parameterizations, new-group prediction, and the distinction between population-level variation and residual noise. You will learn why shrinkage reduces winner's curse and multiple-comparison noise, when it can erase real subgroup structure, how weakly identified group scales create funnels, and why groups with few levels need careful priors. The worked example estimates conversion rates across stores with unequal traffic. The lab implements analytic partial pooling for known variances, verifies limiting cases, and expresses the equivalent PyMC model. Production guidance covers group taxonomy, cold start, fairness, drift, diagnostics, posterior storage, privacy, and rollback.
learningObjectives: Distinguish complete, no, and partial pooling and connect each to assumptions about group variation.
Derive shrinkage weights from within-group uncertainty and between-group variance.
Specify varying-intercept and varying-slope models with defensible exchangeability and hyperpriors.
Diagnose funnel geometry, sparse groups, taxonomy drift, overshrinkage, and new-group predictive behavior.
lessons.labGoal: Implement Normal hierarchical shrinkage with known hyperparameters, verify limiting behavior, and express the equivalent PyMC model.
followUpQuestions: Which groups shrink most?
What is prediction for a new group?
When use noncentered parameterization?

lessons.title: Posterior Predictive Checks & Bayesian Model Criticism
lessons.interviewAnswer: Prior predictive checks sample parameters from the prior and then data, revealing whether assumptions imply plausible outcomes before fitting. Posterior predictive checks sample parameters from the posterior and replicated data from the likelihood, then compare summaries and structure with observations. They can reveal dispersion, tails, zeros, dependence, and subgroup failures but do not prove the model true. Also check MCMC diagnostics, prior sensitivity, simulation-based calibration for the algorithm, and held-out prediction. Predefine important checks, version revisions, and do not treat posterior predictive p-values like ordinary p-values.
keyPoints: Prior predictive checks criticize assumptions before data conditioning
Posterior replication asks whether fitted models reproduce relevant structure
Computation and model fit are separate gates
Discrepancies should reflect decisions and failure modes
Checking drives revision, not certification of truth
lessons.description: Bayesian model checking asks whether data generated from a fitted probability model resemble the observations in scientifically and operationally important ways. Prior predictive checks expose implications before fitting; posterior predictive checks compare replicated datasets with observed data after conditioning; simulation-based calibration audits inference algorithms; sensitivity analysis tests modeling choices; and held-out predictive evaluation measures generalization. This chapter explains what each check conditions on, how to choose discrepancy statistics and graphical diagnostics, why posterior predictive p-values are not ordinary uniform p-values, and how double use of data affects interpretation. You will learn to detect tail, dispersion, zero-inflation, dependence, subgroup, and calibration failures; separate computational from model criticism; compare models without treating one score as truth; and revise models without overfitting the checks. The worked example reveals overdispersion hidden by a Poisson mean fit. The lab generates prior and posterior predictive Beta–Binomial data, checks observed statistics, and verifies reproducibility. Production guidance covers check registries, acceptance gates, drift, privacy, reproducible artifacts, and rollback.
learningObjectives: Distinguish prior predictive, posterior predictive, simulation-based calibration, and held-out predictive checks by what is generated and conditioned on.
Design discrepancy statistics and plots that target domain-relevant aspects of the data rather than only global averages.
Separate sampler convergence from model adequacy and identify tail, dispersion, dependence, subgroup, and calibration failures.
Build a versioned model-revision workflow that avoids optimizing indefinitely against one reused check set.
lessons.labGoal: Generate prior and posterior predictive Bernoulli data, compare observed discrepancies, and verify reproducible predictive calibration checks.
followUpQuestions: What is the difference between prior and posterior predictive checks?
Does a good posterior predictive check prove the model?
What does simulation-based calibration test?

lessons.title: Linear Regression Assumptions & Diagnostics
lessons.interviewAnswer: I do not ask whether linear regression assumptions hold in the abstract; I ask which claim I need. For unbiased conditional coefficients, the central condition is E[epsilon|X]=0 with a correctly specified conditional mean and usable design rank. Homoskedasticity is mainly needed for the classical covariance formula, and normality mainly for exact small-sample inference. Dependence must match the sampling and covariance estimator. I inspect residual patterns, time or group structure, leverage and influence, not only a normality test. Then I address the cause: respecify the mean, use heteroskedasticity- or cluster-robust inference, model dependence, improve data, or narrow the target population. Diagnostics reveal sensitivity; they do not prove causality or future stability.
keyPoints: Assumptions support specific estimands, estimators, intervals, or deployment claims.
E[epsilon|X]=0 is more central to coefficient bias than residual normality.
Leverage is unusual X; residual is unusual Y given X; influence combines both.
Robust covariance changes uncertainty, not fitted coefficients or omitted-variable bias.
Dependence and selection must be represented in splitting and inference.
lessons.description: Regression assumptions are not a ritual checklist that makes a model valid after a few plots. They connect a particular estimand and inferential procedure to a data-generating and sampling process. This chapter separates assumptions needed for unbiased conditional-mean estimation, classical standard errors, prediction, and causal interpretation. You will reason about linearity in the conditional mean, exogeneity, independence or dependence structure, constant variance, rank, outcome tails, and measurement quality. Residual-versus-fitted, scale-location, quantile, leverage, studentized-residual, and Cook-distance diagnostics are explained as targeted probes rather than pass/fail tests. A worked example shows why a high-leverage observation can have a small residual yet materially move a coefficient. The lab computes the hat matrix diagonal, internally studentized residuals, and Cook's distance from first principles, cross-checks fitted values with scikit-learn, and verifies leverage and deletion behavior. Remedies are matched to causes: change the mean specification for nonlinearity, use an appropriate covariance estimator for variance misspecification, represent clusters or time dependence, improve measurement, or change the estimand. Robust standard errors do not repair bias, and deleting inconvenient points without provenance is not diagnosis.
learningObjectives: Map each regression assumption to the claim or calculation it supports.
Interpret residual, leverage, studentized-residual, and influence diagnostics jointly.
Choose remedies that address mean misspecification, variance, dependence, or data quality without conflating them.
Design diagnostics and monitoring that respect time, groups, selection, and deployment conditions.
lessons.labGoal: Compute residual, leverage, studentized-residual, and Cook-distance diagnostics from first principles and verify their geometric and deletion-sensitivity invariants.
followUpQuestions: What is the difference between an outlier and a high-leverage point?
Can OLS be useful under heteroskedasticity?
Why inspect residuals over time?

lessons.title: Ridge, Lasso & Elastic Net
lessons.interviewAnswer: Ridge minimizes squared error plus an L2 coefficient penalty, shrinking correlated or weakly identified directions continuously and improving stability. Lasso uses L1, whose corners can set coefficients exactly to zero, but selection may be unstable among correlated features. Elastic net combines both, often retaining correlated groups while remaining sparse. I standardize continuous features within each training fold, generally exclude the intercept from the penalty, tune alpha and l1_ratio with a split that matches deployment, and reserve a final test set. Regularization trades bias for variance; it does not fix leakage or confounding, and lasso's nonzero set should not be interpreted as a uniquely true or causally important feature list.
keyPoints: Ridge stabilizes all coefficients; lasso can produce exact zeros.
Elastic net combines grouping stability with sparsity.
Penalty strength depends on feature scale and library objective conventions.
Tune the whole preprocessing-plus-model pipeline on honest folds.
Sparse prediction and valid post-selection inference are different goals.
lessons.description: Ridge, lasso, and elastic net regularize linear models by charging for coefficient magnitude. They address variance, ill-conditioning, and high-dimensional representation, but they express different beliefs and produce different stability properties. This chapter derives the penalized objectives, explains ridge as continuous shrinkage, lasso as sparse soft-thresholding, and elastic net as a compromise that can keep correlated groups together. You will learn why scaling must be fit inside the training pipeline, why the intercept is usually not penalized, how cross-validation chooses predictive tuning parameters, and why lasso's selected variables are not automatically scientific discoveries. Coefficient paths and bias-variance trade-offs are connected to design geometry and Bayesian priors. A correlated-feature example shows ridge distributing weight while lasso may arbitrarily choose one representative. The lab implements ridge and coordinate-descent lasso from scratch, compares with scikit-learn, and verifies shrinkage, sparsity, permutation, and convergence invariants. Production guidance covers feature-order contracts, sparse schema evolution, convergence, tuning leakage, coefficient drift, challenger evaluation, and rollback. Regularization can stabilize a prediction system; it cannot create information, fix leakage, or make a conditional association causal.
learningObjectives: Compare ridge, lasso, and elastic-net objectives, geometry, and coefficient behavior.
Implement ridge and lasso mechanisms and verify their solutions against a trusted library.
Design leakage-safe scaling and cross-validation for regularization strength.
Explain why sparse selection can be unstable and why predictive tuning is not valid post-selection inference.
lessons.labGoal: Implement ridge and lasso coordinate descent on standardized data, compare with scikit-learn, and verify shrinkage, sparsity, permutation, and objective convergence.
followUpQuestions: Why does lasso produce exact zeros but ridge usually does not?
When would you prefer elastic net over lasso?
Can regularized coefficients have ordinary OLS p-values?

lessons.title: Polynomial Regression & Splines
lessons.interviewAnswer: Polynomial regression adds powers or other fixed basis functions to a linear model, so it is nonlinear in x but linear in coefficients. High-degree global polynomials are often unstable and extrapolate badly. A regression spline uses low-degree polynomial pieces joined at knots, usually with continuity constraints; B-spline bases provide the same function space with better local support and conditioning. I choose knots or a smoothness penalty inside cross-validation, keep the basis transformation inside the pipeline, inspect boundary and derivative behavior, and define an explicit extrapolation policy. Coefficients depend on the basis, so I interpret the fitted curve, contrasts, or derivatives rather than raw spline coefficients.
keyPoints: Nonlinear in predictors can still be linear in fitted coefficients.
Global polynomials couple the whole domain; splines provide local flexibility.
Knots define representation, while penalties or validation control effective complexity.
Basis coefficients are coordinate-dependent; interpret functions and contrasts.
Boundary support and extrapolation policy are production requirements.
lessons.description: Polynomial regression and splines extend linear regression to curved relationships while keeping estimation linear in coefficients. A raw high-degree polynomial is global: changing one coefficient can alter the curve everywhere, boundary behavior can become extreme, and powers can be badly conditioned. Regression splines instead join low-degree polynomial pieces at knots with continuity constraints, creating local flexibility. This chapter develops polynomial bases, truncated-power and B-spline representations, knot placement, natural boundary constraints, smoothing penalties, effective degrees of freedom, and honest complexity selection. You will distinguish interpolation from regression smoothing and understand why basis coefficients are usually less meaningful than the fitted function and its derivatives. A worked dose-response example shows how a cubic spline captures a plateau without forcing oscillation across the domain. The lab builds a truncated cubic regression-spline basis, uses scikit-learn's local B-spline transformer, and verifies continuity, rank, held-out error, and row-order invariance. Production guidance treats knots, boundaries, scaling, and extrapolation policy as versioned model state. Splines improve a conditional-mean specification over observed support; they do not solve confounding, sparse boundary data, or unsupported extrapolation.
learningObjectives: Explain why polynomial and spline regression remain linear in parameters while modeling nonlinear functions.
Construct a regression-spline basis and relate knots, degree, continuity, and effective flexibility.
Choose complexity using leakage-safe validation and diagnose unstable boundary or extrapolation behavior.
Deploy a basis transform with reproducible knots, scaling, and out-of-range behavior.
lessons.labGoal: Build a truncated cubic regression spline, use a local B-spline pipeline, and verify continuity, rank, row-order invariance, and nonlinear held-out improvement.
followUpQuestions: What is the difference between a regression spline and smoothing spline?
Why are B-splines numerically attractive?
How do you model a nonlinear interaction?

lessons.title: Generalized Additive Models (GAMs)
lessons.interviewAnswer: A GAM models a transformed conditional mean as g(E[Y|X])=beta0+sum_j f_j(X_j), where each f_j is a smooth function represented by a basis and controlled by a roughness penalty. It captures nonlinear marginal effects while preserving an additive structure that is easy to plot and audit. Smooths need centering constraints so the intercept and components are identifiable, and their effective degrees of freedom are selected by cross-validation, REML-like criteria, or related methods. I inspect residuals, boundaries, concurvity, and missing interactions; add tensor-product terms only when justified. Component curves are conditional associations under the fitted model, not causal effects, and deployment must freeze bases, penalties, and extrapolation behavior.
keyPoints: GAMs are additive in learned functions rather than necessarily linear in raw predictors.
Centering smooth components separates them from the intercept.
Penalties control wiggliness and effective degrees of freedom.
Concurvity makes component attribution unstable even when prediction is adequate.
Interactions and boundaries must be modeled and monitored deliberately.
lessons.description: A generalized additive model (GAM) replaces a single linear predictor with a sum of learned smooth component functions while retaining an additive, inspectable structure. In a Gaussian GAM, E[Y|X]=beta0+f1(X1)+...+fp(Xp); with a link function, the additive predictor can model binary, count, and other exponential-family outcomes. This chapter explains identifiability constraints, spline bases, roughness penalties, backfitting, penalized likelihood, effective degrees of freedom, smoothness selection, uncertainty, and the limits of additive interpretation. You will see how concurvity generalizes collinearity when one feature's smooth function can mimic another's, and how tensor-product or varying-coefficient terms add only the interactions the problem needs. A worked energy-demand example separates nonlinear temperature and hour effects while treating weekday as a linear factor. The lab constructs centered spline blocks, fits a ridge-penalized additive model, compares with a scikit-learn pipeline, and verifies additivity, column permutation, and held-out improvement. Production guidance versions each basis and penalty, monitors feature support and component contributions, and routes unsupported combinations. GAM plots are conditional model components, not automatically causal effects or raw-data averages.
learningObjectives: Formulate Gaussian and generalized additive models and explain component identifiability constraints.
Relate spline bases, roughness penalties, backfitting, and penalized likelihood to fitted smooth functions.
Diagnose overfitting, concurvity, missing interactions, boundary weakness, and misleading component plots.
Build and deploy an additive spline pipeline with reproducible component and support monitoring.
lessons.labGoal: Build a centered additive spline design, fit penalized components, compare with an idiomatic scikit-learn pipeline, and verify additivity, permutation, and nonlinear generalization.

visualSummaries.title: Stable prediction can hide unstable attribution

followUpQuestions: What is effective degrees of freedom in a GAM?
How is a GAM different from polynomial regression?
What is concurvity?

lessons.title: Poisson & Count Regression
lessons.interviewAnswer: Poisson regression assumes Y|X has mean mu and log mu=beta0+x^T beta, optionally plus log exposure as a fixed offset. Exp(beta_j) is the conditional multiplicative change in expected count or rate for a one-unit predictor change. The Poisson variance equals its mean, so I check dispersion, residuals, zero and tail calibration, dependence, and exposure construction. Overdispersion may call for robust or quasi-likelihood inference, negative binomial, random effects, or a better mean model; structural zeros may justify hurdle or zero-inflated models only when the process supports them. I evaluate deviance and operational count or rate error on temporal or grouped data and never use ordinary linear regression merely because counts look large.
keyPoints: The log link guarantees positive expected counts and yields rate ratios.
Log exposure is an offset with fixed coefficient one.
Poisson equidispersion is a conditional variance assumption, not a data-summary rule.
Overdispersion has multiple causes and does not dictate one universal alternative.
Validate zeros, tails, dependence, and operational capacity as well as mean deviance.
lessons.description: Poisson regression is a generalized linear model for nonnegative event counts. It models log expected count as a linear predictor, which guarantees positive means and gives multiplicative rate interpretations. The model becomes especially useful when observations have unequal exposure: a fixed log-exposure offset converts counts into rates without treating opportunity as an estimated effect. This chapter derives the Poisson likelihood, score, Hessian, deviance, and iteratively reweighted fitting; distinguishes coefficients on count, rate, and response scales; and explains equidispersion, overdispersion, underdispersion, excess zeros, dependence, and truncation. You will compare Poisson, quasi-Poisson covariance, negative-binomial, hurdle, and zero-inflated reasoning without selecting a model from the fraction of zeros alone. A worked incident example shows how to interpret an exposure-adjusted coefficient. The lab fits Poisson regression with an offset from first principles, compares it with scikit-learn's weighted-rate formulation, and verifies exposure and row-order invariants. Production guidance versions exposure units, count windows, and offset rules; monitors deviance, rate calibration, tail error, zero frequency, and capacity impact. A count model describes conditional event intensity—it does not automatically model distinct events, independence, causality, or future process stability.
learningObjectives: Formulate and fit a Poisson GLM with a log link and exposure offset.
Interpret coefficients as conditional rate ratios and compute response-scale contrasts.
Diagnose overdispersion, excess zeros, dependence, truncation, and exposure errors.
Choose and validate alternative count models based on a data-generating mechanism and deployment loss.
lessons.labGoal: Fit an exposure-offset Poisson model with Newton updates, compare with scikit-learn's weighted-rate formulation, and verify rate, exposure, likelihood, and row-order invariants.

visualSummaries.title: Different sources of extra zeros or variance

followUpQuestions: What does a Poisson coefficient exponentiate to?
When is negative binomial useful?
How do robust standard errors differ from a negative-binomial model?

lessons.title: Robust Regression
lessons.interviewAnswer: Robust regression limits how much atypical observations can dominate a fit. Huber regression uses squared loss for small standardized residuals and linear loss for large ones, often fit by iteratively reweighted least squares; least absolute deviations targets the conditional median, Theil-Sen uses robust slope aggregation, and RANSAC fits consensus subsets. These methods have different estimands and assumptions. A residual-robust loss does not necessarily protect against a high-leverage x point that pulls the line toward itself, so I inspect design support and influence too. I tune the robustness threshold on honest data, compare ordinary and robust fits, investigate provenance, and monitor the fraction and identity of downweighted cases rather than deleting them silently.
keyPoints: Squared loss gives unbounded residual influence; robust losses limit tail contribution.
Huber combines efficient quadratic behavior near zero with linear tails.
Residual robustness and leverage robustness are different problems.
Robust estimators may target means, medians, or consensus relationships differently.
Downweighted observations remain operational signals and require provenance review.
lessons.description: Robust regression reduces the sensitivity of a fitted relationship to contaminated outcomes, heavy tails, and atypical observations. Ordinary least squares squares residuals, so one large miss can dominate the objective. Robust methods change the loss, weighting, or sampling mechanism: Huber M-estimation is quadratic near zero and linear in the tails; least absolute deviations targets a conditional median; Theil-Sen aggregates pairwise slopes; and RANSAC searches for a consensus subset under a declared inlier rule. This chapter explains influence functions, breakdown intuition, scale estimation, iteratively reweighted least squares, and why protection against large residuals does not automatically protect against high-leverage predictor contamination. You will distinguish a data error from a valid rare case and a changed population, compare estimands rather than treating every robust method as interchangeable, and evaluate central and tail performance on clean and stress scenarios. The lab implements Huber iteratively reweighted least squares, compares with scikit-learn, and verifies recovery, bounded sensitivity, and permutation invariants. Production guidance preserves raw-event provenance, logs robust weights, monitors contamination and support, and avoids silently hiding incidents that should trigger investigation.
learningObjectives: Explain how squared, absolute, and Huber losses respond to residual magnitude and which conditional functional they target.
Implement Huber iteratively reweighted least squares and assess sensitivity to response contamination.
Distinguish vertical outliers, high leverage, influence, breakdown, and valid rare populations.
Select and monitor robust methods using provenance, stress tests, and operational loss rather than automatic outlier removal.
lessons.labGoal: Implement Huber iteratively reweighted least squares, compare with scikit-learn, and verify recovery, bounded response sensitivity, and row-order invariance.
followUpQuestions: What controls the Huber robustness-efficiency trade-off?
How is RANSAC different from Huber regression?
What is a breakdown point?

lessons.title: Quantile Regression
lessons.interviewAnswer: Quantile regression models Q_tau(Y|X=x)=x^T beta_tau by minimizing pinball loss rho_tau(r)=tau r for positive residuals and (tau-1)r for negative residuals. Tau 0.5 gives median regression; a high tau targets the conditional upper tail and can reveal effects hidden by mean regression under heteroskedasticity. I fit several declared quantiles, validate pinball loss and exceedance calibration on temporal or grouped data, inspect feature-conditional calibration and crossing, and regularize or use noncrossing methods when needed. A pair of fitted quantiles is not automatically a guaranteed prediction interval, especially after adaptive tuning or distribution shift, and coefficients remain conditional associations unless causal identification is supplied.
keyPoints: Pinball loss asymmetrically prices under- and overprediction for a selected quantile.
Different tau values describe different parts of the conditional outcome distribution.
Quantile coefficients can vary under heteroskedasticity or shape change.
Separately fit quantiles may cross and require joint constraints or post-processing.
Validate exceedance rates conditionally and operationally, not only in aggregate.
lessons.description: Quantile regression estimates a chosen conditional quantile of an outcome rather than its conditional mean. At tau=0.5 it minimizes absolute residual loss and models the conditional median; at tau=0.9 it describes a high conditional outcome boundary. This chapter derives the asymmetric pinball loss, linear-program formulation, coefficient interpretation, sampling uncertainty, and the way multiple quantiles reveal heteroskedasticity and distributional shape. You will distinguish a conditional quantile curve from a marginal percentile, an individual prediction interval, and a conformal coverage guarantee. The chapter treats quantile crossing, tail data scarcity, regularization, censoring, dependence, and calibration over feature and time slices. A worked delivery-time example shows how traffic may have a modest median effect but a much larger upper-tail effect. The lab solves linear quantile regression with SciPy's linear programming interface, compares it with scikit-learn, and verifies pinball optimality, response translation, and empirical calibration. Production guidance versions tau, scaling, penalty, solver, and crossing policy; monitors exceedance rates, interval width, tail loss, subgroup behavior, and operational capacity. Quantile regression is robust to large response residuals relative to squared loss, but not immune to leverage, selection, unsupported tails, or causal confounding.
learningObjectives: Derive the pinball-loss objective and formulate linear quantile regression as a linear program.
Interpret quantile-specific coefficients and explain what coefficient differences reveal about conditional shape.
Diagnose quantile crossing, tail scarcity, leverage, censoring, and conditional miscalibration.
Build and monitor quantile forecasts and intervals without overstating marginal or finite-sample coverage.
lessons.labGoal: Solve linear quantile regression as a linear program, compare with scikit-learn, and verify pinball optimality, translation equivariance, and empirical quantile behavior.

visualSummaries.title: Model-based quantile band versus coverage guarantee

followUpQuestions: Why do quantile-regression lines cross?
How does median regression differ from robust mean regression?
Why are extreme quantiles difficult?

lessons.title: Hierarchical Clustering
lessons.interviewAnswer: Agglomerative hierarchical clustering starts with one cluster per observation and repeatedly merges the pair with smallest linkage distance, producing a dendrogram rather than one fixed partition. Single linkage uses the closest cross-cluster pair and can chain through bridges; complete uses the farthest and favors compact clusters; average uses mean pairwise distance; Ward merges the pair with the smallest increase in within-cluster squared error and is tied to Euclidean geometry. Cutting the dendrogram at a height or cluster count yields a partition. Results depend on scaling, distance, linkage, ties and outliers, and greedy merges cannot be undone. I inspect cophenetic or stability diagnostics, compare cuts with downstream purpose, bootstrap the hierarchy, and avoid treating branch height as time or probability.
keyPoints: A dendrogram encodes a nested sequence of greedy merges; a flat clustering is obtained only after choosing a cut.
Linkage defines distance between clusters and strongly determines shape, chaining and outlier behavior.
Ward linkage minimizes the increase in squared within-cluster dispersion and requires appropriate Euclidean features.
Early erroneous merges are irreversible, and ties can produce implementation-dependent hierarchies.
Branch order and cluster numbers are arbitrary; merge height is dissimilarity under the chosen linkage, not certainty.
lessons.description: Hierarchical clustering builds a nested tree of observations by greedily merging clusters under a linkage rule. This chapter develops agglomerative clustering, dendrogram interpretation, single, complete, average and Ward linkage, and the Lance-Williams perspective on updating distances. It derives Ward's increase in within-cluster sum of squares and explains chaining, compactness, scaling, outliers, ties, connectivity constraints and irreversible early merges. Practical sections cover choosing a cut, cophenetic distortion, silhouette and external utility, bootstrap stability, consensus, large-n memory and approximate alternatives. Worked examples compute three linkage distances and show how one bridge point collapses single linkage. The lab implements agglomerative merging from a distance matrix, compares a Ward partition with scikit-learn, and verifies nesting, merge count and label-permutation invariance. Production guidance versions distance, linkage, cut and leaf identity, monitors assignment support, aligns hierarchies across retrains and defines fallback and rollback. A dendrogram is treated as one model of multiscale similarity, not a discovered organizational chart.
learningObjectives: Compute and contrast single, complete, average and Ward linkage distances.
Interpret a dendrogram and derive flat clusters from an explicit cut.
Diagnose chaining, scaling, outlier, tie and irreversible-merge behavior.
Validate and operate a hierarchy using stability, utility and identity controls.
lessons.labGoal: Implement agglomerative average linkage, compare a Ward cut with scikit-learn, and verify merge and partition invariants.
followUpQuestions: Why does single linkage find irregular shapes?
What does a dendrogram height mean?
How do you compare hierarchies across retrains?

lessons.title: DBSCAN & Density-based Clustering
lessons.interviewAnswer: DBSCAN defines dense regions using an epsilon neighborhood and min_samples. A core point has at least min_samples total weight or points in its eps-neighborhood, commonly including itself. Clusters expand through chains of core points; border points lie within eps of a core but are not themselves core, and remaining points are labeled noise. This finds irregular shapes and does not require k, but one global density threshold struggles with varying densities. Scaling and metric are part of the model, eps is unit-dependent, and border assignment can be order-sensitive. I inspect k-distance plots only as diagnostics, tune with stability and intended use, distinguish noise from anomaly, benchmark neighbor-search memory, and monitor core fraction, noise rate and support drift.
keyPoints: Core, border and noise are density-reachability roles under one metric, eps and min_samples.
Clusters can follow arbitrary connected shapes because expansion chains through core neighborhoods.
A global eps cannot represent all varying-density structures, and high dimension weakens neighborhoods.
Noise means not density-reachable under the fitted settings, not inherently fraudulent or erroneous.
Neighbor-search implementation and eps can produce quadratic memory or latency at scale.
lessons.description: DBSCAN discovers clusters as connected regions of sufficient local density and labels unsupported observations as noise. This chapter defines epsilon neighborhoods, core, border, direct density reachability, density connectivity and noise, then relates the algorithm to a radius-neighbor graph. It explains arbitrary-shape recovery, bridge effects, varying densities, scaling, custom metrics, high-dimensional distance concentration, sample weights, duplicate points, border ambiguity and parameter diagnostics. Worked examples expand a cluster by hand and show why one global eps cannot serve dense and sparse regions. The lab implements DBSCAN from a distance matrix, compares labels with scikit-learn and verifies core, noise, permutation and connectivity invariants. Production guidance covers neighbor-index memory, fit-only prediction semantics, reference-set versioning, support scores, monitoring, poisoning, fallbacks and rollback. Noise is interpreted carefully as failure to satisfy the chosen density model, not a universal anomaly label. You will also learn why border assignments can be ambiguous, how oversampling changes local density, and how a conservative core-based rule can extend a transductive fit to future queries.
learningObjectives: Apply core, border, reachability and noise definitions to a neighborhood graph.
Explain eps, min_samples, metric, scaling and density-variation effects.
Implement and validate DBSCAN while respecting border and label ambiguity.
Design scalable neighbor search and explicit new-point assignment with monitoring and fallback.
lessons.labGoal: Implement DBSCAN expansion from a distance matrix, compare with scikit-learn, and verify core, noise and connectivity invariants.
followUpQuestions: Core versus border point?
Why can border assignment be ambiguous?
When use OPTICS?

lessons.title: Gaussian Mixture Models & EM
lessons.interviewAnswer: A Gaussian mixture models density as p(x)=Σ_k π_k N(x|μ_k,Σ_k) with latent component membership. EM alternates responsibilities r_ik proportional to π_k N(x_i|μ_k,Σ_k) and weighted maximum-likelihood updates for π, means and covariances. Each iteration does not decrease observed-data likelihood, but solutions are local, labels can permute, and unconstrained covariance can collapse around a point with unbounded likelihood. Covariance regularization, adequate component support and repeated initialization are essential. Unlike k-means, GMM provides soft assignments and elliptical covariance, but a component is not automatically a real class. I select covariance structure and component count using held-out likelihood, BIC plus stability and purpose, evaluate calibration of responsibilities cautiously, and monitor log likelihood, weights, covariance conditioning and support drift.
keyPoints: Mixture weights, means and covariances define a density; responsibilities are posterior component probabilities under that model.
EM alternates posterior expectation of latent assignments and weighted maximum-likelihood parameter updates.
Likelihood is nonconvex, component labels are interchangeable, and covariance collapse creates singular solutions.
Covariance type controls geometric flexibility and parameter count: spherical, diagonal, tied or full.
Component count and semantic interpretation require external evidence beyond likelihood improvement.
lessons.description: Gaussian mixture models represent a density as a weighted sum of Gaussian components with latent membership. This chapter derives posterior responsibilities and every expectation-maximization update, explains the evidence lower-bound argument for monotone likelihood ascent, and distinguishes observed likelihood from complete-data likelihood. It covers spherical, diagonal, tied and full covariance, parameter counts, initialization, local optima, label switching, singular covariance collapse, regularization, component death, soft versus hard assignment, sampling, held-out likelihood, AIC, BIC and variational alternatives. Worked examples calculate responsibilities and demonstrate covariance collapse. The lab implements one-dimensional EM in log-stable form, compares fitted means and likelihood with scikit-learn, and verifies normalized responsibilities, monotone likelihood and label-permutation alignment. Production guidance versions transforms and components, monitors likelihood, mixture weights, covariance eigenvalues and support, aligns identities, protects density traces and supports fallback and rollback. Components are treated as approximation units until domain evidence justifies semantic labels. You will also learn why a density component need not equal a population, how regularization prevents unbounded solutions, and why component identities must be aligned before dashboards or downstream policies consume them.
learningObjectives: Derive GMM responsibilities and weighted EM updates.
Explain likelihood ascent, local optima, label switching and singular covariance failure.
Select covariance structure and component count using held-out and stability evidence.
Deploy a stable mixture with component alignment, support monitoring and safe fallbacks.
lessons.labGoal: Implement one-dimensional Gaussian-mixture EM, compare with scikit-learn, and verify responsibilities and monotone likelihood.
followUpQuestions: How is k-means related to GMM?
Why use log-sum-exp?
What is label switching?

lessons.title: t-SNE & UMAP for Visualization
lessons.interviewAnswer: t-SNE and UMAP create low-dimensional embeddings primarily for visualization by preserving neighborhood structure, not by preserving every global distance. t-SNE turns high-dimensional distances into adaptive Gaussian neighbor probabilities and low-dimensional distances into heavy-tailed Student-t similarities, then minimizes KL(P||Q); perplexity controls effective neighborhood scale and the nonconvex layout depends on initialization and optimization. UMAP builds a weighted k-neighbor graph from local distance scales and optimizes a fuzzy-graph cross-entropy; n_neighbors and min_dist control local context and packing. Apparent cluster size, spacing, orientation and sometimes separation can be artifacts. I fit preprocessing without label leakage, run multiple seeds and parameters, quantify trustworthiness and neighbor recall, color by metadata only after the embedding is fixed, and never cluster or make production decisions from a pretty map alone.
keyPoints: Both methods optimize neighborhood representations; two-dimensional Euclidean distance is not a faithful copy of all original geometry.
t-SNE perplexity and UMAP n_neighbors control the neighborhood scale included in the objective.
Nonconvex optimization, initialization and random seeds can change layout while preserving similar local relations.
Cluster size, empty space and axis orientation in the map have weak or no direct original-space meaning.
Visualization must be validated with neighbor metrics, sensitivity runs and original-space evidence before interpretation.
lessons.description: t-SNE and UMAP turn high-dimensional neighborhoods into two- or three-dimensional exploratory maps. This chapter derives t-SNE's adaptive Gaussian affinities, perplexity, symmetrization, Student-t low-dimensional kernel and asymmetric KL objective, explaining crowding and early exaggeration. It then develops UMAP's nearest-neighbor graph, local connectivity, fuzzy memberships, cross-entropy, negative sampling, n_neighbors and min_dist. Practical sections cover scaling, PCA initialization, metrics, seeds, sampling density, disconnected graphs, global-distance and density distortions, transform semantics, parametric alternatives, trustworthiness, continuity, neighbor recall and visual leakage. Worked examples show why cluster gaps and apparent size can be misleading. The lab computes trustworthiness for PCA and t-SNE embeddings, checks determinism under a fixed seed and verifies that local-neighbor preservation is measurable rather than assumed. Production guidance versions embeddings and reference data, monitors neighbor quality and drift, protects coordinates and supports rollback. These methods are treated as visualization algorithms whose claims must return to original space. You will also learn how label-guided parameter selection contaminates exploratory evidence, why unaligned refits create false motion, and how approximation recall and sample density affect the visible neighborhood graph.
learningObjectives: Explain the high- and low-dimensional similarity objectives of t-SNE and UMAP.
Interpret perplexity, n_neighbors, min_dist, initialization and seed sensitivity.
Reject unsupported claims about axes, global distance, density and cluster truth.
Validate embeddings quantitatively and procedurally before communicating patterns.
lessons.labGoal: Create PCA and t-SNE maps, quantify trustworthiness, and verify fixed-seed reproducibility and finite coordinates.
followUpQuestions: What does t-SNE perplexity mean?
Why use a Student-t kernel in low dimension?
How do you validate a map?

lessons.title: Density Estimation & KDE
lessons.interviewAnswer: Density estimation learns a probability density p(x), not a class boundary. A histogram approximates density with bins; kernel density estimation places a normalized kernel at each observation: p_hat_h(x)=1/(nh^d)Σ_i K((x-x_i)/h). Bandwidth h controls smoothing—too small produces spiky high-variance estimates, too large erases modes. Kernels matter less than bandwidth in many low-dimensional settings, but boundaries, scaling and dimension matter greatly. Density values are unit-dependent and often counterintuitive in high dimension; low likelihood is not automatically anomaly risk. I select transforms and bandwidth by held-out log likelihood or a task-specific criterion, use boundary correction or domain transforms, validate normalization and support, and benchmark O(n) query cost or scalable approximations.
keyPoints: A density integrates to one; its pointwise value is not a probability mass and changes under unit transformations.
KDE is a sum of normalized local kernels whose bandwidth sets the bias-variance trade-off.
Boundary bias, feature scaling and high-dimensional sample sparsity can dominate kernel choice.
Held-out log likelihood evaluates predictive density but may not align with anomaly or decision utility.
Exact KDE stores reference points and can require one kernel evaluation per training point per query.
lessons.description: Density estimation models the distribution of observations rather than a conditional label. This chapter distinguishes probability density from probability mass, develops histograms and derives multivariate kernel density estimation with normalized kernels and bandwidth scaling. It explains bandwidth bias and variance, leave-one-out likelihood, kernel choice, adaptive bandwidth, boundary bias, transformations, mixed variables, sampling weights, modes, gradients and high-dimensional failure. Worked examples calculate a Gaussian KDE value and show why a positive-domain boundary loses mass. The lab implements one-dimensional Gaussian KDE, compares log density with scikit-learn, numerically verifies integration and demonstrates bandwidth sensitivity. Production guidance versions reference data, transforms and bandwidth, benchmarks memory and query latency, monitors support and likelihood drift, protects stored examples and separates low-density flags from validated anomaly decisions. The method is framed as a predictive distribution whose units, support and evaluation question must be declared before its scores can be interpreted. You will also learn why a leave-one-out self-kernel is leakage, how Jacobians preserve probability across transformations, and when exact reference-based evaluation must yield to validated scalable approximations.
learningObjectives: Distinguish density values from probability mass and verify normalization.
Derive KDE and explain bandwidth, kernel, boundary and dimensional effects.
Select a density model using leakage-free held-out likelihood or task evidence.
Operate reference-based density scoring with support, privacy, latency and fallback controls.
lessons.labGoal: Implement Gaussian KDE, compare with scikit-learn, verify approximate normalization and expose bandwidth sensitivity.
followUpQuestions: Why divide by h^d?
Why does KDE struggle in high dimension?
How do you evaluate an anomaly threshold from KDE?

lessons.title: Randomized Experiment Design
lessons.interviewAnswer: I start with the causal estimand and target population, then choose the unit at which treatment can be assigned without unacceptable spillover or carryover. I define eligibility before randomization, stable assignment, treatment versions, primary outcomes, guardrails, duration, and exclusions. I use blocking on strong pre-treatment predictors to improve balance and precision, cluster randomization when units interact, and switchbacks when treatment operates at a shared time-varying system level. Analysis follows the assignment mechanism and preserves ITT. I predeclare power, multiplicity, stopping, missingness, and noncompliance handling, then validate assignment and exposure before reading effects.
keyPoints: Design begins with estimand and interference structure
Randomization unit and analysis unit must remain aligned
Blocking can improve precision using pre-treatment information
Cluster and switchback designs trade bias control for effective sample size
ITT, missingness, and treatment versions must be specified before outcomes
lessons.description: Randomized experiment design determines what causal question a test can answer before any statistical model is fit. This chapter develops experimental units, treatment versions, eligibility, potential outcomes, assignment mechanisms, complete and Bernoulli randomization, blocking and stratification, cluster and switchback designs, factorial experiments, unequal allocation, covariate balance, noncompliance, attrition, spillovers, exposure, power, preregistration, and analysis plans. You will learn to align randomization with the interference and delivery structure, separate design-stage balance from post-hoc adjustment, preserve intention-to-treat analysis, and avoid conditioning on variables affected by treatment. A worked marketplace example compares buyer-level, market-level, and time-block assignment under seller competition. The lab implements deterministic blocked randomization, checks allocation and balance invariants, and estimates a known treatment effect over repeated simulations. Production guidance covers assignment services, salts, mutual exclusion, ramps, identity changes, logging, privacy, monitoring, incident response, and rollback. A good design makes a simple estimator credible; no amount of downstream modeling can reconstruct counterfactual evidence destroyed by a flawed assignment or measurement process.
learningObjectives: Choose an experimental unit and assignment mechanism that match treatment delivery, interference, carryover, and the target estimand.
Use blocking, clustering, factorial structure, and unequal allocation with correct analysis and power implications.
Specify intention-to-treat, exposure, attrition, noncompliance, and missing-outcome handling before observing effects.
Implement reproducible blocked assignment and verify determinism, allocation, covariate balance, and estimator behavior.
lessons.labGoal: Implement reproducible blocked assignment, verify allocation and pre-treatment balance, and confirm difference-in-means behavior across repeated randomized assignments.
followUpQuestions: When should you cluster-randomize?
Why block randomization?
What is a switchback experiment?

lessons.title: Sample Ratio Mismatch (SRM)
lessons.interviewAnswer: SRM means the observed variant counts are inconsistent with the planned allocation beyond ordinary random fluctuation. I test assignment-unit counts against expected proportions, usually with a chi-square goodness-of-fit check, before looking at effects. A very small p-value is a smoke alarm, not an effect adjustment: I investigate assignment, eligibility, exposure delivery, missing telemetry, identity changes, redirects, filters, joins, bots, and time of onset. I also distinguish all-assigned SRM from triggered-population SRM. Until the root cause is explained and shown not to bias the estimand, I quarantine the result and normally fix and restart the experiment.
keyPoints: SRM tests allocation integrity, not treatment impact
Expected counts come from the actual design and ramp history
Assignment, exposure, and analysis populations need separate checks
The chi-square p-value detects a symptom but not its cause
A failed SRM gate blocks causal interpretation until diagnosed
lessons.description: Sample ratio mismatch (SRM) occurs when observed experiment allocation counts differ implausibly from the proportions specified by the randomization design. It is one of the highest-value trust diagnostics in online experimentation because many assignment, eligibility, exposure, identity, and logging defects first appear as unexpected arm counts. This chapter derives the multinomial chi-square check, explains its assumptions and scale sensitivity, distinguishes assignment-level from triggered-analysis SRM, and builds a root-cause taxonomy across randomization, delivery, telemetry, filtering, bots, joins, and time. You will learn why SRM is a symptom rather than a correction target, why balanced outcomes cannot rescue a failed trust check, how to localize onset and affected slices, and when unequal counts are expected by design. A worked redirect bug shows how treatment-dependent loss reverses an apparent effect. The lab implements the SRM statistic and p-value, compares it with SciPy, and diagnoses a time-slice failure using invariants. Production guidance covers continuous alerting, multiple looks, minimum counts, ownership, forensic snapshots, restart criteria, and rollback. The rule is simple: do not interpret treatment effects until the mismatch is understood and the causal sample is trustworthy.
learningObjectives: Compute an SRM goodness-of-fit statistic for arbitrary planned allocation proportions and interpret it as a trust diagnostic.
Separate valid random allocation fluctuation from assignment, delivery, exposure, logging, filtering, identity, and join failures.
Localize an SRM by event stage, time, platform, geography, eligibility, and identifier without outcome-driven fishing.
Define automated alert, investigation, restart, and evidence-preservation procedures for an experimentation platform.
lessons.labGoal: Implement a multinomial SRM check, compare it with SciPy, and localize a treatment-specific count loss across time slices.
followUpQuestions: Does unequal arm size always mean SRM?
Can an experiment with SRM still be analyzed?
Why can assignment SRM pass while analysis SRM fails?

lessons.title: Variance Reduction & CUPED
lessons.interviewAnswer: CUPED reduces experiment variance by subtracting the predictable part of an outcome from a pre-treatment covariate. With outcome Y and centered covariate X, define Y_adj=Y-theta(X-E[X]), where theta=Cov(Y,X)/Var(X). Because treatment is randomized and X is measured before treatment, arm means of X are equal in expectation, so the treatment contrast stays unbiased while residual variance falls; with an optimal single covariate the ideal reduction is rho squared. I freeze the pre-period cutoff, estimate theta without outcome-driven selection, handle missing X explicitly, preserve ITT, and verify the adjusted effect against the raw estimate and historical simulations.
keyPoints: CUPED removes outcome variation predictable before treatment
Pre-treatment timing protects the causal contrast
Ideal single-covariate variance reduction is governed by squared correlation
Regression adjustment generalizes CUPED but needs design-aware specification
Precision gains never excuse SRM, leakage, or post-treatment selection
lessons.description: Controlled-experiment variance reduction uses pre-treatment information to make treatment-effect estimates more precise without changing the randomized causal contrast. CUPED (Controlled-experiment Using Pre-Experiment Data) adjusts an outcome by a centered covariate measured before assignment, typically the same user metric in a historical window. This chapter derives the optimal linear coefficient, variance reduction factor, unbiasedness under randomization, cross-fitting and regression adjustment, missing pre-period data, triggered metrics, ratio metrics, multiple covariates, heterogeneity, and failure modes. You will learn why correlation determines precision gain, why post-treatment covariates create bias, why centering and a treatment interaction matter, and how to estimate gains on historical A/A-style data rather than selecting a favorable adjustment after seeing outcomes. A worked revenue experiment shows a large variance reduction with unchanged effect expectation. The lab implements CUPED from first principles, compares it with an OLS treatment coefficient, and verifies unbiased effect recovery plus reduced variance over repeated randomized trials. Production guidance covers cutoff enforcement, leakage checks, coefficient versioning, missingness, metric lineage, monitoring, fallback, and rollback. CUPED creates information by removing predictable noise; it cannot repair broken randomization or measurement.
learningObjectives: Derive the CUPED adjustment coefficient and variance reduction from covariance and correlation.
Choose covariates that are predictive, pre-treatment, consistently available, and unaffected by assignment or exposure.
Connect CUPED to regression adjustment, interactions, cross-fitting, and robust analysis for complex metrics.
Implement and validate an adjustment using unbiasedness, variance, leakage, missingness, and reproducibility checks.
lessons.labGoal: Implement CUPED adjustment, compare it with regression adjustment, and verify effect unbiasedness plus variance reduction over repeated randomized experiments.
followUpQuestions: Why does CUPED remain unbiased?
How much variance can it remove?
What if theta is estimated from the experiment?

lessons.title: Sequential Testing, Peeking & Early Stopping
lessons.interviewAnswer: A fixed-horizon test controls Type I error only for its planned sample and analysis. If I repeatedly peek and stop when p<0.05, I give noise multiple chances to cross the threshold and inflate false positives. Valid options include prespecified group-sequential looks with alpha spending, a sequential probability ratio test for specified alternatives, or anytime-valid p-values, e-values, and confidence sequences. I define the stopping rule, information times, minimum duration, primary metric, multiplicity, and delayed-outcome handling before launch. Safety kill switches can stop exposure immediately, but confirmatory efficacy claims still follow their declared evidence procedure.
keyPoints: Optional stopping changes the sampling distribution
Monitoring schedule and stopping rule are part of the design
Group-sequential methods spend a finite error budget across planned looks
Confidence sequences provide simultaneous coverage over time
Safety stopping and efficacy inference answer different questions
lessons.description: Sequential experimentation allows data-dependent monitoring or stopping while preserving a declared error guarantee. Repeatedly applying a fixed-horizon p-value whenever new data arrive does not do this: optional stopping selects unusually favorable noise and inflates false positives. This chapter develops fixed-horizon designs, group-sequential looks, alpha spending, sequential probability ratio tests, always-valid p-values, e-values, confidence sequences, futility, harm stopping, minimum run constraints, delayed outcomes, and decision-theoretic trade-offs. You will learn why stopping rules are part of the statistical procedure, how time-uniform intervals differ from ordinary intervals, how to choose between planned looks and continuous monitoring, and why operational kill switches should not be confused with efficacy claims. A worked product experiment contrasts naive peeking with an anytime-valid rule. The lab simulates false-positive inflation from fixed-horizon peeking and verifies control from a Bonferroni group-sequential design using SciPy. Production guidance covers dashboards, information time, alpha budgets, metric multiplicity, late data, restarts, safety escalation, audit logs, and rollback. Sequential methods provide flexibility only when the monitoring rule and evidence process are designed together.
learningObjectives: Explain mathematically and through simulation why optional stopping invalidates repeatedly viewed fixed-horizon p-values.
Choose and interpret fixed-horizon, group-sequential, alpha-spending, confidence-sequence, and e-value procedures.
Separate efficacy, futility, harm, operational, and business stopping rules with their distinct guarantees.
Implement and validate a planned-look design using family-wise error simulations and an immutable monitoring schedule.
lessons.labGoal: Simulate false-positive inflation from naive peeking and verify family-wise control from a planned Bonferroni group-sequential design.
followUpQuestions: What is a confidence sequence?
What is alpha spending?
Can you always stop an experiment for harm?

lessons.title: Metric Design: North Star, Driver & Guardrail Metrics
lessons.interviewAnswer: I start from the decision and long-term user/business objective, then create an OEC or primary metric whose direction is credibly aligned with that objective. I add driver metrics for the causal mechanism and guardrails for reliability, safety, fairness, cost, and ecosystem harm. Every metric has a contract: population, unit, numerator, denominator, time window, attribution, aggregation, missingness, direction, and version. I validate sensitivity on historical experiments and directionality against long-term outcomes and known bad changes. I avoid arbitrary composites and average-of-averages, report uncertainty, and treat metric changes like schema migrations because they alter historical and experimental meaning.
keyPoints: Metrics operationalize values and assumptions
OEC, drivers, diagnostics, and guardrails serve different roles
Directionality and sensitivity must both be validated
Population, unit, denominator, and window define the estimand
Metric versions and lineage are part of scientific reproducibility
lessons.description: Metric design translates a product objective into a measurable, sensitive, directionally trustworthy decision system. A North Star or Overall Evaluation Criterion (OEC) should predict long-term value closely enough to guide short experiments, driver metrics explain mechanisms, and guardrails prevent unacceptable harm. This chapter develops metric contracts, populations, units, numerators, denominators, windows, attribution, directionality, sensitivity, validity, reliability, gaming, ratio estimands, heavy tails, missingness, delayed outcomes, composite scores, proxy risk, and metric lifecycle governance. You will learn why more activity is not always better, why per-user and per-event averages answer different questions, how denominator changes can reverse a result, and how to validate short-term proxies against long-term outcomes and known interventions. A worked recommendation-system scorecard separates engagement from satisfaction and ecosystem health. The lab builds a semantic metric contract and ratio-of-sums calculator, rejects grain and denominator errors, and verifies invariants against pandas. Production guidance covers lineage, versioning, backfills, dashboards, experiment inference, access control, alerts, deprecation, correction, and rollback. The goal is not one magical number; it is an auditable map from user and business value to decisions under uncertainty.
learningObjectives: Define a metric through population, unit, event, numerator, denominator, window, attribution, direction, and missingness semantics.
Construct primary, driver, diagnostic, and guardrail metrics that map to a causal product theory rather than a dashboard inventory.
Evaluate directionality, sensitivity, validity, reliability, robustness, gaming risk, and long-term proxy quality.
Implement and test ratio metrics with grain, denominator, reconciliation, and versioning invariants.
lessons.labGoal: Validate a semantic metric contract, compute a ratio of sums at user grain, and verify that aggregation, denominators, and pandas results reconcile.
followUpQuestions: What makes a good OEC?
Why can per-active-user metrics mislead?
Should guardrails be included in a composite?

lessons.title: Funnels & Conversion Analysis
lessons.interviewAnswer: A funnel is a versioned sequence estimand, not just counts by event name. I define the eligible entity and entry cohort, strict or loose order, conversion window, repeat and re-entry rules, identity resolution, and whether conversion is unique entities or event completions. I deduplicate at the chosen unit, require complete follow-up or handle censoring, and reconcile cumulative counts so they cannot increase. I segment only with pre-step attributes for causal interpretation, inspect time-to-transition and alternative paths, and use experiments to test proposed causes. Drop-off shows where progression stops under the definition; it does not prove why.
keyPoints: Funnel definitions construct the population and path
Entity counts and event counts answer different questions
Conversion windows and maturity prevent unequal opportunity
Step drop-off is descriptive, not a causal explanation
Identity and event-contract quality dominate trustworthy funnel analysis
lessons.description: Funnel analysis measures how eligible entities progress through a defined sequence of product states or events and where they fail, branch, repeat, or take too long. A funnel is not an objective map of user behavior: step definitions, order rules, identity, attribution, conversion window, denominator, and re-entry policy construct the result. This chapter develops strict and loose funnels, unique-user versus event conversion, closed versus open cohorts, step and cumulative rates, time-to-convert, competing paths, censoring, segmentation, instrumentation, causal limits, and experimental use. You will learn how repeated events and inner joins inflate conversion, why recent entrants have incomplete opportunity, how to distinguish a product obstacle from selection, and when a state machine or journey analysis is better than a linear funnel. A worked checkout example exposes an identity and window bug. The lab implements a deterministic ordered unique-user funnel from raw events, compares it with pandas, and verifies monotonic counts, window rules, deduplication, and denominator reconciliation. Production guidance covers event contracts, late data, sessionization, privacy, monitoring, metric versions, and rollback. The goal is a reproducible behavioral estimand that guides hypotheses, not a decorative narrowing chart that implies causality.
learningObjectives: Define funnel population, entity, step events, ordering, window, attribution, repetition, and denominator semantics precisely.
Compute cumulative and step conversion without double counting entities or granting unequal observation opportunity.
Diagnose instrumentation, identity, time, competing-path, and selection explanations for apparent drop-off.
Implement and verify an ordered funnel while preserving raw counts, transition times, and alternative paths.
lessons.labGoal: Build an ordered unique-user funnel from event histories, compare counts with pandas, and verify monotonicity, deduplication, and conversion-window semantics.
followUpQuestions: What is a strict funnel?
Why can cumulative counts increase?
How do you compare funnel conversion in an A/B test?

lessons.title: Cohort Retention Analysis
lessons.interviewAnswer: Retention starts with a fixed cohort, usually entities sharing a first value event or acquisition period, and asks what fraction performs a defined return behavior at each age. I specify exact-period versus rolling retention, interval boundaries, identity, denominator, resurrection, and observation cutoff. Recent cohorts do not have mature later ages, so I leave those cells unavailable rather than zero. I compare cohorts at the same age, inspect calendar effects and acquisition mix, and use survival or hazard methods when time-to-churn and censoring matter. A better curve is descriptive until an experiment or causal design supports attribution.
keyPoints: Cohort time and calendar time are separate axes
Retention depends on the value event and denominator contract
Recent cohort cells are censored, not zero
Exact, rolling, and survival retention answer different questions
Composition and identity changes can mimic product retention gains
lessons.description: Cohort retention analysis follows entities from a common starting event and measures whether they return to a value-defining behavior at comparable ages. It separates lifecycle decay from calendar-time shocks, but only when cohort assignment, activity, interval boundaries, identity, denominator, and observation maturity are defined consistently. This chapter develops acquisition and behavioral cohorts, exact-period, rolling, and bracket retention, survival-style retention, resurrection, churn, cohort-age matrices, censoring, composition, seasonality, segmentation, uncertainty, and experimental interpretation. You will learn why recent cohorts form an incomplete triangle, why retention can rise when low-value users never enter the denominator, how identity and late events reshape curves, and when Kaplan-Meier or hazard analysis is more appropriate. A worked subscription example separates acquisition-mix change from product improvement. The lab builds a monthly exact-period retention matrix from first activity and later events, compares with pandas, and verifies cohort size, maturity, identity uniqueness, and denominator invariants. Production guidance covers semantic models, incremental updates, backfills, privacy, monitoring, causal tests, and rollback. The goal is a lifecycle measurement system that reveals durable value, not a color grid interpreted without population or time context.
learningObjectives: Define cohort membership, start event, retained behavior, age interval, denominator, and resurrection semantics.
Compute exact, rolling, and survival-style retention while handling right censoring and incomplete recent cohorts.
Decompose retention changes into cohort composition, lifecycle, calendar time, instrumentation, and product mechanisms.
Implement and validate a cohort matrix with maturity and reconciliation checks.
lessons.labGoal: Build an exact monthly cohort-retention matrix, compare it with pandas, and verify cohort membership, maturity, uniqueness, and denominators.
followUpQuestions: What is rolling retention?
Why is the cohort table triangular?
When should you use survival analysis?

lessons.title: Churn, Lifetime Value & Unit Economics
lessons.interviewAnswer: LTV is expected discounted future contribution margin over a stated horizon, conditional on current information and policy. In subscriptions, churn may be an observed cancellation or nonrenewal; in noncontractual products, inactivity is latent and needs a repeat-purchase/dropout model or an operational lapse rule. I handle right censoring, customer heterogeneity, refunds and variable costs, validate on mature chronological cohorts, and report cohort calibration and uncertainty rather than only individual rank. CAC comparison uses incremental fully loaded acquisition cost. A high predicted LTV does not imply targeting will cause value; intervention decisions need treatment effects and costs.
keyPoints: LTV is a horizon- and policy-dependent expectation
Contribution margin differs from revenue
Churn is observed only in some business settings
Censoring and heterogeneity are central, not edge cases
Predictive value and incremental intervention value are different estimands
lessons.description: Customer lifetime value (LTV or CLV) is the discounted expected contribution margin generated by a customer or cohort over a declared future horizon, while churn describes a contractual cancellation or a modeled loss of future activity. Both are forecasts with behavioral, accounting, censoring, and policy assumptions; neither is a timeless label stored on a user. This chapter develops contractual versus noncontractual settings, retention and hazard, right censoring, revenue versus margin, discounting, acquisition cost, payback, cohort versus individual prediction, BG/NBD-style customer-base models, survival models, calibration, chronological validation, treatment effects, uncertainty, and decision use. You will learn why last activity is not observed churn, why a constant-retention formula can be dangerously optimistic, how heterogeneity changes aggregate value, and why marketing intervention can invalidate passive forecasts. A worked subscription example separates gross revenue from incremental contribution value. The lab implements Kaplan-Meier survival and discounted cohort LTV from first principles, compares grouped calculations with pandas, and verifies censoring and monotonicity invariants. Production guidance covers label maturity, leakage, policy feedback, monitoring, fairness, cost, rollback, and human review.
learningObjectives: Define churn, survival, margin, horizon, discounting, and acquisition cost for contractual and noncontractual businesses.
Estimate retention under right censoring and translate survival or repeat-purchase forecasts into discounted expected contribution value.
