Validate LTV models chronologically with calibration, ranking, aggregate value, policy, and uncertainty metrics.
Distinguish predictive customer value from incremental value caused by a retention or acquisition action.
lessons.labGoal: Implement Kaplan-Meier survival and finite-horizon discounted contribution LTV, compare grouped risk calculations with pandas, and verify censoring and monotonicity.
followUpQuestions: What is right censoring?
How does LTV differ in contractual and noncontractual businesses?
How do you validate LTV?

lessons.title: Potential Outcomes & Average Treatment Effects
lessons.interviewAnswer: The potential-outcomes framework defines Y_i(a) as unit i's outcome under treatment strategy a. For a binary treatment, the individual effect Y_i(1)-Y_i(0) is fundamentally unobservable because only one potential outcome is revealed. We therefore target population quantities such as ATE E[Y(1)-Y(0)], ATT, risk ratio, quantile effect or policy value. Consistency connects observed Y to Y(A); positivity supplies support; exchangeability connects treatment groups to counterfactual outcomes; and SUTVA-style assumptions require well-defined versions and manageable interference. Randomization establishes exchangeability by design, while observational analyses need measured-confounding assumptions or another identification strategy. I specify time zero, treatment versions, population and outcome horizon, distinguish assignment from receipt, report intention-to-treat and adherence estimands clearly, and avoid claiming individual treatment effects are validated from factual outcomes alone.
keyPoints: Potential outcomes define causal effects by comparing intervention states for the same target units.
Only one potential outcome per unit is observed, so individual effects require untestable structure or remain unidentified.
ATE, ATT, CATE, risk ratio, quantile and policy effects are different estimands with different target populations.
Consistency, exchangeability, positivity and interference assumptions connect potential outcomes to observed data.
Assignment, treatment receipt, adherence and treatment versions must not be collapsed into one ambiguous variable.
lessons.description: Potential outcomes make causal questions explicit by defining what each unit would experience under each treatment strategy. This chapter introduces factual and counterfactual outcomes, the fundamental problem of causal inference, consistency, treatment versions, positivity, exchangeability and interference. It distinguishes individual effects from ATE, ATT, ATC, CATE, risk ratios, quantile effects and policy value; separates treatment assignment, receipt and adherence; and contrasts intention-to-treat with per-protocol questions. It derives identification under randomization and measured-confounding adjustment, explains finite-population versus superpopulation targets, and discusses cluster assignment, censoring and repeated outcomes. Worked examples show why the same experiment supports an average effect but not observed individual effects and why vague treatment versions break consistency. The lab simulates complete potential outcomes, hides one per unit, verifies that randomized difference in means recovers the known ATE and quantifies sampling uncertainty. Production guidance versions estimands and treatment protocols, monitors compliance, spillovers, overlap and outcome maturity, and keeps personalized-effect claims separate from observable predictive validation.
learningObjectives: Define potential outcomes and translate decisions into population, treatment, horizon and effect estimands.
Distinguish individual, average, treated-population, conditional and policy effects.
Derive randomized and conditional-exchangeability identification from explicit assumptions.
Design diagnostics for consistency, adherence, positivity, interference and outcome observation.
lessons.labGoal: Simulate complete potential outcomes, reveal one through random assignment, and verify unbiased average-effect recovery and uncertainty behavior.
followUpQuestions: Why is the individual treatment effect unobservable?
What identifies ATE in a randomized trial?
Can ATT equal ATE?

lessons.title: Backdoor Adjustment & Confounding Control
lessons.interviewAnswer: Backdoor adjustment identifies a treatment effect by conditioning on pretreatment variables that block every path entering treatment, while avoiding treatment descendants. If Z is valid, consistency, conditional exchangeability and positivity imply the g-formula E[Y(a)]=E_Z E[Y|A=a,Z]. I choose Z from a reviewed causal DAG rather than p-values or feature importance, prefer a minimal well-measured set with adequate overlap, and define the target population. I can estimate by outcome-regression standardization, stratification, matching, inverse weighting or doubly robust methods; estimator flexibility addresses functional form, not unmeasured confounding. I inspect overlap, balance, model residuals, influential observations and sensitivity to alternative defensible sets. For total effects I do not adjust mediators or post-treatment colliders. When no measured set closes all backdoor paths, I state nonidentification or use another design instead of calling a predictive regression causal.
keyPoints: A valid adjustment set is determined by the causal graph and target effect, not association screening.
The adjustment formula averages treatment-specific conditional outcomes over one declared target covariate distribution.
Outcome regression, weighting and matching estimate the same identified contrast through different modeling choices.
Positivity and measurement quality can favor one valid set over another even when both block confounding.
No estimator or balance table detects confounding by variables absent from the identification set.
lessons.description: Backdoor adjustment turns a causal DAG into an observed-data estimand. This chapter derives the adjustment formula from consistency, conditional exchangeability and positivity; distinguishes graphical validity from statistical estimation; and explains minimal versus sufficient sets, total versus direct effects, precision variables, instruments, proxies and M-bias. It develops stratification, regression standardization, inverse-probability weighting, matching and augmented doubly robust estimation as alternative implementations of the same target contrast. It covers nonlinearity, interactions, marginal versus conditional scales, target-population weighting, practical positivity, measurement error, flexible nuisance models and cross-fitting. Worked examples standardize stratum-specific risks and show why a post-treatment control changes the estimand. The lab simulates measured confounding, computes regression g-computation and inverse weighting, and verifies recovery of the known ATE while the naive difference is biased. Production guidance versions the DAG and adjustment set, asserts pretreatment availability, monitors overlap and weight tails, preserves target-population definitions and reports sensitivity to unmeasured confounding. Every restriction or trimming rule is reported as a population change rather than hidden as numerical cleanup.
learningObjectives: Derive the backdoor adjustment formula for a graph-validated covariate set.
Estimate marginal effects with standardization, weighting and doubly robust scores.
Diagnose adjustment-set, positivity, functional-form and target-population failures.
Separate robustness to nuisance estimation from sensitivity to unmeasured confounding.
lessons.labGoal: Estimate a known confounded treatment effect with g-computation and inverse weighting and verify the naive contrast remains biased.
followUpQuestions: What makes an adjustment set minimal?
Why can extreme propensity weights be a design warning?
When do standardization and IPW target different effects?

lessons.title: Propensity Scores, Matching & Weighting
lessons.interviewAnswer: The propensity score e(X)=P(A=1|X) is the probability of treatment given a valid pretreatment adjustment set. Under conditional exchangeability, conditioning on the true score balances the distribution of X between treatment groups, reducing a multivariate design problem to a scalar balancing score. It does not balance unmeasured confounders and its purpose is causal design, not treatment prediction accuracy. I choose X from a DAG, estimate scores without post-treatment variables, inspect common support, then match, stratify or weight for an explicitly chosen estimand. ATE, ATT, overlap and stabilized weights are different. I check standardized mean differences and distributions after design, effective sample size and extreme weights; iterate the design without outcome-driven cherry-picking. Outcome analysis respects matching or weights and uncertainty. Poor overlap leads to population restriction or redesign, not silent clipping, and sensitivity analysis addresses residual unmeasured confounding.
keyPoints: The propensity score balances measured pretreatment covariates under its causal assumptions; it is not a causal effect.
Covariate choice follows confounding structure, while treatment-model flexibility follows balance and overlap diagnostics.
Matching, subclassification, ATE, ATT and overlap weighting target different populations and require matching inference.
Extreme scores expose weak support; trimming, calipers and clipping change either the population or the estimator.
Good balance on measured X cannot certify exchangeability with respect to unmeasured causes.
lessons.description: Propensity scores support observational-study design by balancing measured pretreatment covariates across treatment groups. This chapter derives the balancing-score result, separates causal covariate selection from statistical score estimation, and explains why treatment-prediction accuracy is not the objective. It compares nearest-neighbor, caliper, exact and full matching; subclassification; inverse-probability, stabilized, ATT and overlap weighting; and augmented doubly robust estimators. It covers common support, extreme weights, effective sample size, replacement, matching ratios, trimming, clipping, balance metrics, cross-fitting and variance estimation. Worked examples derive ATE and ATT weights and show a high treatment-model AUC signaling deterministic assignment rather than a successful design. The lab simulates measured confounding, estimates propensity scores, verifies inverse weighting reduces standardized imbalance and recovers the known effect. Production guidance versions treatment assignment, covariates, score model, target weights and exclusions, monitors overlap and weight tails, and pairs measured-balance evidence with sensitivity to unmeasured confounding. Design quality is judged on the covariates and population the effect actually requires.
learningObjectives: Derive the propensity score's balancing role under conditional exchangeability.
Choose matching, stratification or target-specific weights for a declared population estimand.
Evaluate common support, balance, weight influence and effective sample size after design.
Combine propensity designs with outcome estimation, uncertainty and unmeasured-confounding sensitivity.
lessons.labGoal: Estimate propensity scores, construct ATE weights, and verify improved measured balance and treatment-effect recovery.
followUpQuestions: Why not include post-treatment variables in the propensity model?
What does overlap weighting estimate?
How do you evaluate propensity model quality?

lessons.title: Difference-in-Differences
lessons.interviewAnswer: Difference-in-differences estimates a treatment effect by comparing the treated group's before-after change with the control group's change. The key identifying assumption is parallel trends in untreated potential outcomes for the target groups, possibly conditional on covariates—not equality of outcome levels. In the canonical two-group, two-period design, DID is (Ybar_T,post-Ybar_T,pre)-(Ybar_C,post-Ybar_C,pre). I define treatment timing, anticipation, comparison group, outcome and estimand, plot raw trends and event time, and use inference clustered at the assignment unit. Pretrend tests can reveal contradictions but low power cannot prove parallel trends. With staggered adoption and heterogeneous dynamic effects, ordinary two-way fixed effects may combine inappropriate already-treated comparisons and nontransparent weights, so I estimate group-time effects using never- or not-yet-treated controls and aggregate explicitly. I also test composition, spillovers and concurrent shocks and report sensitivity to trend violations.
keyPoints: DID identifies change relative to a comparison trend, not a generic treatment coefficient.
Parallel trends concerns untreated potential outcomes and remains an assumption after passing pretrend tests.
Treatment timing, anticipation, composition and spillovers determine valid control observations.
Staggered adoption with heterogeneous effects requires group-time estimands rather than naive two-way fixed effects.
Inference must reflect serial correlation and the number and level of treatment-assignment clusters.
lessons.description: Difference-in-differences identifies causal effects from changes in treated and comparison groups under a parallel-trends counterfactual. This chapter derives the canonical two-by-two estimator, regression representation and event-study contrasts; distinguishes equal levels from parallel untreated trends; and analyzes anticipation, treatment reversals, time-varying composition, spillovers and concurrent shocks. It explains why visual pretrends and placebo leads are diagnostics rather than proof, how covariate conditioning changes the assumption, and why scale choice matters. For staggered adoption, it develops cohort-time average treatment effects and explains how ordinary two-way fixed effects can use already-treated controls and combine heterogeneous effects with opaque weights. Worked examples compute a manual DID and expose a differential pretrend. The lab simulates panel outcomes, recovers the known effect by differencing and verifies equivalence with an interaction regression. Production guidance versions cohorts and event times, clusters inference at assignment level, monitors composition and spillovers, reports group-time estimates and aggregates only with decision-relevant weights.
learningObjectives: Derive the two-group, two-period DID estimator and its parallel-trends identification condition.
Diagnose anticipation, differential trends, composition, spillovers and concurrent-shock threats.
Estimate and aggregate staggered cohort-time effects without invalid already-treated controls.
Choose event-time displays, comparison groups and cluster-aware inference for the assignment design.
lessons.labGoal: Simulate a two-period panel, compute DID from group changes, and verify equivalence with a saturated interaction regression.
followUpQuestions: What is the identifying assumption in canonical DID?
Why can already-treated units be bad controls?
What should an event-study plot include?

lessons.title: Instrumental Variables
lessons.interviewAnswer: An instrumental variable Z changes treatment A, is as-if independent of potential outcomes, and affects outcome Y only through A, with monotonicity or an appropriate structural model for interpretation. For a binary instrument and treatment, the Wald ratio [E(Y|Z=1)-E(Y|Z=0)]/[E(A|Z=1)-E(A|Z=0)] identifies the local average treatment effect for compliers under relevance, independence, exclusion and monotonicity. It is not automatically the population ATE. In linear settings, two-stage least squares projects treatment onto instruments and uses only that exogenous variation. I justify each assumption institutionally, report first-stage strength and reduced form, use weak-instrument-robust inference, cluster at assignment level, and inspect whether the instrument has direct pathways or changes sample composition. More instruments or strong treatment prediction do not repair invalid exclusion. I preserve assignment-to-instrument and treatment-receipt definitions and report intention-to-treat alongside LATE.
keyPoints: Relevance is empirically checkable; independence and exclusion are primarily design assumptions.
The Wald estimand is a ratio of reduced-form outcome and first-stage treatment effects.
Under monotonicity, binary IV identifies LATE for compliers, whose population depends on the instrument.
Weak instruments create biased, nonnormal estimates and require robust inference rather than a mechanical F threshold alone.
Two-stage prediction is not ordinary plug-in regression; uncertainty and controls must follow the IV design.
lessons.description: Instrumental variables identify causal effects from treatment variation generated by an external assignment or encouragement. This chapter develops relevance, as-if independence, exclusion, monotonicity and stable treatment definitions; classifies compliance types; derives the binary Wald estimator and its local average treatment-effect interpretation; and separates first stage, reduced form, intention-to-treat and treatment-on-complier effects. It explains two-stage least squares, covariate adjustment, clustered designs, weak instruments, many instruments, overidentification tests and heterogeneous local effects. It also analyzes common failures such as direct instrument pathways, differential attrition, treatment versions and conditioning on post-instrument variables. Worked examples calculate a Wald effect and show why two instruments can target different complier populations. The lab simulates unmeasured confounding, verifies ordinary regression bias, and recovers the known structural effect with manual two-stage least squares. Production guidance versions assignment and receipt, reports first-stage and reduced-form evidence, uses weak-IV-robust uncertainty and keeps causal claims local to the instrument-induced population. Institutional evidence for exclusion remains central even when every numerical diagnostic looks strong.
learningObjectives: State and defend IV relevance, independence, exclusion and monotonicity assumptions.
Derive the Wald ratio, compliance-type LATE and linear 2SLS estimator.
Diagnose weak instruments, direct pathways, attrition, clustering and local-population limits.
Report first stage, reduced form, uncertainty and transport separately from the causal ratio.
lessons.labGoal: Simulate an endogenous treatment with a valid instrument, show OLS confounding, and recover the structural effect using two-stage least squares.
followUpQuestions: What does monotonicity exclude?
Why report the reduced form?
What is a weak instrument?

lessons.title: Regression Discontinuity
lessons.interviewAnswer: Regression discontinuity uses a treatment rule that changes at a cutoff of a running variable. In a sharp design treatment jumps from zero to one; in a fuzzy design its probability jumps and the outcome discontinuity is divided by the treatment discontinuity for a local complier effect. Identification requires potential-outcome regression functions to be continuous at the cutoff absent treatment, no precise manipulation that sorts units around the threshold, and consistent treatment and outcome measurement. I estimate separate local linear regressions on each side with a justified bandwidth and kernel, use robust bias-corrected inference, and show a binned plot only as visualization rather than estimation. I report density and predetermined-covariate continuity checks, placebo cutoffs and bandwidth sensitivity. I avoid high-order global polynomials. The estimand is local to units near the cutoff and should not be extrapolated to distant scores without new assumptions.
keyPoints: RD identifies a local cutoff effect from a discontinuity, not from the overall running-variable slope.
Continuity of untreated and treated potential-outcome functions is the central identification condition.
Manipulation, sorting, other rules at the cutoff and discrete scores threaten the comparison.
Local polynomial order, bandwidth, kernel and robust bias correction determine estimation and inference.
Sharp RD targets assignment at the cutoff; fuzzy RD is a local IV for treatment compliers near the cutoff.
lessons.description: Regression discontinuity identifies a treatment effect at an assignment threshold by comparing limits of outcome functions on either side. This chapter distinguishes sharp, fuzzy, kink and local-randomization designs; derives the cutoff estimand and fuzzy Wald ratio; and states continuity, no-manipulation, exclusion and monotonicity assumptions. It develops boundary-specific local linear and quadratic regression, bandwidth and kernel choice, robust bias-corrected inference, clustered observations and discrete running variables. It explains why bins are for visualization, why global high-order polynomials are dangerous, and how density tests, predetermined covariates, placebo cutoffs, bandwidth sensitivity and donut analyses diagnose specific threats. Worked examples compute sharp and fuzzy effects and expose a second policy at the same threshold. The lab simulates a smooth running-variable response with a known discontinuity, fits separate local slopes through an interaction model and verifies effect recovery across neighboring bandwidths. Production guidance versions score construction and cutoff rules, monitors manipulation and heaping, preserves local support and prevents extrapolation beyond the margin.
learningObjectives: Derive sharp and fuzzy RD estimands from continuity and threshold assignment.
Fit and interpret local polynomial models with bandwidth, kernel and bias-aware inference choices.
Diagnose manipulation, heaping, co-occurring policies, covariate jumps and placebo discontinuities.
Communicate the cutoff-local population and prevent unsupported extrapolation.
lessons.labGoal: Simulate a sharp threshold, estimate separate local slopes, and verify discontinuity recovery and bandwidth stability.
followUpQuestions: Why prefer local linear over high-order global polynomial?
What does a donut RD do?
What population does fuzzy RD identify?

lessons.title: Synthetic Control
lessons.interviewAnswer: Synthetic control estimates the counterfactual trajectory of one or a few treated aggregate units as a weighted combination of untreated donor units. Weights are chosen using only pretreatment outcomes and predictors, commonly constrained to be nonnegative and sum to one, so the synthetic unit lies in the donor convex hull. The post-treatment gap is the estimated effect under assumptions that good pretreatment fit captures the relevant time-varying confounding, donors remain untreated and unaffected by spillovers, and no concurrent treated-unit shock creates the gap. I justify the donor pool and intervention date, show the full treated and synthetic paths, pretreatment RMSPE and weights, and conduct in-space and in-time placebo analyses, often scaling post gaps by pre-fit quality. Poor pre-fit means the counterfactual is unsupported. I do not read ordinary regression standard errors mechanically or generalize a single-unit effect without design evidence.
keyPoints: Synthetic control is a comparative case-study design, not merely a forecasting algorithm.
Donor eligibility, intervention timing, no spillovers and good pretreatment trajectory fit are core assumptions.
Nonnegative sum-to-one weights favor interpretable interpolation and expose convex-hull support.
Post-treatment gaps need placebo, permutation and fit-quality context rather than ordinary large-sample standard errors alone.
Researcher choices about donor pools, predictors and preperiods require transparent sensitivity and no post-outcome cherry-picking.
lessons.description: Synthetic control constructs a transparent counterfactual for an aggregate intervention from a weighted donor pool. This chapter derives constrained donor weights, predictor and pretreatment-outcome matching, convex-hull support and post-treatment gaps. It explains donor eligibility, spillovers, anticipation, time-varying latent confounding, intervention timing and why good pre-fit is necessary but not sufficient. It develops pretreatment RMSPE, leave-one-out donors, alternative windows, in-space and in-time placebos, post/pre fit ratios and researcher-choice sensitivity. It contrasts classical nonnegative simplex weights with regression, augmented and matrix-completion extensions while preserving the target case-study question. Worked examples compute a weighted counterfactual and diagnose an influential donor. The lab fits simplex-constrained weights to a simulated panel, verifies recovery of the donor mixture and known post-treatment effect, and checks that weights are frozen after intervention. Production guidance versions donor pools and source revisions, reports paths and weights, monitors spillovers and concurrent shocks, and avoids automatic causal claims from forecast accuracy.
learningObjectives: Construct and interpret simplex-constrained donor weights and a synthetic counterfactual trajectory.
Diagnose donor contamination, convex-hull failure, poor pre-fit, spillovers and concurrent shocks.
Perform placebo and specification sensitivity appropriate to a comparative case study.
Report weights, paths, fit and local case-study scope without unsupported generalization.
lessons.labGoal: Fit simplex-constrained donor weights on pretreatment outcomes and verify recovery of a known post-treatment counterfactual gap.
followUpQuestions: Why constrain weights to be nonnegative and sum to one?
What if pretreatment fit is poor?
What does an in-space placebo do?

lessons.title: Heterogeneous Treatment Effects & Uplift Modeling
lessons.interviewAnswer: Heterogeneous treatment-effect modeling estimates CATE tau(x)=E[Y(1)-Y(0)|X=x] or learns a treatment policy, not an observable individual-effect label. Identification still needs randomized assignment or conditional exchangeability, positivity, consistency and an interference assumption. S-learners use one outcome model with treatment; T-learners fit separate outcome models; X-, R- and DR-learners use imputation or orthogonal residuals to improve robustness. Causal trees and forests split for effect differences and use honesty or cross-fitting so discovery does not reuse estimation outcomes. I evaluate global ATE recovery, calibration of predicted effects in held-out groups, rank-weighted treatment effects, policy value and overlap—not ordinary RMSE against factual outcomes. I predefine actionable baseline features, separate discovery from confirmation, report uncertainty and subgroup support, and validate any targeting policy prospectively. A high predicted uplift is not a known personal effect.
keyPoints: CATE is a conditional average causal estimand; individual treatment effects remain unobserved.
Meta-learners differ in how they estimate outcome and propensity nuisance functions and handle imbalance.
Honesty, sample splitting and cross-fitting reduce adaptive subgroup and nuisance overfitting.
Evaluate effect ranking, calibration and policy value on held-out causal evidence rather than factual prediction loss alone.
Targeting requires positivity, actionability, capacity, fairness, uncertainty and prospective policy validation.
lessons.description: Heterogeneous treatment-effect and uplift modeling estimates how average causal effects vary with pretreatment features and turns those estimates into constrained policies. This chapter defines CATE, group effects, uplift and policy value while emphasizing that individual causal labels are never observed. It compares S-, T-, X-, R- and doubly robust learners; explains outcome and propensity nuisance estimation, treatment imbalance, cross-fitting and orthogonality; and develops honest causal trees and forests for adaptive subgroup discovery and inference. It covers uplift curves, Qini-style rankings, calibration by predicted-effect groups, best linear projection, RATE, policy-value estimation and prospective validation. Worked examples contrast predictive risk with treatment benefit and expose subgroup search bias. The lab simulates randomized heterogeneous effects, fits separate forest response surfaces and verifies held-out CATE ranking and calibration against known simulation truth. Production guidance restricts features to actionable pretreatment data, monitors overlap and policy capacity, quantifies uncertainty and fairness, preserves exploration and requires randomized confirmation before high-stakes personalized treatment.
learningObjectives: Define CATE, uplift and policy value without treating individual effects as observed labels.
Choose and implement S-, T-, X-, R-, DR- or forest learners for the design and sample regime.
Evaluate held-out heterogeneity through causal calibration, ranking, subgroup effects and policy value.
Deploy bounded targeting policies with overlap, uncertainty, fairness and prospective validation.
lessons.labGoal: Fit a T-learner on randomized heterogeneous effects and verify held-out CATE accuracy, ranking and calibration against known simulation truth.
followUpQuestions: When is a T-learner attractive?
What is honesty in a causal tree?
How do you validate CATE predictions?

lessons.title: Trend, Seasonality, Cycles & Remainder
lessons.interviewAnswer: A time series is often described through level, trend, seasonal patterns, longer cycles, calendar effects, interventions and remainder. An additive representation Y_t=T_t+S_t+R_t fits seasonal amplitude that is roughly constant in target units; a multiplicative representation Y_t=T_t*S_t*R_t, often handled by logs, fits variation proportional to level. Components are modeling constructs, not uniquely observed truths: the decomposition depends on smoothing window, period, transform, endpoints and assumptions. I begin with frequency and timestamp quality, plot raw and transformed series, use domain calendars and spectral or ACF evidence for candidate seasons, and distinguish deterministic repeating seasonality from stochastic dependence. Multiple or evolving seasons need flexible bases or MSTL-like methods. I estimate components inside each training origin, inspect remainder structure and outliers, and never use a full-series decomposition as a leakage-free forecast feature.
keyPoints: Trend, seasonality, cycle and remainder are representation choices whose estimates depend on method and scale.
Additive seasonality has constant amplitude; multiplicative seasonality scales with level and is often modeled on logs.
Calendar effects such as trading days, holidays and moving festivals are not captured by a fixed numeric period alone.
A decomposition is useful only if the remainder and component stability are checked across time and forecast origins.
Full-series smoothing uses future observations and cannot be inserted directly into historical backtests or online features.
lessons.description: Time-series components provide a vocabulary for level, trend, seasonality, cycles, calendar events, interventions and remainder. This chapter compares additive and multiplicative representations, explains log and Box-Cox-style transforms, and distinguishes fixed seasonal periods from holidays, trading-day effects and moving events. It derives moving-average trend and seasonal-index estimates, introduces Fourier bases and multiple seasonality, and discusses changing amplitude, damped trends, structural breaks, outliers and boundary uncertainty. It emphasizes that components are not uniquely observed and that decomposition choices allocate structure differently. Worked examples identify proportional seasonality and distinguish a one-time level shift from a recurring cycle. The lab simulates trend plus monthly seasonality, estimates a centered moving-average trend and phase means, and verifies reconstruction and zero-sum constraints on interior points. Production guidance validates frequency and timezone, versions calendar definitions and transforms, estimates components inside each backtest origin, monitors component drift and retains raw-series baselines when decomposition becomes unstable. The chapter keeps descriptive smoothing separate from the one-sided state available to a live forecaster.
learningObjectives: Identify plausible trend, seasonal, calendar, cycle and remainder structures from domain and diagnostics.
Choose additive, multiplicative or transformed representations from amplitude and support.
Estimate simple trend and seasonal components and understand identifiability and endpoint limitations.
Use component diagnostics without future leakage and monitor their stability in production.
lessons.labGoal: Estimate additive trend and monthly seasonality from a synthetic series and verify normalization and interior reconstruction.
followUpQuestions: How do you choose additive versus multiplicative seasonality?
Why is a centered moving average leaky?
What should remain after decomposition?

lessons.title: Lags, Rolling Windows & Leakage
lessons.interviewAnswer: Lag and rolling features summarize past information, but they must be constructed using only data available at prediction time. Centered windows or post-outcome aggregates silently leak the future.
keyPoints: Shift before rolling when necessary.
Feature availability timestamp matters.
Use the same pipeline in backtests and production.
lessons.description: Lags, Rolling Windows & Leakage is a core topic in Time Series & Forecasting. Lags, Rolling Windows & Leakage appears frequently in data-science work because it connects mathematical assumptions to practical decisions, diagnostics and failure modes. This chapter turns the interview-level summary into a complete engineering and analytical treatment. The starting mental model is: Shift before rolling when necessary. The formal and implementation discussion builds from Shift before rolling when necessary., Feature availability timestamp matters., Use the same pipeline in backtests and production., while keeping the unit of data, objective, assumptions, and failure boundaries explicit. lessons.title: Naive, Seasonal-Naive & Drift Baselines
lessons.interviewAnswer: Forecast baselines are executable hypotheses about persistence. Mean forecasts assume reversion to a stable level; naive forecasts repeat the last observation and are optimal for a random walk under squared loss; drift extrapolates the average first-to-last slope; seasonal-naive repeats the last observed value from the same seasonal phase. I implement every baseline with exactly the data, update cadence and horizon available at each historical origin, and choose seasonal periods from the operational calendar rather than autocorrelation alone. I compare candidate models with paired errors by horizon and series, not only an aggregate. A complex model must beat relevant baselines such as seasonal-naive, current production and a known-future calendar rule after latency and cost. Baselines also serve as fallbacks and monitoring controls: if a model loses to them persistently, the issue may be drift, leakage in development or pipeline failure rather than insufficient architecture.
keyPoints: Each baseline encodes a concrete assumption about level, trend or seasonal persistence.
Naive and seasonal-naive forecasts must be generated recursively and point-in-time for every requested horizon.
A baseline is only fair when it receives the same information, origin schedule and target definition as the model.
Skill should be reported against multiple relevant baselines by horizon and series, with paired uncertainty.
Production baselines are low-dependency fallbacks and sentinels for data, model and regime failures.
lessons.description: Naive forecasting baselines turn simple persistence assumptions into rigorous benchmarks and fallbacks. This chapter derives historical-mean, last-value, drift and seasonal-naive forecasts and explains their links to stable-level, random-walk, linear-drift and repeating-season data-generating processes. It covers multi-step recursion, multiple seasonal periods, transformations, irregular calendars, intermittent demand, panels, cold starts and known-future event rules. It shows how baselines define MASE denominators and relative skill, why comparisons must share forecast origins and information, and how horizon and series aggregation can reverse rankings. Worked examples calculate drift and multi-step seasonal-naive forecasts. The lab implements all four methods over rolling origins, verifies formulas and demonstrates that seasonal-naive beats last-value on a seasonal synthetic series. Production guidance deploys baselines as low-dependency fallbacks, logs paired model-versus-baseline errors, monitors persistent negative skill and distinguishes model failure from data or regime change. Strong business rules and the current production system remain mandatory comparators when they use additional legal information.

Match baseline assumptions and seasonal periods to the operational series and calendar.
Measure paired forecast skill by horizon, series and regime without aggregation artifacts.
Use baselines as production fallbacks and monitoring sentinels with explicit trigger rules.

Translate Forecast Monitoring & Retraining into production controls for versioning, monitoring, resource limits, and rollback.
lessons.labGoal: Build a small, auditable Forecast Monitoring & Retraining example, inspect the key state, and verify a correctness invariant with assertions.

lessons.title: Point, Contextual & Collective Anomalies
lessons.interviewAnswer: A point anomaly is unusual by itself, a contextual anomaly is unusual only relative to conditions such as time or peer group, and a collective anomaly is a sequence or set whose joint pattern is unusual even when each element is ordinary. Before choosing a detector, I define the observation unit, normal reference population, available context, score, alert budget, investigation action, and label process. I fit transformations only on clean historical reference data and avoid future leakage. Detection scores rank cases; thresholds are operational policies chosen from capacity and cost. I monitor score and alert-rate drift, duplicate incidents, group coverage, delayed labels, and the share of alerts caused by data-pipeline failures.
keyPoints: Anomaly is relative to a reference distribution, context, and action.
Point, contextual, and collective anomalies require different features and units.
A continuous anomaly score is separate from the alert threshold.
Reference contamination, future leakage, and cold starts can dominate algorithm choice.
Investigation feedback and alert burden are part of the model system.
lessons.description: An anomaly is an observation or pattern that violates an explicitly defined expectation in a context that matters. Point anomalies are individually unusual, contextual anomalies are unusual only given time, segment, or state, and collective anomalies are ordinary-looking elements whose sequence or group is abnormal. This chapter turns that taxonomy into an engineering contract: define the unit, reference population, context, score direction, contamination assumptions, action, label horizon, and cost of review before choosing an algorithm. You will distinguish anomaly detection from novelty detection, supervised rare-event classification, data-quality validation, and change-point detection. Robust scaling, peer groups, seasonal residuals, sequence windows, and representation choices are connected to the kinds of deviation they expose. A worked payment example shows why the same amount can be normal for one merchant and anomalous for another, while a burst of small transactions can be collectively suspicious. The lab builds contextual median/MAD scores and a collective window score, compares with standardized residuals, and verifies invariance and context behavior. Production guidance prioritizes alert budgets, deduplication, investigation feedback, drift, cold starts, and safe fallback over arbitrary score cutoffs.
learningObjectives: Classify point, contextual, and collective anomalies and connect each type to a valid reference set and representation.
Write an anomaly-detection contract covering unit, context, score, threshold, action, feedback, and failure costs.
Distinguish outlier detection, novelty detection, supervised rare-event prediction, change-point detection, and data validation.
Build and verify robust contextual and collective scores without using future or cross-entity information.
lessons.labGoal: Build robust contextual and collective anomaly scores, compare with standardized residuals, and verify context, translation, and burst-detection invariants.
followUpQuestions: What is the difference between novelty and outlier detection?
How do you evaluate an unsupervised detector with few labels?
Why aggregate alerts into incidents?

lessons.title: Isolation Forest
lessons.interviewAnswer: Isolation Forest creates many random partition trees. Each node chooses a feature and a split within that feature's observed range; points that are few and different tend to be isolated in fewer edges. The anomaly score is roughly 2 raised to minus average path length divided by the expected path length c(psi) for a random binary-search tree of subsample size psi. Subsampling makes training fast and can reduce masking by large normal clusters. Tree scores rank unusualness; contamination generally sets a threshold and does not discover prevalence. I validate feature representation, stability across seeds and reference windows, score direction, alert budget, and labeled or audited incident yield, and I watch for clustered anomalies, duplicates, high-dimensional noise, drift, and unsupported novelty use.
keyPoints: Shorter average isolation path means more anomalous under the fitted forest.
c(psi) normalizes paths across subsample size.
Subsampling is central to both efficiency and detection behavior.
Feature representation shapes the random partitions even without distance metrics.
A threshold and contamination setting are policy layers over a score.
lessons.description: Isolation Forest scores anomalies by how quickly random recursive partitions isolate them. Instead of estimating a density or distance directly, each tree selects a feature and a split between observed minimum and maximum; unusual points tend to reach small leaves along shorter paths. This chapter derives path length, the unsuccessful binary-search-tree normalization c(psi), ensemble scoring, subsampling, feature subsampling, and the separate role of contamination or threshold policy. You will understand why the method is computationally attractive, where axis-aligned random cuts work, and why clustered anomalies, irrelevant high-dimensional features, one-hot representations, duplicates, missing values, and concept drift can defeat it. The chapter distinguishes outlier fitting from novelty scoring and explains score-direction differences in library APIs. A worked telemetry example traces a shallow isolation path. The lab builds a true reusable isolation-tree ensemble from scratch, compares it with scikit-learn, and verifies deterministic, translation, range, and injected-outlier invariants. Production guidance freezes sampling, seed, feature and score conventions; monitors path and alert distributions, support, duplicate rates, and incident yield; and uses a later reference window plus an explicit alert budget rather than presenting contamination as a learned prevalence.
learningObjectives: Build isolation trees and compute normalized ensemble anomaly scores from path lengths.
Explain how subsample size, tree count, feature representation, and contamination affect behavior.
Diagnose masking, clustered anomalies, irrelevant features, duplicates, and drift.
Deploy Isolation Forest with reproducible score direction, thresholds, references, and incident-level monitoring.
lessons.labGoal: Build reusable isolation trees and normalized forest scores, compare with scikit-learn, and verify injected-outlier, determinism, range, and translation invariants.
followUpQuestions: Why use small subsamples?
What happens to duplicate observations?
Is Isolation Forest suitable for novelty detection?

lessons.title: Local Outlier Factor & One-Class SVM
lessons.interviewAnswer: LOF finds points whose local reachability density is low relative to their k nearest neighbors, so a point can be normal inside a sparse cluster even if it is globally far away. A score near one is locally comparable; much above one suggests a local outlier. One-Class SVM instead estimates a regularized support boundary in feature space, often with an RBF kernel; nu controls a trade-off related to training errors and support vectors, while gamma controls boundary scale. I fit scaling on a trusted reference, tune k or gamma/nu on later data and alert capacity, and distinguish LOF's default training-set outlier mode from novelty=True scoring of new points. I monitor distance concentration, neighbor/support-vector stability, reference contamination, score direction, and incident yield.
keyPoints: LOF compares local density with neighbor density rather than using one global threshold.
Reachability distance reduces unstable density estimates around very close neighbors.
One-Class SVM learns a kernel support boundary, not an event probability.
Scaling, metric, k, gamma, nu, and reference purity define the detector.
LOF outlier and novelty modes have different scoring semantics.
lessons.description: Local Outlier Factor (LOF) and One-Class SVM answer two different versions of support-based anomaly detection. LOF compares a point's local reachability density with the densities of its neighbors, making it useful when normal data contain regions of different density. One-Class SVM learns a regularized boundary around reference data in a kernel feature space and is naturally framed as novelty detection. This chapter derives k-distance, reachability distance, local reachability density, LOF, the one-class support-estimation objective, kernel and nu behavior, and the practical difference between transductive training-set outlier detection and scoring unseen observations. You will learn why distance scaling, categorical representation, neighborhood size, curse of dimensionality, reference contamination, kernel bandwidth, and computational cost control results. A worked two-cluster example shows why a global distance score can overflag a sparse legitimate cluster while LOF compares locally. The lab implements LOF from first principles, compares exactly with scikit-learn, adds an RBF One-Class SVM novelty score, and verifies density-ratio, permutation, and injected-outlier behavior. Production guidance freezes reference, scaler, metric, k, kernel, nu, and score direction while monitoring neighbor distances, support vectors, alert burden, and cold-start coverage.
learningObjectives: Compute LOF from k-neighbor reachability distances and explain local density-ratio interpretation.
Explain One-Class SVM support estimation, kernel bandwidth, nu, and decision score semantics.
Distinguish training-set outlier detection from novelty scoring and avoid invalid LOF API use.
Diagnose scaling, high-dimensional distance concentration, reference contamination, and computational constraints.
lessons.labGoal: Implement Local Outlier Factor exactly, compare it with scikit-learn, and verify local-density, permutation, and One-Class SVM novelty behavior.
followUpQuestions: Why use reachability distance instead of raw distance in LOF?
How do you choose k?
What does gamma do in RBF One-Class SVM?

lessons.title: Rare-event Evaluation & Alert Thresholds
lessons.interviewAnswer: For rare events I separate ranking, probability, threshold, and operations. I report precision-recall curves or average precision, recall at the actual top-k review capacity, and threshold-specific counts and cost; accuracy is usually uninformative and ROC AUC can conceal false-positive burden. Precision and AP depend on prevalence, so the evaluation population and sampling weights must match deployment. If scores are probabilities I also test calibration and proper losses. I choose the threshold on validation data from costs, capacity, or a recall constraint, then evaluate once on a later untouched window at the incident level. Because labels are delayed and only alerts may be reviewed, I track unknowns, random-audit nonalerts, and report uncertainty.
keyPoints: Ranking, calibration, threshold performance, and queue operations are different layers.
Precision and the PR baseline change with event prevalence.
Recall at k directly represents a fixed review budget.
Thresholds must be chosen outside the final evaluation window.
Selective and delayed labels require audits and explicit unknown status.
lessons.description: Rare-event evaluation asks whether a score produces useful decisions when positives are scarce, labels are delayed or selective, and false alerts consume real capacity. Accuracy and even ROC AUC can hide failure: predicting every case negative gives high accuracy, while a small false-positive rate can still overwhelm investigators. This chapter derives precision, recall, specificity, false-positive rate, precision-recall curves, non-interpolated average precision, lift, recall at k, calibration, proper scores, expected cost, and threshold selection. It explains why precision and average precision depend on prevalence, why evaluation must use the deployment sampling unit and time window, and why alert deduplication changes the metric denominator. You will handle uncertain labels, review selection, delayed outcomes, incident grouping, confidence intervals, and threshold overfitting. A worked fraud queue example turns a review budget into recall-at-capacity and net value. The lab implements confusion metrics, average precision, top-k recall, and coherent cost selection, then verifies them against scikit-learn. Production guidance versions score and policy separately, monitors queue and incident yield, audits nonalerts, and recalibrates or reselects thresholds when prevalence, cost, capacity, or label processes change.
learningObjectives: Compute and interpret rare-event ranking, threshold, probability, and capacity metrics without conflating them.
Explain how prevalence, sampling, label delay, and incident grouping affect precision-recall evidence.
Select a threshold from coherent costs or operational constraints on data independent of final evaluation.
Design production audits and confidence estimates for selective, delayed, and incomplete labels.
lessons.labGoal: Implement rare-event counts, top-k metrics, average precision, and cost-sensitive threshold selection, then verify against scikit-learn and imbalance invariants.
followUpQuestions: What is the difference between PR AUC and average precision?
When is recall at k preferable?
How do you compare precision across populations?

lessons.title: Censoring, Survival & Hazard Functions
lessons.interviewAnswer: For event time T, survival is S(t)=P(T>t), cumulative incidence without competing risks is F(t)=1-S(t), hazard is the instantaneous event rate among those still event-free, and cumulative hazard H(t)=integral h with S(t)=exp(-H(t)). Right censoring at C observes Y=min(T,C) and delta=I(T<=C), so a censored row contributes evidence of survival through Y, not an event at Y and not no information. Kaplan-Meier and standard likelihoods need censoring independent of event time, often conditional on modeled covariates. I define time origin, event, entry, competing events, and label maturity; use risk sets that respect delayed entry; and inspect censoring and follow-up by segment before modeling.
keyPoints: Censoring preserves partial ordering information and is not ordinary missingness.
Hazard is a conditional rate among survivors, not a probability by itself.
S(t)=exp[-H(t)] in continuous time and F(t)=1-S(t) without competing risks.
Truncation changes who enters the sample; censoring limits what is observed after entry.
Time origin, risk set, censoring, and label maturity define the estimand.
lessons.description: Survival analysis models the time until an event while preserving partial information from subjects whose event time is not fully observed. Right censoring says only that the event occurs after the last observed time; left censoring, interval censoring, delayed entry, and truncation encode different observation mechanisms and require different risk sets or likelihoods. This chapter develops the event time T, survival S(t), distribution F(t), density f(t), hazard h(t), cumulative hazard H(t), and their relationships. You will distinguish a conditional instantaneous hazard from event probability over an interval, state independent or conditionally independent censoring assumptions, and see why dropping censored rows or treating censoring time as the event creates bias. A worked subscription example traces a cohort through events, censoring, and changing risk sets. The lab computes survival, hazard, and cumulative hazard for a discrete event-time distribution, compares an exponential model with SciPy, and verifies monotonicity and algebraic identities. Production guidance fixes time origin, event, horizon, time zones, censoring, delayed entry, competing events, and label maturity; monitors censoring by segment and calendar time; and blocks evaluation beyond supported follow-up. Survival methods use censored information—they do not make informative loss to follow-up harmless.
learningObjectives: Define survival, cumulative distribution, density, hazard, and cumulative hazard and move correctly between them.
Distinguish right, left, interval censoring, left truncation, and delayed entry in both words and risk-set logic.
State the censoring and observation assumptions required for common estimators and diagnose likely informative censoring.
Construct a leakage-safe event-time dataset with explicit origin, event, maturity, entry, and competing-event semantics.
lessons.labGoal: Compute discrete survival, hazard, and cumulative hazard and compare a continuous exponential model with SciPy while verifying algebraic and monotonicity invariants.
followUpQuestions: What is the relationship between hazard and survival?
How is left truncation different from left censoring?
What is restricted mean survival time?

lessons.title: Kaplan–Meier Estimator & Log-rank Test
lessons.interviewAnswer: At each distinct event time t_j, Kaplan-Meier multiplies the previous survival by 1-d_j/n_j, where d_j events occur among n_j subjects at risk just before the time. Censoring does not drop the curve; it removes subjects from later risk sets. The estimate assumes event and censoring times are independent, possibly conditional on group, and tails with few at risk are uncertain. The log-rank test compares observed group events with expected events from pooled risk sets across times and is most sensitive to roughly proportional hazard differences. I show confidence bands and numbers at risk, inspect crossing curves and censoring by group, predeclare the horizon and multiplicity plan, and avoid causal interpretation without an identified treatment comparison.
keyPoints: KM is a product of conditional survival fractions at event times.
Censoring removes later risk membership but does not create a survival drop.
Tail precision depends on numbers at risk, not only the plotted line.
Log-rank tests equality of survival experience with risk-set weighting.
Group curves and p-values do not adjust confounding or establish causality.
lessons.description: The Kaplan-Meier estimator reconstructs a survival curve from right-censored observations by multiplying conditional survival proportions at distinct event times. Censored subjects contribute to risk sets until censoring and then leave without causing a drop. This chapter derives the product-limit estimator, risk-set and tie conventions, Greenwood-style uncertainty, median and restricted-mean interpretation, group curves, and the log-rank test as an observed-minus-expected event comparison over pooled risk sets. You will understand why late tails become unstable when few subjects remain, why visually crossing curves violate the simple proportional weighting intuition of log-rank, and why a significant group comparison is not automatically a causal treatment effect. A worked cohort calculates every product step and a log-rank contribution. The lab implements Kaplan-Meier and log-rank from first principles, uses SciPy for the chi-square tail, and verifies censoring, symmetry, monotonicity, and identical-group invariants. Production guidance publishes number-at-risk tables and supported horizons, versions entry and tie rules, monitors censoring imbalance and label maturity, and avoids displaying or acting on survival tails supported by only a handful of subjects. KM is a marginal nonparametric estimate under censoring assumptions, not a covariate-adjusted prediction model.
learningObjectives: Compute a Kaplan-Meier curve from event counts and changing risk sets, including tied events and censoring.
Interpret survival steps, confidence bands, median survival, number at risk, and restricted mean within supported follow-up.
Derive the log-rank observed-minus-expected statistic and state its null, weighting, and assumptions.
Diagnose crossing curves, small tails, differential censoring, delayed entry, multiplicity, and causal overinterpretation.
lessons.labGoal: Implement Kaplan-Meier and the two-sample log-rank statistic, use SciPy for the chi-square tail, and verify censoring, monotonicity, symmetry, and identical-group behavior.
followUpQuestions: Why is KM a product instead of one minus cumulative observed event fraction?
What happens if the median is not reached?
When is log-rank less powerful?

lessons.title: Cox Proportional Hazards Model
lessons.interviewAnswer: Cox regression models h(t|x)=h0(t)exp(x beta). At each event time, partial likelihood compares the event subject's exp(x beta) with the sum over everyone then at risk, so beta can be estimated without parameterizing h0. Exponentiating a coefficient gives a conditional hazard ratio for a one-unit covariate change if hazards are proportional. After fitting beta, a Breslow-type estimator recovers cumulative baseline hazard and S(t|x)=exp[-H0(t)exp(x beta)]. I check Schoenfeld-residual trends and time interactions, model nonlinear continuous effects, specify ties and delayed entry, use robust or clustered inference when needed, and evaluate discrimination plus calibrated survival at supported horizons. Hazard ratios are not risk ratios, and observational coefficients are not causal effects without an identification design.
keyPoints: Partial likelihood compares each event with its contemporaneous risk set.
The baseline hazard cancels for coefficient estimation but is required for absolute survival.
Hazard ratios are conditional instantaneous-rate ratios, not probability or median ratios.
Proportional hazards is a testable modeling restriction, not a property guaranteed by the algorithm.
Time origin, delayed entry, ties, feature timing, and censoring belong in the model contract.
lessons.description: The Cox proportional-hazards model connects covariates to event timing without requiring a parametric baseline hazard. It writes the hazard as h(t|x)=h0(t)exp(x^T beta), so exp(beta_j) is a multiplicative hazard ratio under the proportional-hazards assumption. This chapter derives the partial likelihood from risk-set comparisons, explains why censored observations still contribute information, and separates coefficient estimation from recovery of the baseline hazard and absolute survival. It covers Breslow and Efron tie handling, delayed entry, time-dependent covariates, penalization, clustered dependence, Schoenfeld residuals, nonproportional effects, and the difference between predictive and causal interpretations. A worked example computes one partial-likelihood term. The lab exposes the mechanism with a one-covariate Newton optimizer, compares it with SciPy's general optimizer, and verifies permutation invariance, gradient convergence, and survival monotonicity. Production guidance treats the risk-set construction, time origin, feature availability, baseline-hazard version, and supported horizon as model artifacts. Cox is often a strong interpretable baseline, but a hazard ratio is neither a probability ratio nor a universal summary when effects vary over time.
learningObjectives: Derive Cox partial likelihood from event-wise risk sets and interpret coefficients as conditional hazard ratios.
Recover a baseline cumulative hazard and individual survival curves after estimating regression coefficients.
Diagnose proportional-hazards violations, tie and entry conventions, nonlinear effects, and dependent observations.
Design leakage-safe validation and deployment contracts for event-time regression.
lessons.labGoal: Expose Cox partial-likelihood mechanics, fit one coefficient with Newton's method, compare SciPy optimization, and verify risk-set and survival invariants.
followUpQuestions: Why does the baseline hazard cancel from partial likelihood?
How do you handle a covariate that violates PH?
What is the distinction between time-varying covariate and coefficient?

lessons.title: Survival Model Evaluation
lessons.interviewAnswer: I evaluate survival models along four axes. Concordance measures whether higher predicted risk precedes observed events among comparable subjects, but Harrell's C can be optimistic under heavy censoring, so I also use IPCW or Uno-style estimates. At prespecified horizons I report cumulative/dynamic AUC for discrimination, time-dependent Brier score for probability error, and calibration of predicted versus observed survival. IPCW estimates the censoring survival distribution on training data and weights observable cases and controls; people censored before a horizon are not treated as event-free. I integrate only over horizons with adequate follow-up, validate on later cohorts, bootstrap at the subject or cluster level, show subgroup event and censoring counts, and connect scores to threshold-specific decisions. One metric never proves ranking, calibration, and utility simultaneously.
keyPoints: Censoring determines which pairs and horizon labels are observable.
Concordance evaluates ordering, not probability calibration or clinical/product utility.
IPCW corrects observable contributions under a censoring model and a positivity condition.
Time-dependent AUC, Brier score, and calibration must be indexed by supported horizons.
Evaluation preprocessing, censoring estimation, horizons, and bootstrap units must avoid leakage.
lessons.description: Survival-model evaluation must respect censoring, time, and the prediction target. Ordinary accuracy and ROC calculations mislabel subjects censored before a horizon, while a single concordance number can reward ranking without calibrated probabilities. This chapter builds an evaluation stack around comparable pairs, Harrell's concordance, inverse-probability-of-censoring weighting, Uno-style concordance, cumulative/dynamic AUC, time-dependent Brier score, integrated Brier score, survival calibration, and decision utility. It explains which subjects define cases and controls at a horizon, why the censoring distribution must be estimated without test leakage, and how heavy censoring or short follow-up limits the estimand. A worked example separates an event case, an event-free control, and an indeterminate early censor. The lab implements comparable-pair concordance and an IPCW Brier score, then uses scikit-learn only on correctly defined horizon labels. Production guidance freezes evaluation horizons, split logic, censoring models, metric orientation, subgroup support, and label-maturity windows. Good evaluation reports discrimination, probability accuracy, calibration, and operational value together rather than declaring a model successful from one censoring-sensitive leaderboard number.
learningObjectives: Construct comparable event-time pairs and explain what Harrell and IPCW concordance estimate.
Define horizon-specific cases, controls, Brier scores, and cumulative/dynamic AUC under censoring.
Assess survival calibration and decision utility at supported horizons instead of relying on ranking alone.
Build temporal, leakage-safe, subgroup-aware evaluation pipelines with explicit censoring assumptions.
lessons.labGoal: Implement comparable-pair concordance and an IPCW horizon Brier score, use scikit-learn on correctly defined horizon labels, and verify orientation and censoring behavior.
followUpQuestions: Why can Harrell's C be optimistic with heavy censoring?
What is the difference between Brier score and calibration?
How should uncertainty be estimated with repeated interval rows?

lessons.title: Lagrange Multipliers, Duality & KKT Conditions
lessons.interviewAnswer: For minimize f(x) subject to g_i(x)<=0 and h_j(x)=0, the Lagrangian is L=f+sum lambda_i g_i+sum nu_j h_j with lambda_i>=0. KKT requires primal feasibility, dual feasibility, stationarity of L, and complementary slackness lambda_i g_i=0. Under a constraint qualification KKT is necessary for a local optimum; for a convex problem it is sufficient, and with Slater's condition strong duality holds. Multipliers are shadow prices: locally they quantify how the optimal value changes when a constraint bound is tightened, but their interpretation depends on units, sign convention, degeneracy, and perturbation size.
keyPoints: The Lagrangian prices constraint violation
KKT combines four conditions, not stationarity alone
Constraint qualifications prevent pathological necessity failures
Convexity turns a KKT point into a global optimum
Dual variables are local sensitivities with units and validity ranges
lessons.description: Lagrange multipliers, duality, and the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions connect constrained optimization to geometry, economic sensitivity, and verifiable optimality. This chapter derives the Lagrangian for equality and inequality constraints, explains feasible directions and active constraints, distinguishes primal and dual problems, and develops weak duality, strong duality, Slater's condition, complementary slackness, constraint qualifications, and dual sensitivity. You will learn when KKT conditions are necessary, when they are sufficient, why multiplier signs depend on convention, and why stationarity alone never proves feasibility or global optimality. A worked resource-allocation problem computes the primal solution and shadow price by hand. The lab builds KKT residual checks for a constrained quadratic, compares the result with SciPy's SLSQP interface, and verifies primal feasibility, dual feasibility, stationarity, and complementarity. Production guidance covers scaling, degeneracy, infeasibility, inaccurate multipliers, solver status, sensitivity ranges, observability, and safe fallbacks. The payoff is the ability to interpret a constrained solver result as a scientific decision and certificate rather than an unexplained vector.
learningObjectives: Construct a Lagrangian with consistent inequality signs and derive stationarity, feasibility, and complementary slackness conditions.
Explain weak versus strong duality and identify conditions under which KKT conditions are necessary or sufficient.
Interpret optimal multipliers as local value sensitivities while stating sign, units, and range limitations.
Diagnose candidate solutions through scaled KKT residuals and solver termination evidence.
lessons.labGoal: Compute and verify the KKT certificate for a binding convex inequality, then compare the candidate with a constrained SciPy solve.
followUpQuestions: What does complementary slackness mean?
When are KKT conditions sufficient?
What is Slater's condition used for?

lessons.title: Linear Programming
lessons.interviewAnswer: An LP minimizes or maximizes c^T x subject to linear constraints and bounds. The feasible set is a convex polyhedron; if a finite optimum exists, at least one extreme point is optimal. Simplex moves among adjacent basic feasible solutions, while interior-point methods travel through the interior. Every LP has a dual whose feasible objective bounds the primal, and under standard feasibility conditions strong duality makes the gap zero. In practice I define variables and units carefully, inspect status, primal residuals, objective reconstruction, dual gap and sensitivity, and explicitly distinguish optimal, feasible-but-uncertified, infeasible, and unbounded results.
keyPoints: Variables and units determine whether the model represents the real decision
LP feasible regions are convex polyhedra
Simplex and interior-point methods exploit different geometry
The dual provides bounds and local resource values
Status, residuals, and dual evidence are part of the output
lessons.description: Linear programming (LP) optimizes a linear objective over linear equality, inequality, and bound constraints. Its simple algebra hides a powerful geometry: feasible solutions form a convex polyhedron, optimal solutions occur on a face containing an extreme point when an optimum exists, and a dual program supplies bounds, shadow prices, and certificates of optimality or infeasibility. This chapter develops modeling from decisions and units through standard forms, slack variables, vertices, simplex intuition, interior-point methods, duality, sensitivity, degeneracy, alternate optima, infeasibility, unboundedness, and numerical scaling. You will learn to translate business rules without reversing signs or mixing units, distinguish model infeasibility from solver failure, and validate solutions using constraint residuals, objective reconstruction, and dual evidence. A worked production-planning example derives candidate vertices and a binding-capacity interpretation. The lab enumerates every 2D vertex from scratch, compares the optimum with SciPy's HiGHS-backed `linprog`, and verifies feasibility and objective agreement. Production guidance covers sparse models, solver statuses, tolerances, warm starts, time limits, security, drift, safe fallbacks, and rollback.
learningObjectives: Translate a decision problem into linear variables, an objective, constraints, bounds, units, and explicit assumptions.
Explain LP geometry, extreme points, simplex and interior-point intuitions, and the primal-dual certificate.
Diagnose optimal, infeasible, unbounded, degenerate, and multiple-optimum outcomes from evidence rather than guesswork.
Implement vertex enumeration for a small LP and validate a library solution using independent invariants.
lessons.labGoal: Enumerate a two-variable LP's vertices from first principles, compare with SciPy linprog, and verify primal feasibility plus objective agreement.
followUpQuestions: Why does an LP optimum occur at a vertex?
What does unbounded mean?
What is degeneracy?

lessons.title: Integer & Mixed-Integer Optimization
lessons.interviewAnswer: A mixed-integer program combines linear constraints and objective terms with some variables restricted to integers, often binary. The LP relaxation drops integrality and gives a bound. Branch-and-bound partitions the feasible set by branching on fractional variables, solves relaxations at nodes, prunes nodes whose bounds cannot beat the incumbent, and uses cuts and heuristics to tighten bounds or find feasible solutions. Rounding is not generally valid. In production I build tight formulations, use indicator constraints when available, set explicit time and gap limits, and report the feasible incumbent, best bound, relative gap, residuals, and solver status separately.
keyPoints: Integrality models choices and logic, not just rounded quantities
LP relaxations supply bounds but not necessarily feasible decisions
Branch-and-bound tracks incumbent and global bound
Strong formulations and symmetry breaking can dominate solver tuning
A time-limited feasible solution is not automatically optimal
lessons.description: Integer and mixed-integer optimization represents indivisible choices, logical rules, fixed costs, assignments, schedules, and network designs that continuous models cannot express faithfully. This chapter develops binary, integer, continuous, semi-continuous, and mixed variables; strong formulations; LP relaxations; integrality gaps; branch-and-bound; cutting planes; primal heuristics; constraint programming and CP-SAT; big-M, indicator, and logical constraints; symmetry; decomposition; and solver certificates. You will learn why rounding an LP solution can violate constraints or destroy value, how bounds turn exponential search into a quantifiable optimality gap, and how formulation strength often matters more than solver tuning. A worked knapsack example contrasts integer, relaxed, and rounded decisions. The lab enumerates a small binary portfolio from scratch, compares it with SciPy's `milp`, and verifies feasibility, optimality, and a nonzero relaxation gap. Production guidance covers time limits, incumbent-versus-bound semantics, deterministic replay, solution pools, infeasibility, numerical scaling, licensing, monitoring, safe fallbacks, and rollback. The objective is to ship auditable discrete decisions, not merely obtain a solver vector.
learningObjectives: Model discrete decisions and logical relationships with explicit variable domains and tight linear constraints.
Explain LP relaxation, branch-and-bound, cuts, heuristics, integrality gaps, and termination certificates.
Recognize weak big-M formulations, symmetry, scaling, and horizon choices that make otherwise correct models intractable.
Validate feasible incumbents and optimality gaps independently before operational use.
lessons.labGoal: Solve a binary knapsack by enumeration, compare it with SciPy milp, and verify domains, capacity, objective, and relaxation gap.
followUpQuestions: What is an integrality gap?
Why is big-M dangerous?
What can you return at a time limit?

lessons.title: Bayesian Optimization for Expensive Objectives
lessons.interviewAnswer: Bayesian optimization is useful when objective evaluations are expensive and gradients are unavailable. It fits a probabilistic surrogate, commonly a Gaussian process, to observed configurations and outcomes. An acquisition function such as expected improvement or UCB combines predicted performance with uncertainty, is optimized cheaply to choose the next evaluation, and the posterior is updated after observing it. I define the search space and budget, seed with a space-filling design, model noise and constraints, compare against random search over repeated runs, and monitor regret, feasibility, cost, failed trials, and calibration. It is usually best in modest dimensions, not a default for cheap or massively high-dimensional objectives.
keyPoints: BO optimizes evaluation choice, not just a fitted response surface
Posterior uncertainty drives exploration
The acquisition is cheap to optimize but can itself be multimodal
Noise, constraints, batches, and fidelity change the correct decision rule
Repeated-budget comparisons against simple baselines are essential
lessons.description: Bayesian optimization (BO) is a sequential strategy for optimizing a costly black-box objective when each evaluation consumes meaningful time, money, compute, or risk. It fits a probabilistic surrogate to observed evaluations, uses posterior uncertainty to score the value of candidate experiments, evaluates a selected candidate, and repeats. This chapter develops Gaussian-process surrogates, priors and kernels, noisy observations, exploration versus exploitation, probability of improvement, expected improvement, upper-confidence-bound and information-based acquisitions, acquisition optimization, initialization, constraints, batch and asynchronous experiments, multi-fidelity evaluation, high-dimensional and mixed spaces, stopping, and honest evaluation. You will learn when BO is preferable to random search or gradient methods, how model misspecification and overconfident uncertainty can waste a budget, and why the acquisition is a decision rule rather than the real objective. The lab implements a one-dimensional Gaussian-process posterior and expected-improvement loop, compares it with scikit-learn, and verifies uncertainty and simple-regret improvement. Production guidance covers experiment identity, failed trials, concurrency, reproducibility, cost, safety, monitoring, and rollback.
