lessons.title: Database Normalization: 1NF to 3NF
lessons.interviewAnswer: Normalization organizes attributes around keys and functional dependencies to reduce redundancy and update anomalies. 1NF requires atomic relation-valued design in the chosen model; 2NF removes dependencies on only part of a composite candidate key; 3NF removes non-key attributes depending transitively on keys, with a formal dependency condition; BCNF requires every nontrivial determinant to be a superkey. A decomposition must also be lossless, and dependency preservation is desirable. Denormalize only for a measured workload and define how duplicate facts stay consistent.
keyPoints: Dependencies come from semantics
Candidate keys may be composite
Decomposition must be lossless
3NF and BCNF differ
Denormalization creates maintenance duty
lessons.description: Relational normalization uses keys and functional dependencies to place facts where they can be inserted, updated, and deleted without contradictory copies. First, second, and third normal form are not a ritual of splitting tables; they are tests against a declared meaning of attributes. This chapter defines superkeys, candidate keys, prime attributes, determinants, functional and transitive dependencies, then derives 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, and Boyce-Codd normal form (BCNF). It explains lossless decomposition and dependency preservation, because individually clean-looking tables can still fail to reconstruct the original relation or enforce a rule locally. You will normalize an order-line relation, identify update, insertion, and deletion anomalies, and preserve historical prices rather than incorrectly deriving them from a current product table. The design section connects normalized operational schemas with foreign keys, temporal validity, generated identifiers, JSON, star schemas, materialized views, performance, and governance. The objective is to model one fact once under the correct key, then denormalize only for a measured read or analytics need with explicit ownership and refresh semantics.
learningObjectives: Derive candidate keys and functional dependencies from domain semantics rather than sample coincidences.
Normalize a relation through 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, and BCNF while checking lossless join and dependency preservation.
Choose deliberate denormalization for operational or analytical workloads with integrity, history, refresh, lineage, and performance controls.
lessons.labGoal: Use SQLite constraints to model normalized orders and verify uniqueness, references, historical price stability, and revenue reconciliation.

visualSummaries.title: Normalized source and denormalized read model

followUpQuestions: How do 3NF and BCNF differ?
What is lossless decomposition?
Why preserve dependencies?

lessons.title: Query Plans & SQL Performance
lessons.interviewAnswer: The optimizer transforms declarative SQL into a physical operator tree using statistics and a cost model. Read from leaf scans upward, tracking estimated rows, actual rows per loop, join algorithms, filters, sorts, memory, buffers, and spill. `EXPLAIN` estimates without running; `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` executes and can have side effects for writes. Large estimated-versus-actual cardinality errors often cause poor join order or memory choices. Costs are planner units, not milliseconds, so validate with representative runtime and workload impact before changing SQL, indexes, statistics, or configuration.
keyPoints: Plan is a physical operator tree
Cardinality drives choices
Actual rows times loops matters
Cost units are not time
Fix evidence, not node names
lessons.description: A query plan is the database's chosen physical program for a declarative SQL statement. It specifies scans, filters, joins, sorts, aggregates, exchanges, and materialization, with estimated rows and costs derived from statistics and a cost model. This chapter teaches plan reading from leaves to root, distinguishes estimated `EXPLAIN` from execution-producing `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`, and shows how cardinality errors cascade into bad join order, algorithm, memory, and parallelism choices. It covers sequential and index scans, nested-loop, hash, and merge joins, sorts and spills, hash aggregation, predicate pushdown, projection, sargability, prepared-plan/parameter effects, and why estimated cost is not milliseconds. You will diagnose a slow join by comparing estimates with actual rows and buffers, then fix the underlying distribution, predicate, statistics, index, or query semantics rather than blindly forcing a node. Production sections address safe plan capture, workload baselines, plan changes after upgrades, memory and temp I/O, concurrency, and regression monitoring. The goal is evidence-led optimization without cargo-cult hints.
learningObjectives: Read physical plans from data sources to root and explain cardinality, loops, rows, cost, buffers, memory, and spill evidence.
Connect estimation errors and predicate/index shape to scan, join order, algorithm, aggregation, sorting, and parallel choices.
Optimize safely with representative execution evidence, workload-level measurement, reversible changes, and plan-regression monitoring.
lessons.labGoal: Use SQLite plan output and timing to verify index eligibility, result equivalence, and the difference between selective and broad predicates.

visualSummaries.title: Read a plan from leaves to root

followUpQuestions: Why can estimated and actual rows differ greatly?
Why might an index scan be slower for many rows?
What is the risk of EXPLAIN ANALYZE on UPDATE?

lessons.title: Transactions & Isolation Levels
lessons.interviewAnswer: Isolation controls how concurrent transactions appear to execute. Read Committed commonly gives each statement a fresh committed snapshot; repeatable/snapshot levels hold a stable transaction view but can still permit write skew in some systems; Serializable aims to make committed outcomes equivalent to some serial order and may abort transactions that threaten that guarantee. MVCC lets readers see versions rather than blocking every writer, but old snapshots have cleanup cost. Choose isolation from the invariant, use explicit locks or constraints where appropriate, and retry serialization failures and deadlocks as whole idempotent transactions.
keyPoints: Name the invariant first
Isolation controls histories
MVCC uses version visibility
Snapshot can allow write skew
Serializable requires retry handling
lessons.description: Transaction isolation defines which concurrent interleavings a database permits and what each transaction may observe. It is not equivalent to atomicity, and level names alone are insufficient because implementations differ. This chapter builds a history-based model, then explains dirty reads, nonrepeatable reads, phantoms, lost updates, write skew, and serialization anomalies. It covers multiversion concurrency control (MVCC), snapshots, locks, optimistic validation, PostgreSQL's current Read Committed, Repeatable Read, and Serializable behavior, serialization failures, deadlocks, and retry design. You will trace an on-call schedule where two individually valid updates violate a cross-row invariant under snapshot-style execution, then prevent it with a serializable transaction or explicit locking/materialized constraint. The operations section addresses transaction scope, deterministic lock order, read-only replicas, connection pools, long snapshots, timeouts, idempotency, metrics, and chaos testing. The objective is to choose the weakest level and explicit controls that actually preserve named invariants, then treat abort and retry as a normal part of concurrent correctness.
learningObjectives: Classify concurrent histories by dirty read, nonrepeatable read, phantom, lost update, write skew, and serialization behavior.
Explain snapshot/MVCC visibility and compare target-engine isolation guarantees without relying solely on standard level names.
Implement invariant-preserving transactions with locks or serializable validation, bounded idempotent retries, timeouts, and contention monitoring.
lessons.labGoal: Simulate write skew and verify that a shared guard lock/serial critical section preserves the cross-row invariant.
followUpQuestions: What is write skew?
Why can MVCC create bloat?
How do deadlock and serialization failure differ?

lessons.title: Columnar Storage, Parquet & Predicate Pushdown
lessons.interviewAnswer: Parquet stores data by column within row groups. Each row group has one contiguous column chunk per field, split into encoded and compressed pages, with footer metadata describing schema and locations and often statistics. Analytical readers can avoid unprojected columns and skip row groups or pages whose metadata proves a predicate cannot match. Similar adjacent values compress effectively through encodings such as dictionary and run-length encoding. Performance still depends on engine support, file and row-group size, sort order, statistics, filter form and object-store requests. Parquet is a file format, not a transaction manager; reliable tables need metadata, atomic commits, schema policy and compaction around the files.
keyPoints: Row groups partition rows
Column chunks make projection cheap
Pages carry encoding and compression
Statistics can prove non-matches
A file format is not a table transaction layer
lessons.description: Apache Parquet is an open columnar file format for analytical data. A file is divided horizontally into row groups; each row group contains one contiguous column chunk per column, and column chunks contain encoded and compressed pages. That hierarchy lets readers project only required columns and use metadata statistics, dictionaries, page indexes and partition information to skip data that cannot match a predicate. This chapter derives the I/O and compression benefits, explains definition and repetition levels for nested structures, and separates file-format capabilities from query-engine behavior. You will learn why predicate pushdown is not the same as file pruning, how row-group size and sort order affect selectivity, why thousands of tiny files damage planning and throughput, and why a Parquet file alone does not provide table transactions, schema governance or safe concurrent updates. A worked event dataset estimates bytes avoided under projection and time-range pruning. Production guidance covers types, timestamps, nulls, dictionary fallback, compression, encryption, object-store requests, compaction, statistics, corruption, schema evolution and table formats. The aim is to reason from the query and physical layout to measured scan cost instead of assuming the `.parquet` suffix automatically makes analytics fast.
learningObjectives: Explain Parquet's file, row-group, column-chunk and page hierarchy and how it supports projection, encoding, compression and parallel reads.
Distinguish partition pruning, row-group/page skipping and predicate pushdown, then diagnose why an intended filter still scans data.
Choose and operate file size, row-group layout, sort order, schema, encoding and table metadata from real workloads and reliability needs.
lessons.labGoal: Expose dictionary encoding and min/max row-group pruning, then compare the result with an idiomatic PyArrow Parquet scan (Use It requires `pyarrow`).

visualSummaries.title: How a selective analytical scan avoids work

followUpQuestions: What is a row group?
Why does sorting help pruning?
Why are tiny files harmful?

lessons.title: Warehouse vs Data Lake vs Lakehouse
lessons.interviewAnswer: A warehouse integrates managed relational storage, SQL compute, transactions, optimization and governance for analytical workloads. A data lake stores varied data in scalable object storage and open formats for many engines, but bare files lack atomic table updates and consistent metadata. A lakehouse adds a transactional metadata/table layer over open files, providing snapshots, schema and partition evolution, time travel and data skipping while retaining direct multi-engine access. The right choice depends on workload, latency, governance, interoperability, skills and total operating cost. Evaluate concrete guarantees—especially commits, deletes, concurrency, catalog consistency and rollback—not the architecture label.
keyPoints: Architecture is a capability bundle
Files are not tables
Snapshots make publication atomic
Open access trades against centralized control
One storage copy can still have many semantics
lessons.description: A data warehouse, data lake and lakehouse are architectural patterns assembled from storage, metadata, transaction, governance and compute capabilities—not quality rankings. A warehouse offers managed relational tables, SQL optimization, transactions and governance with controlled storage and strong workload integration. A data lake places diverse data in scalable object storage with open files and multiple compute engines, gaining flexibility while requiring explicit metadata, quality and publication discipline. A lakehouse adds a transactional metadata/table layer over directly accessible open files to provide snapshots, atomic updates, schema and partition evolution, time travel and improved optimization. This chapter separates file format from table format, catalog, engine and semantic model; compares coupling, latency, interoperability, cost and operational burden; and explains why “one copy” does not mean one consistent interpretation. You will learn to select an architecture from workloads and ownership, design bronze/raw through curated publication without turning layers into dumping grounds, and manage small files, compaction, concurrent writes and rollback. A worked multi-engine platform uses immutable object storage plus snapshot metadata and reconciled marts. The goal is to evaluate concrete guarantees and failure behavior instead of choosing a fashionable label or assuming a lakehouse automatically replaces every operational and analytical system.
learningObjectives: Compare warehouse, lake and lakehouse patterns across storage access, metadata, transactions, governance, workload support and operational ownership.
Explain how an open table format turns immutable files into atomic snapshots with evolution, pruning, concurrent commit and rollback.
Design a governed multi-workload analytical platform with explicit publication, reconciliation, security, cost, reliability and exit strategy.
lessons.labGoal: Model an immutable-file table snapshot, verify atomic pointer publication and rollback, and show why directory listing is not a consistent table view.
followUpQuestions: What does a table format add above Parquet?
When is a warehouse still a strong choice?
What is the small-file problem?

lessons.title: LDA & QDA
lessons.interviewAnswer: LDA and QDA are generative classifiers that model each class as multivariate Gaussian and apply Bayes' rule. QDA estimates a separate covariance Σ_k for every class, producing quadratic log-posterior boundaries. LDA assumes one shared covariance Σ, so quadratic x terms cancel and boundaries are linear. LDA estimates fewer parameters and is usually more stable with limited data; QDA can capture class-specific orientation and scale but needs much more data and regularization. Priors shift intercepts and decisions. I standardize only when justified by the feature pipeline, fit covariance and shrinkage inside validation, inspect conditioning, compare Gaussian NB's diagonal assumption, evaluate calibration and subgroup errors, and avoid causal interpretations of discriminant directions.
keyPoints: Both methods model class priors and Gaussian class-conditional densities, then maximize posterior probability.
Shared covariance makes LDA boundaries linear; class-specific covariance makes QDA boundaries quadratic.
Covariance estimation, conditioning and shrinkage dominate performance when features are numerous relative to samples.
Gaussian NB is the diagonal class-specific covariance special case; it is not the same as LDA.
LDA classification and supervised dimensionality reduction are related but distinct outputs.
lessons.description: Linear and quadratic discriminant analysis classify by combining Gaussian class-conditional densities with class priors. This chapter derives QDA's quadratic discriminant score and shows how a shared covariance cancels quadratic terms to produce LDA's linear boundary. It covers Mahalanobis distance, determinant volume penalties, priors, covariance parameter counts, singularity, SVD solvers, shrinkage, robust alternatives, Gaussian Naive Bayes, logistic regression, calibration and supervised LDA projection. Worked examples compute a one-dimensional boundary and show why QDA collapses with a rare class in high dimension. The lab implements stable log discriminants with solved linear systems, compares predictions with scikit-learn and verifies that shared covariance matches LDA while unequal covariance can change the boundary. Production guidance versions units, class mapping, priors, covariance strategy and solver; monitors conditioning, prevalence, distance, calibration, drift and subgroup outcomes; and defines fallbacks and rollback. The emphasis is on the assumption-capacity trade-off: covariance flexibility is useful only when the data can estimate it.
learningObjectives: Derive LDA and QDA discriminant scores from Gaussian class-conditionals and Bayes' rule.
Explain how shared versus class-specific covariance changes boundary shape and parameter count.
Use shrinkage and stable solvers when covariance estimates are ill-conditioned.
Distinguish LDA classification, LDA projection, Gaussian NB and logistic regression.
lessons.labGoal: Implement Gaussian LDA and QDA log scores, compare with scikit-learn, and verify covariance and probability behavior.
followUpQuestions: Why is LDA's boundary linear?
When does Gaussian NB relate to QDA?
Why can LDA outperform QDA?

lessons.title: AdaBoost
lessons.interviewAnswer: AdaBoost builds a weighted vote of weak binary classifiers. It begins with uniform observation weights, fits a learner to minimize weighted error ε_t, assigns it vote α_t=0.5 log((1-ε_t)/ε_t), then multiplies weights by exp(-α_t y_i h_t(x_i)) so misclassified points receive more attention. The final score is Σ_t α_t h_t(x), usually thresholded at zero. For a learner better than random, α is positive; perfect and chance-level cases need explicit handling. AdaBoost minimizes exponential loss stagewise and can keep improving margins after training error reaches zero, but exponential weighting is sensitive to mislabeled points and outliers. I validate depth, rounds, learning rate, weights and thresholds with leakage-safe splits and monitor margins, calibration, subgroup error and weight concentration.
keyPoints: Training weights are an optimization device that changes which observations the next weak learner emphasizes.
A learner's vote grows with its edge over random guessing; chance-level learners contribute no useful direction.
The multiplicative update is equivalent to greedy reduction of exponential loss.
Margins help explain continued improvement after zero training error, but they are not calibrated probabilities.
Label noise and outliers can capture extreme weight and destabilize later rounds.
lessons.description: AdaBoost creates a strong binary classifier by repeatedly fitting weak learners to adaptively weighted observations and combining them with reliability-based votes. This chapter derives weighted error, the closed-form alpha vote, the multiplicative update, exponential loss and signed margins. It contrasts AdaBoost with bagging and gradient boosting, explains stumps, learning rate, round count, multiclass extensions, sample-weight contracts, class imbalance, label noise, outliers, calibration and early stopping. Worked examples calculate one complete weight update and show how a mislabeled case can dominate later rounds. The lab implements weighted decision stumps and binary AdaBoost from scratch, compares it with scikit-learn and verifies normalization, finite votes and training improvement. Production guidance versions label encoding, weak-learner and weight semantics, monitors margin and weight concentration, evaluates threshold and calibration separately, and defines canaries, fallbacks and rollback. The method's central strength and weakness are the same: it refuses to ignore repeatedly misclassified observations, whether they represent a valuable hard boundary or corrupt data.
learningObjectives: Derive AdaBoost's learner vote and multiplicative observation-weight update.
Explain its exponential-loss and margin interpretations and contrast it with bagging.
Diagnose weak-learner, chance-error, label-noise and class-weight failure modes.
Evaluate and deploy boosted votes with explicit calibration, threshold and monitoring layers.
lessons.labGoal: Implement binary AdaBoost with weighted stumps, compare with scikit-learn, and verify votes, normalization and error reduction.
followUpQuestions: Why must the weak learner beat chance?
What does learning rate do?
Why is AdaBoost sensitive to noise?

lessons.title: Probability Calibration
lessons.interviewAnswer: A probabilistic classifier is calibrated when predictions near p are positive about p of the time in the target population. Calibration is distinct from discrimination: a monotonic transform preserves ranking and AUC while changing probability meaning. I evaluate probabilities on untouched natural-prevalence data using reliability diagrams plus proper scores such as log loss and Brier score, remembering that those scores also reflect resolution and prevalence, not calibration alone. Post-hoc Platt scaling fits a logistic mapping and is data-efficient but shape-restricted; isotonic regression is flexible and monotone but can overfit small calibration sets. Calibration must be fitted on predictions from data not used to fit the base model, using a separate split or cross-fitting. I then choose action thresholds from cost on separate evidence when necessary, monitor calibration by probability range and cohort with uncertainty, and recalibrate only after confirming label maturity and population shift.
keyPoints: Calibration asks whether probability values match frequencies; discrimination asks whether scores rank cases.
Reliability diagrams depend on binning and need counts and uncertainty, especially in high-risk tails.
Brier and log loss are proper scores but mix calibration with sharpness, resolution and base-rate difficulty.
Fit calibrators on held-out or out-of-fold predictions, never on the base model's in-sample predictions.
Class weighting, resampling, prior shift and subgroup mixture can all change probability meaning.
lessons.description: Probability calibration gives classifier scores an empirical risk meaning. This chapter separates calibration from discrimination and sharpness, defines population calibration, and explains why perfect ranking, perfect calibration and useful decisions are different properties. It builds reliability diagrams with equal-width and equal-frequency bins, includes counts and uncertainty, and warns that expected calibration error is bin-dependent. It derives Brier and log loss as proper scoring rules while explaining their dependence on resolution and prevalence. It compares Platt scaling, isotonic regression, cross-validated calibration and prior-shift adjustment, with strict separation between base-training, calibration and final-test data. Worked examples show a monotonic score transform preserving AUC while damaging probabilities and a constant-prevalence forecast that is calibrated but uninformative. The lab intentionally distorts logits, fits a sigmoid calibrator on a separate split and verifies improved held-out Brier loss without changing ranking. Production guidance monitors probability-range support, delayed labels, cohort reliability, decision value and recalibration governance. Special attention goes to sparse high-risk regions where a smooth global average can conceal the decisions with greatest consequence.
learningObjectives: Distinguish probability calibration, discrimination, sharpness and downstream decision utility.
Construct and critique reliability diagrams and bin-based calibration summaries.
Fit sigmoid or isotonic calibration without reusing base-training or final-test outcomes.
Monitor probability semantics across prevalence, cohort, label delay and policy changes.
lessons.labGoal: Distort a well-ranked score, fit sigmoid calibration on separate data, and verify held-out probability improvement without ranking change.
followUpQuestions: When would you choose isotonic over Platt scaling?
Can a model be calibrated within every subgroup?
Why is Brier score not a pure calibration metric?

lessons.title: Decision Thresholds & Cost-sensitive Classification
lessons.interviewAnswer: Threshold tuning converts a fixed score into an action policy. The model estimates a ranking or probability; the threshold should follow false-positive and false-negative costs, benefits, review capacity, safety constraints and abstention options. For calibrated probability p with false-positive cost C_FP and false-negative cost C_FN and no other utility terms, predict positive when p exceeds C_FP/(C_FP+C_FN). Real systems often need constraints or empirical utility instead. I select thresholds on validation or inner cross-validation predictions, lock the policy, and estimate it on untouched data; maximizing test-set F1 is leakage. I report the entire operating point—threshold, confusion counts, prevalence, queue volume, uncertainty and slice constraints—not just a metric. I also monitor score and prevalence drift because a fixed numeric threshold can produce changing workload, and I version rollback thresholds separately from the model.
keyPoints: A threshold is a decision policy, not an intrinsic property of a classifier score.
Expected-cost thresholds require calibrated probabilities and explicit, correctly oriented costs.
Select thresholds on development predictions and estimate the locked policy on independent outcomes.
Capacity, minimum-recall and safety constraints often describe the problem better than maximizing F1.
Ties, abstention, subgroup policies, delayed labels and changing prevalence need explicit governance.
lessons.description: Threshold tuning turns classifier scores into operational decisions. This chapter derives the cost-optimal cutoff for calibrated binary probabilities, generalizes to empirical utility and constrained optimization, and explains why 0.5 and maximum F1 are not default truths. It covers minimum-recall, maximum-false-positive and fixed-capacity policies; top-K selection; accept-review-reject bands; abstention; ties; per-group policies and their governance implications. It separates model fitting, probability calibration, threshold selection and final assessment so test labels never choose the reported operating point. Worked examples derive a 1/11 cutoff from asymmetric costs and show how a fixed threshold changes queue volume under drift. The lab searches thresholds on validation data, verifies the utility calculation and evaluates the locked threshold on a separate test set. Production guidance versions costs, constraints, tie rules and cohort definitions, monitors workload and threshold-level confusion counts, backfills delayed outcomes, canaries policy changes and retains independent model and policy rollback controls. It treats workload and safety limits as explicit constraints rather than after-the-fact dashboard commentary.
learningObjectives: Derive probability thresholds from asymmetric costs and formulate constrained alternatives.
Select a policy from validation or inner out-of-fold predictions without test leakage.
Evaluate thresholds using counts, workload, utility, uncertainty and critical slices.
Operate fixed, capacity-based and abstaining policies under prevalence and score drift.
lessons.labGoal: Select a cost-aware threshold on validation scores, lock it, and verify utility and independent test evaluation.
followUpQuestions: When is a top-K policy preferable?
Should calibration happen before threshold tuning?
How do you handle tied scores at capacity K?

lessons.title: Regression Metrics: RMSE, MAE, MAPE & R²
lessons.interviewAnswer: Regression metrics answer different questions. MAE and RMSE measure error in target units, with RMSE emphasizing large misses. R-squared compares squared error with a constant-mean baseline on the evaluated sample; it can be negative out of sample and is not a percentage of predictions that are correct. MAPE measures relative absolute error but is undefined at zero, explodes near zero and asymmetrically penalizes underprediction. WAPE is total absolute error divided by total absolute actual volume, so high-volume observations dominate and cancellation is avoided; sMAPE has bounded-looking formulas but multiple conventions and awkward zero behavior. For forecasts I also use scaled errors such as MASE against a training-only naive baseline. I choose a metric from decision cost and aggregation level, report complementary scale, relative, bias and tail measures, preserve time/entity structure, and verify denominators, weights and inverse transformations.
keyPoints: Absolute, squared, relative, explained-variance and scaled metrics encode distinct estimands and weights.
Out-of-sample R-squared may be negative because a model can lose to the evaluation-set mean baseline.
MAPE is invalid at zero and gives tiny actual values extreme influence; it is also directionally asymmetric.
WAPE is a ratio of aggregates, not the mean of percentage errors, and weights large actual volumes more.
A production scorecard needs scale-dependent error, signed bias, tails, slices and a decision-relevant baseline.
lessons.description: Regression evaluation requires more than choosing between MAE and RMSE. This chapter organizes scale-dependent, percentage, relative, scaled and baseline-relative metrics around the decisions they represent. It derives R-squared and explains negative out-of-sample values, intercept effects and why R-squared is not an accuracy percentage. It dissects MAPE's zero denominator, near-zero explosion and underprediction asymmetry; distinguishes WAPE from a mean of ratios; documents competing sMAPE conventions; and introduces MASE, RMSLE, signed bias, quantile loss and tail error. Worked examples show metric rankings reversing across low- and high-volume series and a model losing to the mean. The lab implements the major formulas, checks them against scikit-learn where applicable, and verifies scale and zero invariants. Production guidance fixes target units, transforms, baselines, horizon and entity weights, reports paired uncertainty and relevant slices, and treats each denominator or aggregation change as a metric-version change. It also separates portfolio performance from the experience of a typical series or entity, preventing accidental weighting from becoming an unstated product decision.
learningObjectives: Compute and interpret R-squared, MAPE, WAPE, sMAPE, scaled error and signed bias.
Diagnose zero, scale, asymmetry, weighting and aggregation failures in normalized metrics.
Choose complementary regression measures from operational costs and baseline performance.
Design grouped and time-aware evaluation with paired uncertainty and versioned definitions.
lessons.labGoal: Implement R-squared and common relative regression metrics, verify library agreement, and expose zero and scale behavior.
followUpQuestions: When is MASE useful?
Why can R-squared be negative?
How would you evaluate asymmetric inventory cost?

lessons.title: Scaling & Encoding Features
lessons.interviewAnswer: Encoding and scaling translate raw fields into a representation whose geometry matches the estimator. Standardization centers and divides by training standard deviation; robust scaling uses quantiles; min-max scaling fixes a training range but future values may exceed it. Distance-, gradient- and regularization-based models are scale-sensitive, while ordinary tree splits usually are not. One-hot encoding represents nominal categories without fake order; ordinal encoding is appropriate only when order is real; target or count encodings need fold-local construction and smoothing to prevent label leakage. I fit every learned statistic and vocabulary inside the training fold with a ColumnTransformer or equivalent pipeline, define behavior for missing and unseen categories, preserve sparse output where useful, and version feature names. Scaling does not make a skewed distribution Gaussian and encoding does not create semantic equivalence; both are production contracts that must remain identical online and offline.
keyPoints: Representation should match estimator geometry, regularization and the semantic type of each field.
Means, variances, quantiles, category vocabularies and target statistics are learned state and must fit on training data only.
One-hot avoids arbitrary nominal order but can create high-dimensional sparse features and unstable rare levels.
Target encoding requires nested or out-of-fold values for training rows plus smoothing and unseen-category fallback.
Unknown, missing, infrequent and structurally inapplicable categories need distinct, versioned handling when semantics differ.
lessons.description: Encoding and scaling define the numerical representation consumed by machine-learning estimators. This chapter compares standard, min-max, max-absolute, robust, unit-norm, logarithmic, power and quantile transforms and explains which alter units, distances, tails or distribution shape. It connects scale to gradient optimization, regularization, kernels, nearest neighbors, PCA and tree models. For categorical data it distinguishes nominal one-hot, ordinal, hashing, count, frequency and target encodings; addresses high cardinality, rare levels, missing values and unseen categories; and derives smoothed out-of-fold target statistics. It shows why every fitted statistic and vocabulary belongs inside cross-validation and why sparse matrices should not be centered blindly. Worked examples expose unit-dominated distance and self-leaking target encoding. The lab builds a typed ColumnTransformer, verifies training statistics and unknown-category behavior, and confirms manual standardized values. Production guidance versions schemas, categories, feature names and transforms, tests extremes and unknowns, monitors range and vocabulary drift, and guarantees online-offline parity. The representation is treated as a fitted, testable component of the model rather than disposable cleaning code.
learningObjectives: Choose numeric scaling and transformation from estimator geometry and data semantics.
Encode nominal, ordinal and high-cardinality categories without invented order or target leakage.
Build typed fold-local preprocessing pipelines with stable sparse output and unknown handling.
Version and monitor production representations, feature names, ranges and vocabularies.
lessons.labGoal: Build a typed numeric and categorical transformer, verify training-only statistics, and test stable unseen-category behavior.
followUpQuestions: Which models usually require scaling?
How do you handle unseen categories?
Why avoid centering sparse one-hot matrices?

lessons.title: Interactions & Domain Feature Engineering
lessons.interviewAnswer: A feature interaction means the effect of one feature depends on another. In a linear predictor, adding x1*x2 makes the slope with respect to x1 equal beta1+beta12*x2, so main effects should usually remain for hierarchy and interpretation. Polynomial features capture smooth curvature and interactions but expand combinatorially, increase collinearity and extrapolate aggressively; scaling and regularization are essential. Splines model nonlinear main effects with local basis functions, and tree or neural models can learn interactions implicitly, though capacity and data support still matter. I propose interactions from domain mechanisms, fit their generation inside the pipeline, compare against a main-effects baseline on legal validation splits, and inspect support across the joint feature space. I avoid target-guided interaction mining outside CV and do not interpret a predictive interaction causally without an identification argument.
keyPoints: Interactions encode conditional effects; nonlinear main effects should not be mistaken for interactions.
Respect hierarchy by retaining constituent main effects when including their product unless a strong constraint says otherwise.
Polynomial degree and interaction count grow rapidly, requiring scaling, regularization and sufficient joint support.
Domain-motivated interactions are easier to validate and govern than exhaustive target-guided crosses.
Predictive interaction, statistical significance and causal effect modification are different claims.
lessons.description: Feature interactions represent situations where one predictor's contribution depends on another. This chapter derives product terms, marginal slopes and mixed derivatives; explains hierarchy, centering and interpretation on linear and logistic link scales; and distinguishes interaction from nonlinear main effects. It compares pairwise crosses, polynomial bases, splines, categorical interactions, tree partitions and neural representations while quantifying combinatorial feature growth, collinearity and sparse joint support. It develops domain-driven screening, hierarchical regularization, fold-local generation and nested selection so exhaustive target-guided crosses do not leak. Worked examples show a product term changing a slope and a missing joint quadrant causing dangerous extrapolation. The lab builds manual quadratic terms, verifies PolynomialFeatures output and shows that the interaction model recovers a synthetic response better than an additive baseline. Production guidance versions basis definitions and feature names, monitors joint-support and range drift, tests unknown category combinations, and retains an additive fallback when high-order behavior becomes unstable. Interpretation always stays tied to the model's link scale and observed joint data support.
learningObjectives: Derive and interpret continuous and categorical interaction terms under model hierarchy.
Distinguish conditional interaction from nonlinear main effects and link-scale artifacts.
Generate, regularize and validate interaction bases without target or split leakage.
Diagnose joint-support, extrapolation, stability and production drift risks.
lessons.labGoal: Construct quadratic and interaction features manually, verify library output, and test their predictive value against an additive baseline.
followUpQuestions: Why center variables before interaction regression?
What is model hierarchy?
How do you test whether an interaction helps?

lessons.title: Change-point Detection
lessons.interviewAnswer: A change point is a boundary where a distributional parameter changes persistently; a point anomaly is an isolated deviation. Offline methods segment a complete series by minimizing within-segment cost plus a penalty per change. Exact dynamic programming is quadratic in a basic form, PELT prunes candidates and can be near linear under conditions, and binary segmentation is faster but greedy. Online detectors such as CUSUM trade false-alarm average run length against detection delay. I residualize known seasonality and trend using past information, choose cost, penalty, minimum segment and tolerance on historical incidents or simulation, and evaluate boundary precision/recall plus delay. In production I group duplicate alarms, connect releases and data-pipeline changes, and define confirm, reset, cooldown, and rollback actions.
keyPoints: A change point marks persistent regime structure, not merely a large residual.
Cost specifies what changes; penalty controls how many boundaries appear.
PELT is exact for its objective while pruning candidates under stated conditions.
Online detection balances false alarms and delay and needs reset semantics.
Seasonality, dependence, and logging changes must be modeled or contextualized.
lessons.description: Change-point detection locates times where the data-generating regime changes, such as a shift in mean, variance, trend, covariance, or event rate. It is different from point anomaly detection: one extreme observation is transient, while a change point marks a boundary after which many observations follow a new pattern. This chapter develops offline segmentation as penalized cost minimization, cumulative-sum evidence, exact dynamic programming, PELT pruning, binary segmentation, online detection delay, minimum segment length, penalty selection, and tolerance-based evaluation. You will learn how seasonality, trend, autocorrelation, missingness, logging changes, and multiple related series can create false boundaries or hide real ones. A worked latency example distinguishes a release-induced persistent shift from a short spike and connects detection to rollback. The lab implements exact penalized mean-shift segmentation, compares its strongest boundary with a vectorized CUSUM statistic, and verifies localization, translation, constant-series, and penalty behavior. lessons.title: Supervised Rare-event Modeling
lessons.interviewAnswer: For rare events, I first protect the label, split, and evaluation design. I can retain all positives and subsample negatives for efficiency, but I store inclusion probabilities and either weight the likelihood or correct and calibrate probabilities on representative data. Class weights and oversampling change the training objective; they may help ranking or optimization but do not automatically produce population probabilities. Duplicating positives adds no new information, and synthetic examples can violate temporal, categorical, or causal constraints. I evaluate PR/AP, recall at review capacity, calibration, and cost on a later untouched population, tune thresholds separately, audit nonalerts, and monitor prevalence, label maturity, hard-negative mix, subgroup support, and queue outcomes.
keyPoints: Event diversity and label quality matter more than raw class ratio alone.
Negative subsampling changes the sample prior and usually the probability intercept.
Weights, resampling, calibration, and thresholding solve different problems.
Validation must preserve deployment prevalence, time, groups, and label maturity.
Selective review and hard-negative mining create feedback that requires audits.
lessons.description: Supervised rare-event modeling uses labeled positives and negatives to learn a ranking or event probability when positives are scarce. The central problem is not that algorithms cannot see a minority class; it is that effective information is limited by the number, diversity, and labeling quality of events, while naive sampling and weighting can distort probabilities and validation. This chapter develops rare-event logistic behavior, case-control and negative subsampling, inverse-probability weighting, prior or intercept correction, class weights, hard-negative mining, resampling, calibration, cost-sensitive thresholds, and temporal or grouped evaluation. You will understand why oversampling duplicates does not create new positive information, why synthetic interpolation can be invalid for mixed or temporal data, and why weighting the training loss is different from choosing a decision threshold. A worked fraud example shows how a model trained on all positives and sampled negatives can preserve ranking yet overstate prevalence until corrected or calibrated. The lab reproduces that intercept shift with scikit-learn, applies a log-odds prior correction, and verifies prevalence, ranking, and cost-policy invariants. Production guidance versions inclusion probabilities, label maturity, calibration and policy separately; audits nonalerts; monitors prevalence, hard-negative mix, calibration, queue yield, and subgroup event support.
learningObjectives: Design case-control, weighted, or resampled training data without corrupting evaluation or probability interpretation.
Apply and explain prior-log-odds correction after random negative subsampling.
Separate representation, ranking objective, probability calibration, and cost-sensitive threshold policy.

lessons.title: Accelerated Failure Time Models
lessons.interviewAnswer: An AFT model writes log T=x beta+sigma epsilon, so exp(beta_j) is a time ratio when other covariates are fixed. A positive coefficient stretches every modeled time quantile; for example exp(0.2)=1.22 means about 22 percent longer time under the model. The error distribution determines survival and hazard shape: Weibull, log-normal, and log-logistic are common choices. For an observed event the likelihood contributes the density f(t|x); for right censoring it contributes S(t|x), because only survival past the censor time is known. I compare distributions with residuals, calibration, likelihood-based criteria and held-out horizon scores, inspect nonlinear and time-varying acceleration, and avoid unsupported tail extrapolation. Time ratios are not automatically causal, and a convenient parametric curve does not replace censoring, entry, or competing-risk design.
keyPoints: AFT coefficients multiply the event-time scale rather than the instantaneous hazard.
Censored rows contribute survival probabilities, not event densities or negative labels.
The chosen error distribution determines hazard shape and extrapolated tails.
Weibull is both AFT and PH; log-normal and log-logistic generally are not PH.
Communicable time ratios remain conditional, model-based, and noncausal without identification.
lessons.description: Accelerated failure-time models place covariate effects directly on event time rather than on instantaneous hazard. In a log-linear AFT model, log T=x^T beta+sigma epsilon, so exp(beta_j) is a time ratio: values above one stretch the event-time distribution and values below one accelerate failure. This chapter derives censored likelihood contributions, compares Weibull, exponential, log-normal, and log-logistic assumptions, and explains when Weibull AFT is simultaneously a proportional-hazards model. It covers quantiles, survival and hazard recovery, residual and distributional diagnostics, nonlinearities, heterogeneity, delayed and interval censoring, extrapolation risk, and causal limits. A worked example translates a coefficient into median-time change. The lab implements a censored Weibull AFT likelihood, fits it with SciPy, verifies parameter recovery and time-unit invariance, and turns fitted parameters into survival predictions. Production guidance versions the time unit, distribution, censoring contribution, feature encoding, optimizer, supported horizon, and tail policy. AFT models provide unusually communicable duration effects, but that clarity depends on an adequate distribution and common acceleration structure.

lessons.title: Competing Risks
lessons.interviewAnswer: With competing risks, an event of one cause prevents a different cause from being the first event. The cause-specific hazard is the instantaneous rate of cause k among subjects still free of every event. The cumulative incidence F_k(t)=P(T<=t,J=k) is the actual probability of cause k by t. Aalen-Johansen estimates it by adding S(t-)d_k/n at each event time while updating event-free survival by all-cause events. Treating competing events as censored and plotting 1-KM overestimates cause probability because it imagines those subjects could later experience the cause. Cause-specific Cox models the rate among event-free subjects; Fine-Gray models a subdistribution risk set to connect covariates directly to CIF. I select by estimand, report cause-specific calibrated probabilities, account for censoring and cause adjudication, and avoid causal claims without an intervention framework.
keyPoints: A competing event removes the possibility of another event being the first outcome; it is not ordinary loss to follow-up.
CIF accumulates cause-specific events weighted by probability of still being event-free from every cause.
One minus cause-specific Kaplan-Meier is generally not the real-world cause probability.
Cause-specific and subdistribution hazard ratios use different risk sets and answer different questions.
All cause probabilities plus event-free survival must reconcile within one coherent state system.
lessons.description: Competing risks arise when one subject can experience several mutually exclusive first events and one event prevents the others from occurring first. Churn, upgrade, and account closure; failure from different components; or death from different causes are not ordinary independent censoring categories. This chapter separates overall survival, cause-specific hazard, cumulative incidence, and subdistribution hazard; derives the Aalen-Johansen cumulative-incidence update; and shows why one minus Kaplan-Meier overestimates a cause's real-world probability when competing events are censored. It compares cause-specific Cox regression with Fine-Gray regression, emphasizing that their coefficients answer different questions and need not agree. It covers censoring assumptions, delayed entry, ties, multi-state extensions, recurrent outcomes, composite endpoints, intervention interpretation, evaluation, and calibration by cause. A worked example follows probability mass from event-free survival into two causes. The lab implements Aalen-Johansen and verifies probability conservation, monotonicity, cause-label symmetry, and the naive Kaplan-Meier bias direction. Production guidance versions cause taxonomy and adjudication, reconciles all cause probabilities, monitors unknown and late-coded outcomes, and reports supported horizons rather than hazard ratios alone.
learningObjectives: Distinguish cause-specific hazards, cumulative incidence functions, and subdistribution hazards by estimand and risk set.
Compute Aalen-Johansen cumulative incidence while conserving probability across event-free and cause states.
Choose cause-specific or Fine-Gray regression according to etiologic, prediction, or policy questions.
Handle censoring, cause coding, evaluation, interventions, and multi-state extensions without probability contradictions.
lessons.labGoal: Implement Aalen-Johansen cumulative incidence, contrast it with naive cause-specific one-minus-KM, and verify probability conservation, monotonicity, and cause-label symmetry.

lessons.title: Multi-objective Optimization & Pareto Trade-offs
lessons.interviewAnswer: In multi-objective optimization, a feasible point dominates another if it is no worse on every objective and strictly better on at least one. Pareto-optimal points are not dominated, so the result is generally a frontier rather than one answer. Weighted sums are simple and can recover supported points on convex fronts, but may miss nonconvex regions and hide stakeholder preferences. Epsilon constraints or lexicographic rules are often clearer for hard limits and priorities; evolutionary algorithms such as NSGA-II approximate broader fronts. I normalize only with declared meaning, include uncertainty and feasibility, evaluate coverage/diversity, and treat selection from the frontier as a separate governed decision.
keyPoints: Pareto optimal means not dominated, not universally best
Decision space and objective space are different
Scalarization embeds preferences and can miss parts of a front
Front quality requires convergence and diversity evidence
Choosing one point is a policy decision after optimization
lessons.description: Multi-objective optimization handles decisions where several criteria conflict and no single scalar score is scientifically or organizationally sufficient. Rather than pretending one configuration is universally best, it identifies feasible trade-offs through dominance, Pareto optimality, fronts, scalarization, epsilon constraints, lexicographic priorities, evolutionary methods, hypervolume, and multi-criteria decision analysis. This chapter develops decision space versus objective space, weak and strict dominance, supported and unsupported Pareto points, normalization, preference elicitation, constraints, uncertainty, many-objective difficulties, and post-optimization selection. You will learn why weighted sums expose only part of a nonconvex front, why objectives should preserve units until preferences are explicit, how NSGA-II uses nondominated sorting and crowding distance, and why optimizing a frontier is separate from choosing a policy. A worked model-selection example balances error, latency, cost, and fairness guardrails. The lab implements nondominated filtering and hypervolume in two dimensions, uses a SciPy epsilon-constraint sweep, and verifies invariance and known fronts. Production guidance covers stakeholder governance, metric drift, robust feasibility, monitoring, rollback, and transparent decision records.

Separate frontier generation from preference-based selection and audit the final decision under uncertainty.

lessons.title: Query Understanding: Spelling, Intent & Filters
lessons.interviewAnswer: I retain the raw query, then apply a versioned locale-aware analyzer to produce normalized tokens and protected spans such as quotes, SKUs, URLs and names. Spelling correction uses candidates from edit or phonetic indexes and ranks them with frequency plus query context; high-confidence suggestions can be applied, while risky changes are shown as `did you mean` or searched in parallel. Intent classification and entity extraction produce confidence and provenance, not hard truth. Structured constraints become typed filters only after units, dates, ranges and negation are resolved. Synonyms and expansions are field- and intent-specific with budgets. I evaluate rewrite precision and recall, exact-token preservation, intent F1, filter accuracy and downstream retrieval on locale and tail slices. Sensitive logs are minimized, access controlled and retained briefly; ambiguous high-cost queries trigger clarification.
keyPoints: Preserve the raw query and annotate every rewrite so failures are reversible and explainable.
Spelling candidates need contextual ranking; minimum edit distance alone can corrupt valid rare entities.
Exact identifiers, quotes, exclusions and structured operators require stronger preservation rules than ordinary words.
Intent and filter predictions should carry confidence and support clarification or parallel retrieval.
Query logs are biased, sensitive behavioral data and require privacy, security and evaluation discipline.
lessons.description: Query understanding converts a short, noisy user string plus context into a retrieval plan without silently changing the user's intent. It spans Unicode and locale normalization, tokenization, spelling correction, segmentation, language detection, intent classification, entity and attribute extraction, structured filters, units and dates, synonyms, abbreviations, query expansion, routing and clarification. This chapter develops noisy-channel spelling as candidate generation plus contextual ranking, distinguishes correction from suggestion, and shows how exact identifiers and quoted terms require preservation. It treats intent and filter extraction as uncertain predictions with confidence, provenance and safe fallback, not unquestionable facts. Worked examples parse a misspelled product query and an ambiguous temporal request. The lab implements edit distance, frequency-aware suggestions, quoted/excluded/filter parsing and a small scikit-learn intent classifier, then verifies exact-token protection and deterministic output. Production guidance versions dictionaries and rewrite rules, evaluates changes by error type and locale, protects sensitive query logs, caps expansion, resists operator and injection abuse, and asks for clarification when the cost of a wrong rewrite is high. Good query understanding improves recall while preserving an inspectable route back to the original request.

Implement and evaluate spelling correction, segmentation, synonyms and expansion with exact-identifier safeguards.

Monitor rewrite precision, zero results, reformulation, latency, fairness, privacy and security in production.

lessons.title: Sampling Design: Random, Stratified & Cluster Sampling
lessons.interviewAnswer: A probability sample gives each frame unit a known nonzero inclusion probability. Simple random sampling selects units directly; stratification samples within homogeneous subgroups to guarantee coverage and often improve precision; cluster sampling selects groups for cost efficiency but induces correlation and often increases variance; multistage designs combine them. Estimate population quantities with design weights, typically inverse inclusion probabilities, and compute design-aware variance using strata, clusters, finite-population corrections, or replicate weights. Large convenience samples do not have these guarantees.
keyPoints: The frame is not automatically the target population
Known inclusion probabilities enable design-based weighting
Strata seek internal homogeneity; clusters are often internally heterogeneous but correlated
Weights affect point estimates and effective information
Variance must reflect every sampling stage
lessons.description: Sampling design determines which population units can enter a dataset and with what probability. Simple random, systematic, stratified, cluster, multistage, and unequal-probability samples trade cost, coverage, and precision differently; their weights and dependence structure must flow into estimation and uncertainty. This chapter defines target and frame populations, inclusion probabilities, base weights, stratification gains, cluster design effects, finite-population correction, probability-proportional-to-size sampling, and design-based versus model-based inference. You will learn why stratification and clustering are not opposites, how self-weighting designs can emerge across stages, why convenience and quota samples do not acquire probability-sample guarantees from large n, and how nonresponse adjustments and calibration alter both bias and variance. The worked example estimates a company-wide mean from disproportionate department strata. The lab implements a Horvitz–Thompson-style weighted mean, verifies recovery on a finite population, and demonstrates stratification variance reduction. Production guidance covers frame snapshots, inclusion-probability lineage, replicate variance, privacy, monitoring, and survey lifecycle controls.
learningObjectives: Map target population, sampling frame, unit, stages, strata, clusters, and inclusion probabilities before analysis.
Explain when stratification improves precision and when cluster sampling reduces cost while increasing variance.
Compute design-weighted estimates and understand finite-population and design-effect adjustments.
Diagnose coverage, unequal weighting, nonresponse, and variance-estimation failures in complex samples.

lessons.title: Selection, Coverage & Nonresponse Bias
lessons.interviewAnswer: Selection bias occurs when inclusion depends on variables related to the outcome after conditioning on what the analysis uses. Coverage bias comes from the frame missing or duplicating target units; nonresponse bias comes when sampled respondents differ from nonrespondents on the estimand. Bias is not determined by response rate alone: it depends on response–outcome association. Weighting or imputation can correct differences explained by observed variables with overlap and valid models, but not unknown unmeasured selection without assumptions. Compare to frame benchmarks, model response, conduct targeted follow-up, and report sensitivity analyses.
keyPoints: Large n attacks variance, not systematic selection
Response rate is a risk indicator, not a bias estimate
Adjustment needs outcome-relevant observed variables and positivity
Conditioning on a collider can create association
Residual selection uncertainty requires sensitivity and external evidence
lessons.description: Selection, coverage, and nonresponse bias arise when observed units differ systematically from the target population in ways related to the outcome or estimand. More rows reduce sampling variance but do not automatically reduce these biases; a massive opt-in dataset can be precisely wrong. This chapter decomposes total survey error, distinguishes target population, frame coverage, unit nonresponse, item nonresponse, attrition, and conditioning on selection, and explains why response rate alone does not determine bias. You will learn to draw selection diagrams, compare respondents with frame benchmarks, use inverse-probability weighting, calibration, imputation, follow-up samples, and sensitivity analysis, while stating the untestable assumptions each method needs. The worked example shows how differential response reverses an apparent support rate and how weighting helps only with observed adjustment variables. The lab simulates outcome-related response, quantifies bias, applies poststratification, and verifies when correction succeeds or fails. Production guidance covers contact paradata, consent, privacy, weight lineage, monitoring, bounded corrections, and transparent residual-uncertainty reporting.
learningObjectives: Separate undercoverage, overcoverage, unit nonresponse, item nonresponse, attrition, and measurement error in a total-error framework.
Explain why response rate and sample size alone do not identify nonresponse or selection bias.
Apply weighting, calibration, imputation, follow-up, and sensitivity methods with explicit exchangeability and positivity assumptions.

lessons.title: Grid, Random & Bayesian Hyperparameter Search
lessons.interviewAnswer: Hyperparameter tuning searches choices that are not learned by the estimator's ordinary fit, such as regularization, tree depth or learning rate. I first define a leakage-safe pipeline, a deployment-faithful splitter, a primary metric and a bounded search space, usually on meaningful log scales. Grid search is suitable for a few discrete choices; randomized search explores larger spaces more efficiently because every trial samples all dimensions; resource-aware methods stop weak candidates early but need comparable learning curves. Each trial is a noisy estimate, so selecting the maximum creates optimism that grows with search breadth. I log all trials, seeds, failures, fit time and secondary constraints, use identical folds for paired comparison, and inspect sensitivity rather than trusting one sharp optimum. The final test set never drives the search. If I need an unbiased estimate after extensive tuning, I use nested CV or a held-out final test, then refit the chosen complete procedure on all development data.
keyPoints: Search the complete preprocessing-plus-model procedure on deployment-faithful folds.
Parameterize spaces using domain geometry, often logarithmic for scale parameters and conditional for architecture choices.
The best observed validation score is a noisy maximum and becomes more optimistic as trials increase.
Track compute, latency, memory, calibration and stability alongside the primary predictive metric.
Selection data choose the configuration; independent outer or final-test data estimate the selected process.
lessons.description: Hyperparameter tuning is statistical model selection under a finite compute budget. This chapter distinguishes learned parameters from configuration choices and turns preprocessing, model family, regularization, optimization and threshold settings into one searchable procedure. It compares grid, randomized, Bayesian and successive-halving strategies; explains logarithmic and conditional search spaces; and derives why the best observed validation score is optimistically biased. It covers reproducible split manifests, common random folds, multiple metrics, refit rules, failed trials, early stopping, warm starts, resource fairness and latency or memory constraints. Worked examples show why random search beats a Cartesian grid when only a few dimensions matter and why a broad search can select noise. The lab manually evaluates a regularization grid, verifies GridSearchCV's scores and selected parameter, and confirms that the final test remains untouched. Production guidance logs every trial and environment, chooses stable Pareto-feasible configurations, separates search from final estimation, refits the complete pipeline on all development data, and preserves the selected settings and rollback model.
learningObjectives: Design bounded, correctly scaled and conditional hyperparameter search spaces.
Compare grid, randomized, Bayesian and resource-aware search from their assumptions and budgets.
Diagnose winner's optimism, split noise, failed trials and unstable optima.
Select and package a reproducible procedure under predictive and operational constraints.
lessons.labGoal: Implement a paired regularization search, verify GridSearchCV results, and keep an untouched final test outside selection.

lessons.title: Nested Cross-validation
lessons.interviewAnswer: Nested cross-validation separates model selection from performance estimation. For each outer split, I treat the outer validation fold as unseen, run the entire search—including preprocessing, feature selection, hyperparameters, calibration and threshold policy—only within the outer training data, fit the selected procedure on that outer training set, and score it once on the outer holdout. Inner scores choose; outer scores estimate the generalization of the selection algorithm. Tuning once on all data and then evaluating the chosen configuration with ordinary CV is not nested because outer folds have already influenced the choice. I use group- or time-aware splitters at both levels where needed, record selected configurations and out-of-fold outer predictions, and aggregate at the independent unit. Nested CV is computationally expensive and does not create a permanent test set, but it is valuable when data are limited and search adaptivity would bias a single CV estimate.
keyPoints: The complete selection process is repeated independently inside every outer training fold.
Inner validation chooses a procedure; outer holdouts estimate the procedure's post-selection performance.
Outer observations must not influence preprocessing, search space adaptation, early stopping, calibration or thresholding.
Different outer folds may select different configurations; this is evidence about selection stability, not an error.
Group, time, label-horizon and independent-unit constraints apply to both nesting levels.
lessons.description: Nested cross-validation evaluates a model-selection procedure without reporting the optimistic score that selected its winner. This chapter constructs outer assessment and inner selection loops, specifies exactly which preprocessing, feature engineering, search, early stopping, calibration and threshold decisions must be nested, and explains why tuning globally before outer evaluation is invalid. It adapts the design to grouped entities and ordered time, estimates computational cost, distinguishes outer predictions from inner scores, and interprets varying selected hyperparameters as stability evidence. Worked examples trace a three-by-four nested search and expose a fake nested design. The lab performs manual nested CV for a scaled logistic-regression search, verifies scikit-learn's nested result and asserts complete, disjoint outer predictions. Production guidance freezes search spaces before nesting, logs every inner and outer artifact, aggregates by independent unit, compares selection algorithms on shared outer folds, refits a documented final configuration on all development data and preserves truly external evidence when available.
learningObjectives: Implement outer assessment and inner selection without information crossing the outer boundary.
Identify every adaptive modeling decision that belongs inside the nested procedure.
Interpret outer estimates, predictions, computational cost and configuration stability.
Adapt nesting to grouped and temporal data and finalize a reproducible deployment procedure.

lessons.title: Bagging, Blending & Stacking
lessons.interviewAnswer: Bagging, voting, blending and stacking combine models for different reasons. Bagging averages resampled versions of an unstable learner to reduce variance. Voting or averaging combines independently trained model outputs using fixed or learned weights. Stacking trains a meta-model on out-of-fold base predictions so it can learn where models complement one another; using in-sample base predictions leaks fit quality and usually overweights flexible learners. Blending uses a dedicated holdout for meta-training and sacrifices data. For classification I align class order and use probabilities or decision scores consistently, with calibration when needed. I require every base and meta feature to be available at the same prediction cutoff, use grouped or temporal folds, compare against the best single model and simple average, and ship fallbacks for partial model failure.
keyPoints: Ensembling helps when component errors are usefully diverse, not merely when model names differ.
Stacking meta-features must be out-of-sample with respect to each base model.
Fold design must preserve time, groups and preprocessing boundaries for the entire two-level pipeline.
Probability scales and class-column order must be compatible before averaging or meta-learning.
A production ensemble needs dependency, latency, fallback and version-skew contracts.
lessons.description: Ensembling combines predictors through resampling, fixed aggregation or learned meta-models. This chapter distinguishes bagging, hard and soft voting, weighted averaging, blending and stacking, then derives why error covariance determines ensemble gain. It develops the complete out-of-fold stacking algorithm, including fold-local preprocessing, class-column alignment, optional passthrough features, meta-regularization and final base-model refitting. Worked examples calculate the variance of correlated predictors and expose leakage from in-sample meta-features. The lab builds regression stacking with explicit out-of-fold predictions, compares it with scikit-learn and verifies one-time fold coverage, finite meta-features and performance against a mean baseline. Production guidance treats the ensemble as a dependency graph: artifact lineage, parallel execution, deadlines, partial failures, version skew, feature cutoffs, monitoring, canaries and rollback are explicit. The standard of evidence is strict: a stack should beat the best component and a simple average on honest data by enough to justify its added complexity. You will also learn how class-column ordering and score calibration affect aggregation, why outer evaluation must wrap the entire stack construction, and how an atomic manifest prevents incompatible base and meta-model versions.
learningObjectives: Explain when bagging, voting, averaging, blending and stacking can reduce error.
Construct leakage-free out-of-fold meta-features under grouped or temporal folds.
Align probability scales, class order and final refitting between training and inference.
Design an ensemble serving graph with resource budgets and partial-failure fallbacks.
lessons.labGoal: Construct leakage-free out-of-fold regression meta-features, fit a stack and verify fold coverage and baseline improvement.
followUpQuestions: Why refit base models after creating OOF features?

lessons.title: Permutation Importance, PDP & SHAP
lessons.interviewAnswer: SHAP and permutation importance answer different questions. Permutation importance is global model reliance: how much a chosen held-out score drops when a feature or feature group is disrupted for a fixed fitted model. SHAP assigns one prediction's difference from a background expectation among features using Shapley-value axioms and a chosen missing-feature game. SHAP values sum to the explained output relative to the baseline, but they depend on model output scale, background population and whether absent features are handled interventionally or conditionally. Correlated features can share or redirect credit, and neither method establishes causality. I use held-out grouped permutation for global necessity, SHAP for local decomposition and interaction exploration, validate local efficiency and global stability, preserve encoded-to-raw lineage, and never treat a force plot as proof of why the real-world outcome occurred.
keyPoints: Permutation measures score reliance after a perturbation; SHAP distributes a prediction difference under a feature-coalition game.
SHAP's baseline, output scale, background sample and missing-feature semantics are part of the explanation.
Local additivity does not imply causal truth, unique semantic credit or stable ranking under correlated features.
Aggregate SHAP summaries answer different questions from held-out permutation and retraining ablation.
Explanations require fidelity checks, uncertainty, feature lineage, privacy review and human-readable limitations.
lessons.description: SHAP and permutation importance inspect fitted models through complementary estimands. This chapter derives Shapley values from coalition marginal contributions and explains efficiency, symmetry, dummy and additivity, then maps the game to model outputs, background expectations and feature-missing conventions. It distinguishes interventional from conditional explanations, output probability from log-odds scale, local signed attribution from global mean absolute summaries, and main effects from SHAP interaction values. It contrasts those allocations with held-out permutation score degradation, grouped perturbations and drop-column retraining. Correlation, one-hot fragmentation, off-manifold masking, background choice, approximation error, privacy and causal misinterpretation receive explicit treatment. The lab computes exact two-feature Shapley values for a model with an interaction, verifies local efficiency and symmetry, and contrasts them with permutation reliance. Production guidance versions explainer and background artifacts, checks additivity and stability, maps encoded features to governed concepts, limits sensitive disclosure and treats explanations as diagnostic evidence rather than automatic causal or legal justification.
learningObjectives: Derive exact Shapley values and interpret the local efficiency baseline contract.
Choose background, output scale, feature grouping and dependence semantics deliberately.
Contrast local SHAP allocation with global permutation and retraining importance.
Validate explanation fidelity, stability, privacy and communication limitations in production.
lessons.labGoal: Compute exact two-feature Shapley values, verify axioms for an interaction model, and contrast local allocation with global permutation reliance.

lessons.title: Dashboard & BI Design
lessons.interviewAnswer: I design a dashboard around who decides what, how often, and what action follows. I create a hierarchy from outcome and guardrail KPIs to diagnostic drivers, with definitions, units, denominators, targets, uncertainty, sample support, freshness, and ownership. The default screen answers current state, change, significance/impact, and where to investigate; details live in drill-downs. I use simple comparable charts, consistent filters and time windows, accessible redundant status encodings, and explicit stale/partial-data states. The semantic model, row-level security, tests, performance, alerts, and rollback are part of the design.
keyPoints: Decisions and actions determine dashboard scope
KPIs need targets, denominators, uncertainty, and freshness
Overview and diagnosis need different levels of detail
Status must distinguish harm, uncertainty, and missing/stale data
The semantic and operational system is part of the interface
lessons.description: A dashboard is an operational decision interface over a semantic metric layer, not a collage of charts. Its design begins with audience, decisions, monitoring cadence, actions, and failure behavior; visual hierarchy and interaction then make the relevant state legible. This chapter develops audience and task analysis, KPI trees, leading and lagging indicators, targets and guardrails, overview-to-detail structure, freshness and provenance, chart selection, alert semantics, filters, drill-down, mobile and accessibility behavior, performance budgets, and governance. You will learn why a single number needs context, why red/green status cannot replace uncertainty or impact, how denominator and refresh mismatches create false narratives, and how to separate monitoring from exploratory reports. The worked example redesigns a model-health dashboard whose green average hides slice harm and stale labels. The lab builds a dashboard-card state engine with freshness, sample-size, interval, and threshold checks and verifies safe behavior. Production guidance covers semantic models, caching, row-level security, observability, testing, ownership, incident response, and rollback.

Design KPI hierarchy with estimates, targets, guardrails, denominators, uncertainty, freshness, and diagnostic drill-down.
Specify filters, interaction, accessibility, responsive layout, performance, and secure data behavior as product requirements.
Operate dashboards through semantic contracts, tests, observability, incident response, and versioned rollback.
