lessons.title: MinHash & Jaccard Similarity
lessons.interviewAnswer: Jaccard similarity compares sets as |A∩B|/|A∪B|. MinHash compresses a large set into k minimum values under independent random permutations or suitable hash functions. For one component, the probability that two sets choose the same minimum equals their Jaccard similarity, because the first element in a random ordering of A∪B is uniformly likely and matches both signatures exactly when it lies in A∩B. The fraction of matching components is therefore an unbiased estimator with variance J(1−J)/k under independence. I define shingling and canonicalization first, choose k from the uncertainty required near the decision threshold, use stable versioned hashes, and evaluate false merges and misses on labeled pairs. Plain MinHash represents set Jaccard, not cosine similarity, edit distance, multiplicity, or weighted Jaccard.
keyPoints: Jaccard measures intersection relative to union and ignores multiplicity in ordinary sets.
A MinHash collision is a Bernoulli observation whose expectation equals Jaccard similarity.
More independent signature rows reduce sampling variance but increase storage and hashing work.
Shingle construction, normalization and hash quality often matter more than the estimator formula.
MinHash estimates similarity; LSH is a separate indexing layer that avoids comparing every signature pair.
lessons.description: MinHash is a randomized sketch for estimating Jaccard similarity between large sets. This chapter begins with set construction, token normalization, character and word shingles, binary incidence and the difference between resemblance and containment. It proves the central collision identity from the minimum element of a random permutation and derives the estimator's expectation, variance and concentration behavior. It explains how seeded hash functions replace explicit permutations, why all compared objects must share the same hash family, and how signature length controls storage, compute and uncertainty. Edge cases include empty sets, duplicate tokens, tiny sets, hash collisions, correlated rows and adversarial or unstable hashing. The chapter distinguishes ordinary MinHash from weighted MinHash, one-permutation variants, bottom-k sketches and semantic embeddings, and distinguishes similarity estimation from LSH candidate retrieval. A worked document example interprets error near a deduplication threshold. The lab creates deterministic universal-hash signatures, compares them with exact and library Jaccard, and verifies identity, disjointness, permutation invariance and improved accuracy with longer signatures. Production sections cover preprocessing contracts, hash-family versioning, backfills, threshold calibration, exact second-stage checks, privacy, skew, monitoring and rollback.
learningObjectives: Derive the MinHash collision probability and the sampling uncertainty of a signature estimate.
Construct stable shingles and signatures while handling duplicates, empty sets and hash-family versioning.
Select a signature length and decision workflow from error tolerance and labeled merge or miss costs.
Distinguish MinHash from LSH, weighted similarity, exact verification and semantic retrieval.
lessons.labGoal: Build deterministic MinHash signatures, compare them with exact and library Jaccard, and test core estimator invariants.
followUpQuestions: Why does the minimum collision probability equal Jaccard?
How many rows should a signature have?
What is the difference between MinHash and LSH?

lessons.title: Locality-Sensitive Hashing (LSH)
lessons.interviewAnswer: Locality-sensitive hashing is a candidate-generation framework in which nearby objects collide more often than far objects. For MinHash signatures, divide k=br rows into b bands of r rows; a pair is a candidate if every row matches in at least one band. If row agreement is s and independence is a useful approximation, candidate probability is 1−(1−s^r)^b. Larger r demands stronger within-band agreement and improves precision; more bands create more chances and improve recall. The S-curve is not a hard threshold, and candidates still require full scoring or exact verification. I tune b and r on labeled pairs, report candidate recall and candidate volume separately from final ranking metrics, version the hash family, handle hot buckets, and never describe LSH as universally optimal across metrics.
keyPoints: An LSH family is metric-specific: close pairs have higher collision probability than far pairs.
MinHash banding performs an OR over bands of ANDs within a band.
The probability 1−(1−s^r)^b produces a soft S-curve, not deterministic thresholding.
LSH generates candidates; a second stage computes or learns the final similarity and decision.
Measure candidate recall, bucket skew, memory and latency before downstream ranking quality.
lessons.description: Locality-sensitive hashing is a family of randomized indexes for approximate near-neighbor retrieval. This chapter defines locality sensitivity through collision probabilities, explains why an LSH family must match the target distance or similarity, and derives MinHash banding as an OR-of-AND amplification scheme. It works through the candidate probability 1−(1−s^r)^b, the resulting S-curve, the effects of bands and rows, and the difference between an approximate transition and a guaranteed threshold. It connects the construction to the Indyk–Motwani near-neighbor framework and distinguishes MinHash LSH for Jaccard from random-hyperplane hashing for angular similarity and p-stable methods for certain Lp distances. The chapter treats multi-probe lookup, multiple tables, candidate deduplication, exact rescoring, recall–latency trade-offs and the limitations of correlated hashes. The lab builds band buckets over deterministic MinHash signatures, verifies theoretical monotonicity and retrieves similar sets while excluding a disjoint set. Production guidance covers labeled tuning, candidate recall, bucket skew, memory, hot keys, online updates, backfills, hash versioning, adversarial flooding, privacy and rollback. LSH is positioned as a retrieval component, not a final similarity metric or universal nearest-neighbor solution.
learningObjectives: Derive MinHash banding's candidate probability and explain the roles of b and r.
Match an LSH family to Jaccard, angular or Lp geometry without conflating their collision laws.
Tune and evaluate candidate generation independently from exact scoring or downstream ranking.
Design a versioned, observable index that handles hot buckets, updates, abuse and rollback.
lessons.labGoal: Build a banded MinHash index, derive its collision curve, and verify candidate retrieval on similar and disjoint sets.
followUpQuestions: What do more bands do?
What do more rows per band do?
Why exact-score candidates after LSH?

lessons.title: Bloom Filters
lessons.interviewAnswer: A Bloom filter is an insert-only approximate-membership structure with an m-bit array and k hash locations per key. Insert sets all k bits; lookup returns definitely absent if any bit is zero and possibly present if all are one. Under the model of independent uniform hashes after n distinct insertions, the false-positive probability is approximately (1−e^(−kn/m))^k and the optimal integer k is near (m/n)ln2. A correct ordinary filter has no false negatives only while its hash and bit-state contract is preserved and bits are never cleared. I size from expected cardinality and target error, version hashing and capacity, rebuild before saturation, verify positives against an authoritative store, and monitor fill ratio and empirical false positives. Deletion needs a counting or deletion-capable alternative, not clearing shared bits.
keyPoints: Negative answers are definitive; positive answers require confirmation when correctness matters.
False positives arise because unrelated keys can collectively set every queried bit.
Capacity, bit count and hash count jointly determine error; overfilling invalidates the target rate.
The no-false-negative claim assumes stable hashing, completed writes, intact bits and no unsupported deletion.
Filters can reduce expensive negative I/O, but they are not key-value stores and cannot enumerate members.
lessons.description: Bloom filters provide compact approximate membership with one-sided error. This chapter develops the bit-array and multi-hash mechanism, proves why a zero bit certifies absence, derives expected occupancy and the standard false-positive approximation, and obtains the near-optimal number of hashes and memory-sizing formula. It distinguishes planned distinct insertions from events, explains why overcapacity raises error, and examines finite-hash collisions, double hashing, stable serialization and adversarial keys. The no-false-negative guarantee is stated with its real assumptions: identical hash configuration, durable completed insertion, uncorrupted state and no clearing of shared bits. Variants include counting, scalable, blocked, partitioned and stable Bloom filters, plus Cuckoo and quotient filters, with attention to deletion and cache locality. The lab implements deterministic double hashing, checks every inserted key, measures empirical false positives against theory and verifies serialization-relevant determinism. Production design treats the filter as a negative cache in front of an authoritative store, monitors fill and observed error, rebuilds through versioned snapshots, coordinates updates, handles warmup and rollback, and protects against collision flooding. It also explains when a plain set, sorted structure or exact database index is a better choice.
learningObjectives: Derive Bloom-filter occupancy, false-positive probability, memory sizing and optimal hash count.
Explain the precise assumptions behind one-sided error and why ordinary deletion is unsafe.
Choose among ordinary, counting, scalable, blocked, Cuckoo or exact membership structures.
Operate a versioned filter with empirical error monitoring, authoritative confirmation and safe rebuilds.
lessons.labGoal: Implement a deterministic Bloom filter, size it from an error target, and test one-sided membership and empirical false positives.
followUpQuestions: How do you choose m and k?
Can two Bloom filters be unioned?
When is a Bloom filter a bad choice?

lessons.title: Count-Min Sketch & Heavy Hitters
lessons.interviewAnswer: A Count-Min sketch summarizes a nonnegative frequency vector in a d×w counter table. Each update adds its amount to one bucket per hash row; a point query returns the minimum of those counters. In a cash-register stream the estimate never undercounts, because each chosen counter contains the target frequency plus collision mass. With width about e/ε and depth about ln(1/δ), the overestimate is at most ε times total stream mass with probability at least 1−δ under the standard hash assumptions. Rows reduce failure probability; width reduces collision error. Sketches with identical dimensions and hashes merge by elementwise addition. I distinguish this contract from signed turnstile streams, version the hashes, prevent overflow, validate heavy hitters against exact samples, and monitor error as distribution and total mass change.
keyPoints: The minimum removes rows with unusually large positive collision noise.
Nonnegative updates give one-sided overestimation; signed updates need a different analysis or sketch.
Width controls additive error and depth controls the probability that every row is bad.
Linearity enables merge only when counter shape, hash family, encoding and update semantics match.
Heavy-hitter discovery also needs a candidate mechanism because the sketch cannot enumerate original keys.
lessons.description: The Count-Min sketch is a fixed-memory streaming summary for approximate point frequencies and related aggregate queries. This chapter models a stream as updates to a frequency vector, constructs the depth-by-width counter array, and explains why querying the minimum yields a one-sided estimate under nonnegative updates. It derives the standard width and depth choices from ε additive error and δ failure probability, clarifies constants and hash-independence assumptions, and interprets error relative to total L1 mass rather than individual count. It covers weighted updates, conservative update, inner-product and merge operations, and distinguishes the cash-register model from strict and general turnstile streams. It explains why a sketch cannot enumerate keys, so heavy-hitter systems need a candidate structure, and why negative updates, counter overflow and incompatible hash versions can invalidate expectations. The lab implements deterministic rows, compares estimates with exact Counter values, verifies non-underestimation and merge equivalence, and checks a practical error envelope. Production guidance addresses parameter budgets, key encoding, distributed merge manifests, skew, candidate tracking, exact audits, saturation, concurrency, adversarial hashes, privacy and rollback. Comparisons with Bloom filters, Count Sketch, Misra–Gries and HyperLogLog reinforce that each structure answers a different query.
learningObjectives: Implement Count-Min updates, point queries and compatible merges from the frequency-vector model.
Derive and correctly interpret the ε||f||1 additive-error and δ failure guarantee.
Distinguish nonnegative, strict-turnstile and signed-stream behavior and select alternatives when needed.
Build a heavy-hitter service with candidate tracking, exact audits, versioned schemas and safe failure behavior.
lessons.labGoal: Implement Count-Min frequency estimates, verify their one-sided behavior, and prove compatible distributed merge equivalence.
followUpQuestions: Why take the minimum rather than the mean?
What does ε control?
Count-Min or Count Sketch for signed updates?

lessons.title: HyperLogLog & Distinct Counting
lessons.interviewAnswer: HyperLogLog estimates the number of distinct elements using a uniform hash and m=2^p registers. The first p hash bits select a register; the remaining bits provide a rank equal to the position of the first one. Each register stores its maximum observed rank. Rare long zero prefixes imply many distinct trials. HLL combines registers with a bias-corrected harmonic-mean estimator, applies small-range correction such as linear counting when many registers are zero, and has standard error roughly 1.04/√m in its classical regime. Compatible sketches merge by register-wise maximum, so duplicates and partitions do not double count. I version precision, hash and encoding, monitor zero registers and saturation, validate against exact samples, and rebuild rather than merge incompatible sketches. It estimates cardinality, not identities, membership, frequency, intersections without extra machinery, or deletions.
keyPoints: Hash prefixes assign independent-looking substreams; suffix ranks encode rare-event evidence.
Register maxima are duplicate-insensitive and merge through elementwise maximum.
The harmonic mean limits domination by exceptionally large registers.
Precision p sets m=2^p, relative error near 1.04/√m, and memory that grows linearly in m.
Small-range, bias and large-range corrections are part of a practical implementation, not optional decoration.
lessons.description: HyperLogLog is a fixed-memory probabilistic algorithm for distinct counting. This chapter builds from the probability of leading-zero runs in uniform hashes to stochastic averaging across 2^p registers. It specifies register selection and rank calculation, explains maximum updates and duplicate invariance, derives the raw harmonic-mean estimator and interprets its normalization constant. It covers linear-counting correction for small ranges, empirical bias correction in modern variants, finite hash-width behavior and the classical relative standard error near 1.04/√m. It proves union merge as register-wise maximum and explains why differences, deletions and small intersections are not directly supported. Comparisons with exact sets, bitmaps, linear counting and bottom-k sketches clarify when HLL is appropriate. The lab implements a deterministic 64-bit version with small-range correction, verifies duplicate invariance and partition merge equality, and compares estimates with exact cardinality. Production guidance covers precision and hash versioning, sparse-to-dense storage, serialization, distributed aggregation, register saturation, exact audits, uncertainty-aware thresholds, privacy, corrupted state and rollback. The emphasis is on the full sketch contract: cardinality semantics, canonical identities, uniform hashes, compatible registers and corrections must all align.
learningObjectives: Implement register indexing, leading-zero rank updates, raw estimation and small-range correction.
Explain the 1.04/√m precision law and choose p from memory and decision uncertainty.
Prove duplicate invariance and compatible union merge while recognizing unsupported deletion and difference queries.
Operate versioned sketches with exact audits, serialization checks, privacy controls and rollback.
lessons.labGoal: Implement a 64-bit HyperLogLog with small-range correction, then verify duplicates, accuracy and max-merge semantics.
followUpQuestions: Why use a harmonic mean?
What does increasing p do?
How do HLL sketches merge?

lessons.title: PageRank & Link Analysis
lessons.interviewAnswer: PageRank is the stationary distribution of a random-surfer Markov chain. From page j, follow one of its outgoing links with probability α and teleport according to distribution v with probability 1−α. Dangling pages need an explicit transition, commonly v. With a column-stochastic matrix P, r=αPr+(1−α)v; teleportation makes the usual finite chain well behaved and power iteration converges. I normalize orientation, deduplicate or weight edges deliberately, handle dangling mass, iterate until a residual or rank-change tolerance, and compare with an independent solve on small graphs. PageRank measures recursive prominence under this browsing model—not relevance, truth, causality or safety. Production systems combine it with content and quality signals, defend against link farms, version graph snapshots, monitor convergence and slices, and keep rollback and explanation paths.
keyPoints: PageRank is an eigenvector or stationary-distribution problem on a normalized directed graph.
Teleportation prevents rank traps and usually supplies uniqueness and convergence under standard conditions.
Dangling nodes must redistribute their probability mass rather than leaking it.
Row-versus-column conventions are equivalent only when equations and multiplication match.
Recursive link prominence is one signal and is vulnerable to graph construction choices and manipulation.
lessons.description: PageRank is a graph-centrality algorithm defined by the stationary distribution of a damped random-surfer process. This chapter constructs a directed transition matrix from links, makes row and column conventions explicit, distributes each source's vote over outgoing edges, and handles self-links, duplicates, weights and dangling nodes. It derives the fixed-point and linear-system forms, explains teleportation, irreducibility, aperiodicity and convergence, and implements sparse-style power iteration with change and residual checks. Personalized PageRank, topic-sensitive teleportation and incremental or approximate computation extend the basic method. The chapter distinguishes PageRank from HITS, degree, shortest-path centralities, content relevance and causal authority. It examines link farms, sybil structures, temporal staleness, popularity feedback, graph incompleteness and fairness across cohorts. The lab builds a stochastic matrix, compares power iteration with a direct linear solve, verifies probability conservation, residual and permutation invariance, and exercises dangling behavior. Production guidance covers graph contracts, snapshot manifests, distributed sparse multiplication, convergence diagnostics, spam defenses, canaries, feature combination, explanations, monitoring, privacy and rollback. The central message is that PageRank is mathematically precise about one browsing model, not universally authoritative about page quality or truth.
learningObjectives: Construct a valid transition matrix with explicit orientation, edge weighting and dangling policy.
Derive PageRank's fixed point and compute it with converged power iteration and residual checks.
Explain how damping, teleportation and personalization change reachability and interpretation.
Design a scalable, manipulation-aware graph-ranking pipeline with reproducible snapshots and rollback.
lessons.labGoal: Build PageRank with dangling redistribution, compare power iteration with a direct solve, and verify conservation, residual and relabeling invariance.
followUpQuestions: Why is teleportation necessary?
How do you handle dangling nodes?
How would you validate an implementation?

lessons.title: Vector vs Raster Spatial Data
lessons.interviewAnswer: Vector data represents discrete features as points, lines and polygons with attributes; raster data represents a regularly sampled field as cells in one or more bands. I choose from the phenomenon and operations, not from file extension. Boundaries, networks and identifiable objects often fit vector topology; imagery, elevation, temperature and continuous surfaces fit rasters. Resolution is a measurement and aggregation choice: a pixel records support over an area, not an infinitely precise point. Conversions are lossy—rasterization depends on grid alignment and inclusion rules, while polygonization inherits pixel stair-steps. In production I preserve CRS, extent, affine transform, resolution, nodata mask, band units, geometry validity and lineage; tile and window large rasters, spatially index vectors, and test mass or class conservation across transformations.
keyPoints: Vector geometries model discrete objects; rasters model sampled fields on a grid, though many phenomena admit both views.
A raster cell has spatial support, resolution, alignment, CRS, bands, datatype and nodata semantics.
Vector validity and topology distinguish mere coordinate arrays from trustworthy spatial features.
Rasterization, resampling and polygonization introduce scale- and rule-dependent information loss.
Cloud-efficient processing depends on spatial windows, tiles, overviews, chunk alignment and metadata contracts.
lessons.description: Spatial data is commonly represented as vector features or raster grids, and the choice determines storage, operations and error. This chapter defines point, line, polygon, multi-geometry and geometry-collection models alongside raster width, height, bands, datatype, transform, CRS, resolution and nodata masks. It explains feature attributes, geometry validity, rings and holes, topology, dimensionality and the distinction between a conceptual feature and its file encoding. For rasters it covers pixel-center versus pixel-area interpretation, north-up affine transforms, multi-band imagery, categorical versus continuous values, masks, scale, offset and overviews. It compares vector indexing with raster tiling and window reads, and it analyzes rasterization, polygonization, vectorization, resampling and zonal statistics as lossy transformations with explicit inclusion rules. The lab creates a synthetic grid and polygon, performs center and fractional-style aggregation, and verifies affine coordinates, masks and area totals using NumPy and Shapely. Production guidance covers GeoPackage, Parquet and GeoTIFF-style metadata, cloud-optimized layouts, chunking, compression, schema and CRS validation, invalid geometries, nodata leakage, lineage, privacy and reversible rebuilds. The goal is to make representation a deliberate measurement decision rather than an accidental consequence of whichever file arrived first.
learningObjectives: Choose vector, raster or a hybrid representation from phenomenon, query and error requirements.
Interpret affine transforms, resolution, pixel support, bands, datatype and nodata masks correctly.
Evaluate information loss and conservation when rasterizing, polygonizing, resampling or computing zonal summaries.
Design scalable tiled or indexed storage with validated spatial metadata and lineage.
lessons.labGoal: Represent a raster grid and vector polygon, map cells through an affine transform, and verify masked zonal aggregation and area semantics.
followUpQuestions: When would you choose raster over vector?
What is the difference between pixel center and pixel area?
How do you validate a vector-to-raster conversion?

lessons.title: Coordinate Reference Systems & Projections
lessons.interviewAnswer: A coordinate reference system gives coordinates meaning through a datum or reference frame, ellipsoid, coordinate system, axes, units and possibly a map projection. Geographic longitude–latitude coordinates are angular; a projected CRS maps the curved Earth to a plane and introduces distortion in some combination of area, shape, distance and direction. I assign a CRS only when metadata is known; I reproject when transforming coordinates. For measurement I choose a local or regional projected CRS whose distortion properties suit the task, or use ellipsoidal geodesics. I never compute meters directly from EPSG:4326 degrees or assume Web Mercator is metric everywhere. In production I persist authoritative WKT or authority code, axis order, coordinate epoch, transformation pipeline and grids, test known control points and round trips, and fail closed on missing CRS.
keyPoints: Coordinates without a CRS are ambiguous numbers; assigning and transforming are different operations.
A datum or reference frame locates the ellipsoid relative to Earth and can vary with time.
Every planar projection distorts; choose properties and area of use from the operation.
Longitude–latitude axis order, units and antimeridian behavior are common silent failure modes.
Transformation accuracy depends on the selected operation, grids, software database and coordinate epoch.
lessons.description: Coordinate reference systems connect numeric coordinates to positions on and around Earth. This chapter separates ellipsoid, geoid, datum or dynamic reference frame, geographic coordinate system, projected coordinate system, vertical CRS and compound CRS. It explains authority identifiers and WKT, axis order and units, area of use, coordinate epoch and why EPSG:4326, CRS84 and Web Mercator are not interchangeable labels. Projection families are compared through conformal, equal-area, equidistant and azimuthal properties, with Tissot-style distortion reasoning and the special limits of EPSG:3857. The chapter distinguishes assigning missing metadata from transforming coordinates and follows a modern PROJ-style operation pipeline through inverse projection, datum transformation and forward projection. It covers grid shifts, operation selection, missing resources, antimeridian and polar issues, and metric versus geodesic measurement. The lab implements spherical Mercator, validates inverse round trips, compares against pyproj and quantifies scale growth with latitude. Production guidance requires authoritative CRS metadata, always-XY policy where appropriate, transformation and database versions, control points, bounds and round-trip tests, precision, epoch handling, lineage and rollback. The result is a workflow in which coordinates remain physically interpretable across files, services and analyses.
learningObjectives: Decompose a CRS into reference frame, ellipsoid, axes, units and projection components.
Choose a projected or geodesic method from area of use and distortion requirements.
Distinguish CRS assignment from coordinate transformation and verify an operation pipeline.
Prevent axis, unit, epoch, grid and antimeridian failures in production spatial systems.
lessons.labGoal: Implement spherical Mercator forward and inverse transforms, compare with pyproj, and quantify latitude-dependent scale distortion.
followUpQuestions: How would you choose a CRS for area calculation?
Why can longitude and latitude be swapped?
What does a datum transformation do?

lessons.title: Spatial Joins & Predicates
lessons.interviewAnswer: A spatial join attaches records using a geometric predicate rather than key equality. I first align both layers to the same suitable CRS, validate geometries and state the predicate precisely: intersects, within, contains, covers, touches, crosses, overlaps or within-distance have different boundary semantics. The engine normally uses a spatial index to generate bounding-box candidates and then evaluates the exact predicate. Cardinality is not necessarily one-to-one: a point on a boundary can match multiple polygons under intersects, and overlapping polygons multiply rows. I define tie-breaking or aggregation, preserve unmatched rows as required, test boundary and empty geometries, and reconcile output counts and unique IDs. A join proves spatial relation at the encoded accuracy, not causal exposure or administrative truth.
keyPoints: Predicate semantics and argument direction determine which geometry and boundary relationships match.
A bounding-box index filters candidates; exact geometry evaluation removes false candidates.
One-to-many and many-to-many matches require an explicit output grain and resolution policy.
CRS mismatch, invalid geometry, precision and dateline handling can silently corrupt results.
Post-join reconciliation should account for matched, unmatched, duplicate and ambiguous source IDs.
lessons.description: Spatial joins relate features through geometry predicates rather than ordinary equality keys. This chapter defines intersects, disjoint, within, contains, covers, covered-by, touches, crosses, overlaps and distance-based matching using interior, boundary and exterior semantics. It explains predicate direction, especially point-in-polygon boundary cases, and introduces the DE-9IM conceptual model behind interoperable simple-feature behavior. The execution path is decomposed into spatial-index candidate generation with minimum bounding rectangles and exact predicate refinement, clarifying why an index improves speed without changing correct results. One-to-zero, one-to-one, one-to-many and many-to-many outcomes are treated as data-model decisions, with aggregation, priority and ambiguity policies. The chapter covers CRS alignment, planar versus geodesic distance, invalid and empty geometries, multipart features, precision grids, antimeridian crossings and prepared geometries. The lab uses Shapely and GeoPandas to compare within and intersects for interior, boundary and exterior points and verifies join cardinality. Production guidance versions both layers and predicates, validates geometries, estimates candidate explosion, partitions work, reconciles source IDs, logs ambiguity and supports audit and rollback. The join result is presented as a derived dataset with measurable geometric assumptions, not an unquestionable geographic fact.
learningObjectives: Select and explain topological or distance predicates including their boundary and direction semantics.
Trace spatial-index candidate filtering and exact predicate refinement.
Control join cardinality, ambiguity, invalid geometry and CRS-related failure modes.
Validate and operate a scalable spatial join as a versioned derived dataset.
lessons.labGoal: Compare exact spatial predicates on interior, boundary and exterior points and verify GeoPandas join cardinality.
followUpQuestions: How do you handle a point on a polygon boundary?
Why can bounding boxes create many false candidates?
What output checks would you run?

lessons.title: Spatial Indexes, Geohash & H3
lessons.interviewAnswer: Spatial indexes reduce candidate search; they do not replace exact geometry or distance checks. An R-tree groups object minimum bounding rectangles hierarchically, pruning branches whose envelopes cannot satisfy a query. A geohash or quadtree maps locations into hierarchical rectangular cells; prefix locality helps partitioning but neighboring locations can cross prefix boundaries. H3 maps the sphere through an icosahedral, mostly hexagonal hierarchy with resolutions and twelve pentagons; cells support aggregation and neighborhood operations, but cell equality is not exact polygon containment. I choose by workload: dynamic geometry windows, point bucketing, spherical neighborhood analytics or distributed partition pruning. I always refine candidates, handle adjacent cells and distortion, monitor hot cells and index health, and version resolution, encoding and geometry semantics.
keyPoints: R-trees index bounding rectangles of arbitrary geometry and answer window candidates dynamically.
Hierarchical cell IDs turn spatial proximity into prefixes or parent–child relationships with boundary caveats.
Geohash rectangles vary physically with latitude; H3 cells are mostly hexagonal with unavoidable pentagons.
Index resolution trades candidate volume, storage, boundary duplication and aggregation stability.
Exact predicates and geodesic distances remain the refinement stage after candidate retrieval.
lessons.description: Spatial indexes accelerate geometric and proximity queries by organizing candidate regions. This chapter derives minimum bounding rectangle tests and follows an R-tree through hierarchical nodes, overlap, insertion, split quality and search. It compares R-trees with quadtrees and fixed grids, then explains geohash bit interleaving, prefix cells, neighbor lookups and latitude-dependent physical dimensions. H3 is introduced as an icosahedral aperture-seven hierarchy of mostly hexagonal cells, including resolution choice, parent and child relations, neighborhood rings, cell area variation and the twelve pentagons present at every resolution. The chapter separates logical cell membership from approximate parent containment and from exact feature topology. It covers polygon coverings, compacting, boundary duplication, multi-resolution aggregation, hot cells, antimeridian and polar behavior. The lab uses Shapely STRtree to compare indexed candidates with brute-force exact intersections and verifies no missed results and meaningful pruning. Production guidance selects indexes from query shape, update rate and distribution; versions geometry, CRS and resolution; measures candidate-to-exact ratios, skew and rebuild lag; and maintains exact refinement, privacy and rollback. Index keys are treated as query accelerators and partition hints rather than substitutes for geography.
learningObjectives: Explain R-tree envelope hierarchy and why exact refinement remains necessary.
Compare geohash, quadtree and H3 hierarchy, neighborhood and distortion behavior.
Choose resolution and covering policy from recall, candidate, storage and aggregation requirements.
Operate versioned indexes under skew, updates, adversarial inputs and rebuilds.
lessons.labGoal: Use an STRtree as an envelope candidate index and verify exact query equivalence and pruning against brute force.
followUpQuestions: R-tree or H3 for polygon intersection?
Why probe neighboring geohash cells?
How do you evaluate an index?

lessons.title: Geodesic Distance & Spatial kNN
lessons.interviewAnswer: Distance must match the surface and decision. Euclidean distance in a suitable projected CRS is efficient and accurate within its design region; longitude–latitude degrees are not a metric. Great-circle or haversine distance models a sphere and is often adequate at moderate accuracy; ellipsoidal inverse geodesics use a reference ellipsoid and handle global and near-antipodal cases robustly. Network travel time, barriers and anisotropic cost surfaces may be more relevant than straight-line distance. For spatial kNN, I use an index whose metric matches the query—such as BallTree haversine on radians—retrieve candidates, apply exact ellipsoidal or route refinement, and define ties and maximum radius. I validate known pairs, symmetry, identical points, antimeridian and polar cases, and monitor units and coverage.
keyPoints: Longitude and latitude are angular coordinates; Euclidean degree distance has latitude-dependent meaning and wrap errors.
Haversine computes spherical central angle; ellipsoidal geodesics improve accuracy and robustness.
Straight-line, geodesic, network and cost distance answer different operational questions.
Nearest-neighbor indexes are metric-specific and approximate retrieval may require exact refinement.
Radians, axis order, Earth radius, antimeridian, poles, ties and duplicate points need explicit tests.
lessons.description: Spatial distance depends on the geometry of Earth and on what movement or exposure the application represents. This chapter contrasts Euclidean distance in projected coordinates, spherical great-circle distance, the haversine formula, ellipsoidal geodesics and chord distance, then extends the comparison to road-network travel time, barriers and raster cost distance. It derives the haversine central angle with longitude wrapping and explains Earth-radius conventions, ellipsoid choice, forward and inverse geodesic problems, azimuths and near-antipodal robustness. Projection distortion and local tangent approximations are tied to explicit error budgets. Spatial nearest-neighbor search is developed with brute force, kd-trees for suitable planar metrics, BallTree haversine search, cell and R-tree candidate filters, exact refinement, ties and radius constraints. The lab implements haversine, compares it with pyproj's ellipsoidal Geod and uses scikit-learn BallTree to recover nearest cities, testing symmetry, identity and antimeridian behavior. Production guidance covers units, radians, axis order, metric and index compatibility, routing freshness, uncertainty, caching, privacy, benchmarks, fallbacks and rollback. The final question is always whether the chosen distance corresponds to the decision, not merely whether the code is fast.
learningObjectives: Choose planar, spherical, ellipsoidal, network or cost distance from the spatial decision and error budget.
Derive and implement haversine distance with stable units and longitude wrapping.
Match kNN index geometry to the metric and apply exact or route-based refinement.
Validate global edge cases and operate a distance service with uncertainty, freshness and fallback controls.
lessons.labGoal: Implement haversine distance, compare spherical and ellipsoidal results, and verify spherical nearest-neighbor retrieval.
followUpQuestions: When is a local projection adequate?
How do you query spherical kNN with BallTree?
Why refine candidates geodesically?

lessons.title: Spatial Autocorrelation & Moran’s I
lessons.interviewAnswer: Spatial autocorrelation asks whether values at locations connected by a specified weights matrix are more similar or dissimilar than expected. Global Moran's I is I=(n/S0)[Σ_iΣ_j w_ij(z_i−z̄)(z_j−z̄)]/[Σ_i(z_i−z̄)^2]. Positive values indicate neighboring deviations tend to share sign, negative values indicate contrast, and interpretation depends on W, scaling and the null. Under a common randomization null E[I]=−1/(n−1), not zero. I define neighbors from the process—contiguity, distance, kNN or network—handle islands and row standardization, examine a Moran scatterplot, and use permutation inference that reassigns values while holding W fixed. Global significance does not locate clusters or establish causation. I test residual autocorrelation, multiple local statistics and boundary sensitivity before production use.
keyPoints: Spatial dependence is defined relative to a weights matrix, not inherent in a column alone.
Moran's I compares cross-products of centered neighboring values with global variance.
Randomization expectation is often −1/(n−1); permutation design must match the null.
Global I summarizes overall association and can hide local clusters, outliers and nonstationarity.
Residual spatial autocorrelation signals missing structure and invalid independent-error assumptions, not a specific remedy.
lessons.description: Spatial autocorrelation measures dependence between values linked through geography. This chapter develops spatial weights matrices from rook and queen polygon contiguity, fixed distance, inverse distance, k-nearest neighbors and network relations, including binary versus weighted edges, row standardization, symmetry, islands and boundary effects. It derives global Moran's I as a normalized quadratic form of centered observations, interprets positive and negative association, and explains why its randomization expectation is usually −1/(n−1). Moran scatterplots connect standardized values with spatial lags. Analytical and permutation inference are compared, with the permutation scheme tied to the exchangeability null. The chapter distinguishes global I from local indicators of spatial association, Getis–Ord statistics and variograms, covering local high-high, low-low and spatial-outlier patterns with multiple testing. It shows how trends, population denominators, rates, heteroskedasticity and the modifiable areal unit problem affect interpretation. The lab constructs a rook weights matrix, computes I, runs a deterministic permutation test and verifies that spatially smooth values exceed shuffled arrangements. Production guidance versions geography and W, tests sensitivity, monitors residual dependence, handles islands, protects small-area data and separates descriptive clustering from causal explanation.
learningObjectives: Construct and audit spatial weights from process-relevant neighbor definitions.
Derive Moran's I, its randomization expectation and spatial-lag interpretation.
Perform permutation inference and distinguish global from local spatial diagnostics.
Use residual and sensitivity analysis without overstating cluster or causal claims.

lessons.title: Spatial Cross-Validation & Geographic Leakage
lessons.interviewAnswer: Random cross-validation assumes examples are exchangeable enough for the intended deployment. Spatially nearby rows often share outcomes, covariates, sensors, entities or duplicated context, so random folds place near twins in train and validation and estimate interpolation rather than transfer. I begin with a deployment estimand: new points inside mapped regions, new neighborhoods, new cities, or future regions. Then I group or block by geography at a scale larger than the residual dependence range, optionally add a buffer between train and test, keep preprocessing and feature selection inside each fold, and combine temporal order when required. I report random and spatial results as different questions, map fold coverage and covariate support, quantify distance to training and residual autocorrelation, and reserve a final geographically untouched holdout. Blocking reduces leakage but can introduce extrapolation, which may be exactly the real task.
keyPoints: Validation design estimates a deployment scenario; random and spatial folds answer different questions.
Spatial dependence, repeated entities, shared rasters and neighborhood features create geographic leakage.
Block size and buffer should reflect dependence range and operational separation, not arbitrary map aesthetics.
All learned preprocessing, target encoding, imputation and feature construction must be fit inside training folds.
Report geographic coverage, support shift and distance-to-training alongside aggregate metrics and uncertainty.
lessons.description: Spatial cross-validation aligns model evaluation with geographic deployment under dependence and distribution shift. This chapter explains why random folds can underestimate error when nearby observations share latent processes, repeated entities, imagery, sensors, administrative attributes or engineered neighborhoods. It distinguishes interpolation within sampled territory, prediction into spatial gaps, transfer to new regions and space-time forecasting. Designs include leave-location or group-out, regular and environmental blocks, buffered leave-one-out, spatial clustering, leave-one-region-out and nested spatial cross-validation for tuning. Block size is linked to residual autocorrelation, sampling design and operational separation, while buffers reduce near-boundary leakage. The chapter covers fold balance, disconnected regions, covariate support, extrapolation, target-weighted aggregation and uncertainty across a small number of geographic folds. It traces pipeline leakage through global imputation, scaling, feature selection, target encoding, raster composites, graph neighborhoods and hyperparameter tuning. The lab simulates a smooth spatial field, compares random K-fold with blocked folds using a distance-based regressor and verifies optimistic random error. Production guidance adds immutable split manifests, spatial and temporal cutoffs, final region holdouts, subgroup maps, distance-to-training and out-of-support monitoring, fallback and rollback. Spatial blocking is treated as an estimand decision, not a ritual that automatically makes any metric unbiased.
learningObjectives: Define whether deployment requires interpolation, spatial gap filling, regional transfer or space-time forecasting.
Construct group, block and buffer splits at a defensible dependence scale.
Prevent preprocessing, feature, graph, raster and tuning leakage inside spatial folds.
Report spatial performance, uncertainty and support diagnostics and operate geographic fallback policies.
lessons.labGoal: Simulate a spatial field and demonstrate why random folds can look better than leave-region-out validation.

lessons.description: ML Testing & Quality Gates is a core topic in MLOps & Production ML. Many ML failures are data/interface failures rather than architecture failures. This chapter turns the interview-level summary into a complete engineering and analytical treatment. The starting mental model is: A service can be healthy while receiving impossible feature values, so API tests alone are insufficient. The formal and implementation discussion builds from Unit/integration tests, Data tests, Model gates, Critical slices, while keeping the unit of data, objective, assumptions, and failure boundaries explicit. The original technical core is preserved: Promotion gates can require schema compatibility, baseline improvement, minimum critical-slice metrics and system constraints before a model becomes deployable. Rather than treating those statements as isolated facts, the chapter connects them to data preparation, evaluation design, numerical or systems behavior, and choices that change under scale or distribution shift. You will work through two concrete scenarios, a runnable Python lab with assertions, and two original conceptual visuals. The lab is intentionally small enough to run locally while still exposing an invariant that should remain true in a larger implementation. The production section translates the concept into monitoring, versioning, rollback, and failure-handling requirements. Run cheap deterministic checks in CI and heavier validation inside train/deploy pipelines. The broader module context is experiment tracking, deployment, monitoring, registries, ci/cd and lifecycle management. The goal is not memorization: by the end, you should be able to define the contract, explain the mechanism, choose a defensible evaluation, diagnose common errors, and describe what has to be true before shipping the idea in a real Data, ML, or AI system.

lessons.title: Kernel Methods & the Kernel Trick
lessons.interviewAnswer: Kernel methods replace explicit feature vectors with pairwise inner products K(x,z)=φ(x)ᵀφ(z), allowing linear algorithms in a feature space to express nonlinear functions. A valid Mercer-style kernel produces a symmetric positive-semidefinite Gram matrix, so the associated optimization remains well behaved. The RBF kernel exp(-γ||x-z||²) encodes local smoothness; polynomial kernels encode interactions. Kernel ridge solves (K+λI)α=y and predicts k(x)ᵀα, while SVMs use sparse support-vector coefficients. Scaling and kernel parameters define geometry. Exact methods need O(n²) kernel storage and often O(n³) solves, with O(n) prediction for dense expansions, so I benchmark sample size and use Nyström or random Fourier approximations when needed. I validate kernel and regularization jointly, audit support and never treat similarity as causality.
keyPoints: A kernel specifies inner products in an implicit feature space and therefore a strong similarity prior.
Symmetric positive semidefinite Gram matrices preserve the convex geometry used by standard kernel algorithms.
Kernel parameters and preprocessing jointly control smoothness and locality.
The representer form makes predictions depend on training examples, creating quadratic storage and potentially linear-in-n inference.
Approximate features trade kernel fidelity for bounded memory and fast linear-model training and serving.
lessons.description: Kernel methods express nonlinear learning through pairwise inner products in an implicit feature space. This chapter derives the Gram matrix, positive-semidefinite validity and representer form, then develops linear, polynomial and RBF kernels and their geometry. It shows kernel ridge regression's dual solution, relates kernels to SVM support vectors and Gaussian-process covariance functions, and explains centering, scaling, regularization, composite kernels, domain-specific similarity and indefinite-kernel risk. Worked examples verify a Gram matrix and show how RBF gamma changes effective neighborhoods. The lab implements RBF kernel ridge regression with a stable linear solve, compares predictions with scikit-learn, and verifies symmetry, positive eigenvalues, interpolation behavior and permutation invariance. Production coverage includes O(n²) memory, factorization cost, expansion latency, cache and privacy concerns, Nyström and random Fourier approximations, drift, canaries and rollback. The practical decision is explicit: use the richest valid geometry whose evaluation and serving costs remain justified by measured gain. You will also learn why checking one Gram matrix cannot prove universal validity, how centering conventions alter fitted functions, and when an explicit approximate feature map is safer to version and serve.
learningObjectives: Explain kernelization as replacing feature-space inner products with a valid kernel function.
Test finite Gram matrices for symmetry and positive semidefiniteness and interpret the limitation of that test.
Derive and implement kernel ridge prediction and tune geometry with regularization.
Choose exact, Nyström or random-feature approaches from quality, memory and latency evidence.
lessons.labGoal: Implement RBF kernel ridge regression, compare with scikit-learn, and verify Gram and prediction invariants.
followUpQuestions: Why must the Gram matrix be PSD?

lessons.title: Perceptron & Online Learning
lessons.interviewAnswer: The perceptron is an online linear classifier for labels ±1. For each example, it predicts sign(wᵀx+b); if y(wᵀx+b)≤0, it updates w←w+ηyx and b←b+ηy. On linearly separable data with ||x||≤R and separator margin γ, the classic mistake bound is at most (R/γ)² under the normalized setup. On nonseparable data it may cycle and has no calibrated probability. Averaging weight vectors often improves stability, while margin-based passive-aggressive or regularized SGD methods handle noisy streams more deliberately. In production I define event order, feature and label timing, update eligibility, checkpointing and rollback; evaluate prequentially before learning each label; monitor mistake and update rates, margins, drift, delayed labels and poisoning risk; and keep a frozen fallback.
keyPoints: The perceptron updates only on mistakes or nonpositive margins, making training naturally online.
Its finite mistake bound requires linear separability, bounded feature norm and a positive margin.
Data order affects the fitted vector, especially when classes overlap.
Averaging reduces oscillation, but perceptron scores remain uncalibrated.
Online learning requires pre-update evaluation, temporal feature correctness and secure update governance.
lessons.description: The perceptron learns a linear boundary from a stream by updating only when an example is misclassified or has nonpositive margin. This chapter derives the update geometrically and proves the classical finite mistake bound under bounded norm and positive separability margin. It explains bias terms, feature scaling, data order, nonseparable cycling, pocket and averaged variants, multiclass updates, kernel perceptrons, hinge-loss SGD and passive-aggressive learning. Worked examples trace updates and construct contradictory points that force oscillation. The lab implements standard and averaged perceptrons from scratch, compares with scikit-learn and verifies separable convergence, deterministic replay and margin signs. Production coverage designs a prequential predict-then-update loop with event-time features, delayed labels, idempotency, checkpointing, update-rate and margin monitoring, drift policy, privacy, poisoning defense, canaries and rollback. The perceptron is deliberately simple so the core online-learning contract is impossible to miss: every update changes future decisions and therefore needs the same lineage and safety controls as a deployment.
learningObjectives: Implement the perceptron update and explain its effect on signed margin.
Prove the mistake bound and state every separability, norm and margin condition.
Compare final, pocket, averaged and margin-based online linear learners.
Build leakage-free prequential evaluation and checkpointed update operations.
lessons.labGoal: Implement standard and averaged perceptrons, compare with scikit-learn, and verify separable convergence and deterministic replay.

lessons.title: Factor Analysis
lessons.interviewAnswer: Factor analysis models centered observations as x=Λz+ε, where low-dimensional latent factors z explain shared covariance and feature-specific noise ε has diagonal covariance Ψ. Under the standard Gaussian model, Cov(x)=ΛΛᵀ+Ψ. Unlike PCA, FA does not seek maximum total variance or minimum reconstruction error; it separates common variance from uniqueness. Loadings are rotationally non-identifiable: ΛR gives the same covariance for orthogonal R, so varimax or oblique rotations aid interpretation but do not prove latent causes. I choose factor count using held-out likelihood, parallel analysis and stability, check residual correlations and uniqueness, fit preprocessing inside validation, and avoid causal or psychological labels without measurement-theory evidence and invariance across groups.
keyPoints: FA explains covariance through common latent factors plus diagonal feature-specific uniqueness.
PCA decomposes total variance for reconstruction; factor analysis is a probabilistic covariance model.
Loadings are not uniquely oriented, so rotations change interpretation while preserving fit under corresponding assumptions.
Factor count, communalities and residual covariance require model checks and independent evidence.
Latent factors are statistical constructs, not automatically causal entities or fair scores.
lessons.description: Factor analysis explains observed covariance through a small number of Gaussian latent factors and feature-specific noise. This chapter derives x=mu+Lambda z+epsilon, the covariance Lambda Lambda transpose plus Psi, posterior factor scores, communalities and uniqueness. It contrasts FA with PCA, probabilistic PCA and ICA; explains maximum-likelihood or EM estimation, diagonal-noise assumptions, Heywood cases, rotational non-identifiability, varimax and oblique rotation, factor-count selection, parallel analysis, residual covariance and confirmatory structure. Worked examples reconstruct a covariance matrix and show two rotated loading solutions with identical fit. The lab simulates known factors, fits scikit-learn FactorAnalysis, verifies positive uniqueness, covariance approximation and improved held-out likelihood over a diagonal Gaussian. Production guidance versions item coding and loadings, monitors score and residual drift, checks measurement invariance, protects sensitive latent scores and supports rollback. Factor names are treated as hypotheses supported by theory and replication, not facts created by an optimizer. You will also learn why posterior scores remain uncertain, how residual correlations expose local dependence, and why group comparisons are invalid until the measurement model demonstrates sufficient invariance.
learningObjectives: Derive the factor-analysis covariance and posterior score formulas.
Distinguish shared communality, uniqueness, PCA variance and probabilistic assumptions.
Explain rotational ambiguity and use rotations without overclaiming identification.
Select, check and deploy a factor model with invariance, uncertainty and privacy controls.
lessons.labGoal: Simulate a factor model, fit FactorAnalysis, and verify uniqueness, covariance fit and held-out likelihood against an independence model.
followUpQuestions: Why is Psi usually diagonal?
What is a Heywood case?
Why test measurement invariance?

lessons.title: Independent Component Analysis (ICA)
lessons.interviewAnswer: ICA assumes observed centered signals are linear mixtures x=As of statistically independent, mostly non-Gaussian sources and estimates an unmixing W so s_hat=Wx has maximally independent components. Centering and whitening remove mean and second-order correlation; ICA then uses higher-order non-Gaussianity through negentropy-like contrasts, kurtosis or fixed-point FastICA updates. Identifiability is only up to permutation and scale or sign, and at most one source may be Gaussian in the classical model. Independence is stronger than uncorrelatedness. I choose component count and nonlinearity, inspect convergence and source stability across seeds, validate separation with domain or synthetic mixtures, and reject causal source labels without evidence. In production I version whitening and unmixing together, align components across refits and monitor reconstruction, independence diagnostics and drift.
keyPoints: ICA seeks statistically independent latent sources, while PCA only decorrelates orthogonal directions.
Whitening reduces the remaining mixing to an orthogonal rotation but does not itself create independence.
Non-Gaussianity enables source identification; multiple Gaussian sources are rotationally indistinguishable.
Recovered components have arbitrary order, sign and scale and must be aligned before comparison.
Convergence, independence contrasts and domain separation all need validation because the linear noiseless model can fail.
lessons.description: Independent component analysis separates a linear mixture into statistically independent, non-Gaussian latent sources. This chapter derives the mixing and unmixing model, distinguishes independence from zero covariance, and explains why centering and PCA whitening leave an orthogonal rotation to identify. It develops non-Gaussianity, kurtosis, negentropy approximations and symmetric FastICA fixed-point updates, including normalization and decorrelation. Practical sections cover component count, noise, over- and undercomplete mixtures, multiple Gaussian sources, scale, sign and permutation ambiguity, convergence, seed stability, temporal mixtures, artifact removal and leakage. Worked examples unmix synthetic Laplace and uniform sources and show why Gaussian rotations are unidentified. The lab uses scikit-learn FastICA on a known mixture, aligns recovered components by correlation and verifies reconstruction, decorrelation and source recovery. Production guidance versions centering, whitening and unmixing, aligns refits, monitors reconstruction and independence, protects sensitive sources and supports rollback. Recovered components are treated as model-dependent signals, not automatically causal generators. You will also learn why whitening alone cannot separate non-Gaussian sources, how sign and permutation matching prevents false drift, and when reverberation, dependence or sensor noise invalidates the instantaneous linear mixture.

lessons.interviewAnswer: Time-series foundation models pretrain on large collections of sequences and adapt or zero-shot forecast new series. They can reduce per-series modeling work, but still need comparison with strong naive/statistical baselines and careful domain-shift evaluation.
